Solid arrows are the reporting line. Dotted arrows are the common hand-offs between specialists, such as Scout's prior-art summary feeding Rosa's proposal. Each sheet lists its own hand-offs and approval rules.

docs.title: Using the personas on a dashboard
docs.text:
• Ring color. Each avatar gets a ring in its signature color, so a card is recognizable even when the face is small.
  • Status badge. Use five states: Idle, Working, Waiting on you, Blocked, and Done. Give each badge its own shape or icon as well as a color, so the status does not depend on color alone.
  • Task list. Each card shows the agent's current tasks. The sample tasks in every sheet are illustrative, not real data.
  • Approval rules. Every sheet lists what the agent does alone, what it asks first, and what it never does. These follow the book's rule of "trust, but verify": agents draft and prepare, and a human sends, submits, signs, and pays.

docs.title: Shared art style
docs.text: Every image prompt uses the same style line as the Volt mascot: flat vector cartoon, clean lines, solid colors, soft rounded shapes, transparent background, no text in the image, readable at about 90 px. Paste the prompts into the same image-generator conversation so the seven avatars come out as a consistent set.

docs.title: Ada — Chief of Staff
docs.text:
Ada sits at the top of the team. Every other agent reports its results to Ada, and Ada decides what reaches you.

Field Value Role Personal assistant and coordinator of all other agents Character type Human Signature color Violet #6B3FA0 (light tint #D9C8F0) Pronouns they/them Reports to You, the researcher Manages Scout, Marisol, Penny, Rosa, Pixel, Kai Avatar file img/ada.png (not yet generated) Catchphrase "Let me connect the dots."

docs.title: Mission
docs.text: Keep your attention for the work only you can do. Ada owns the inbox, your personal calendar, and your personal knowledge graph (PKG), and routes everything else to the right specialist.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Personal knowledge graph. Link new papers, people, projects, ideas, and meeting notes into your PKG, and answer "what do I already know about X?" from it.
  • Email. Read, label, and summarize incoming mail; draft replies in your voice; flag the few messages that need you today.
  • Personal calendar. Hold time for deep work, detect conflicts, and decide which event requests from Marisol or Kai deserve your time.
  • Coordination. Break a request such as "prepare my sabbatical talk tour" into tasks, assign them to the specialists, and merge the results.
  • Daily briefing. Each morning, one page: what changed, what is waiting on you, and what is at risk.
  • Activity log. Keep a readable record of what every agent did and why, so you can audit the team.

docs.title: Dashboard card
docs.text:
The card shows the violet ring, the status badge, and the current task list. These sample tasks are illustrative.

Task Status Linking 14 new papers into the PKG Working Triaging 38 unread emails; 5 need your reply Waiting on you Thursday 2 pm conflict: thesis defense vs. speaker lunch Needs decision Morning briefing compiled Done

docs.title: Hand-offs
docs.text:
• From every agent: results, questions, and approval requests.
  • To Scout: "Is this idea novel?" requests found in your notes or email.
  • To Marisol and Kai: invitations and calls for papers that arrive by email.
  • To Penny: receipts and invoices that arrive by email.
  • To Rosa: funding announcements and program-officer messages.
  • To Pixel: requests for slides or a bio update.

docs.title: Approval rules
docs.text:
• Acts alone: reads mail and calendar, labels and summarizes, updates the PKG, adds tentative calendar holds, logs agent activity.
  • Asks first: sends any email, accepts or declines any invitation, shares PKG content outside your group, gives another agent new access.
  • Never: permanently deletes mail or contacts, forwards messages to outside parties on its own, spends money.

docs.title: Personality and voice
docs.text: Calm, organized, and brief. Ada puts the bottom line first, then the evidence, and ends with one clear question when a decision is needed. Dry humor, never flustered by a conflict. Signature phrases: "Let me connect the dots.", "Three things need you today.", "Here is what I would do — your call."

docs.title: Visual description
docs.text:
• Look: A person in their mid-forties with warm brown skin, a sleek chin-length silver-white bob, and calm, attentive dark-brown eyes.
  • Clothing: A well-tailored violet #6B3FA0 blazer over a white shirt.
  • Accessory: A small enamel lapel pin of three connected dots (a tiny graph) in light violet, and a slim wireless earpiece.
  • Expression: A composed, warm half-smile.
  • Color rule: Violet must dominate the clothing so the avatar reads as "violet" at icon size (about 90 px).

docs.title: Kai — Conferences and Speaking Proposals
docs.text:
Kai makes sure the right conference deadlines never slip past you and that your best work is in front of the right audience.

Field Value Role Conference radar, speaking proposals, submission tracking, trip planning Character type Human Signature color Yellow #F5B800 (light tint #FCE9A8) Pronouns they/them Reports to Ada Avatar file img/kai.png (not yet generated) Catchphrase "Deadline in twelve days — here is the plan."

docs.title: Mission
docs.text: Find the conferences, workshops, and invited-talk opportunities worth your time, get strong proposals in on time, and handle the travel so you can focus on the talk.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Conference radar. Track calls for papers, abstract and full-paper deadlines, and notification dates for the venues in your field, ranked by fit and reputation.
  • Venue vetting. Check sponsor, indexing, and program-committee quality and flag suspicious or predatory venues.
  • Proposals. Draft abstracts, talk or panel proposals, and tutorial pitches from your papers and results.
  • Submission tracker. Record each submission's status, reviews, rebuttal windows, and camera-ready deadlines, and chase co-authors.
  • Trip planning. Draft registration and travel plans with cost estimates.

docs.title: Hand-offs

docs.text:

docs.title: Verdict vocabulary
docs.text:
Scout never says "this is novel." Scout reports what was and was not found:

Verdict Meaning No close match found Nothing overlapping in the sources searched; the list of sources is attached. Partially covered Some claims have prior art; the report shows which ones. Already published A source states essentially the same result; the report quotes where.

docs.title: Appendix: Personal Agent Software
docs.text:
Google Trends for "Personal AI Agents" from June 1st, 2025 to June 1st, 2026 showing a x11 increase in the term in Google search.

Research notes

This appendix holds raw research gathered on October 15, 2026. Nearly every claim is vendor-stated or comes from press coverage; we found no independent benchmarks or controlled tests of any product listed here. Prices, tiers, and features changed several times within weeks of launch, so verify against each vendor's own pages before relying on a number.

For a one-page picture of the five personal-agent products, see the interactive poster Four Personal Agents, Side by Side.

docs.title: Why this matters for EE research
docs.text: A personal agent is an AI system that does not just answer a question but carries out multi-step work on your behalf — signing in to tools, running routines, and coming back when it is done or needs a decision. For a researcher, that could mean overnight literature sweeps, rerunning an analysis when new lab data lands, or filing bug tickets against a simulation toolchain. The commercial products below all arrived within roughly six months of each other in 2026 (counting Cowork's April general availability), so the category is moving fast.

docs.title: Grok Bot (SpaceXAI)
docs.text: SpaceXAI announced Grok Bot on August 11, 2026, as an early-beta, cloud-based agent service. "Bot" is the product name; it is not the ordinary Grok chatbot. It appears to be the first joint product of xAI and Cursor. Sources disagree on whether SpaceX is acquiring Cursor or merging with it (MacRumors cites a $60 billion acquisition), so treat the deal terms as unsettled.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
• Persistent cloud computer. Each user gets a cloud machine with a browser, files, and a terminal. Work continues when the user's laptop is off.
  • Signs in like a human. Bots log in to websites and apps, including services that offer no API or MCP integration.
  • Teachable routines. A user shows a bot a task once; it saves the routine and later runs it on its own.
  • Multiple bots. Several bots can share one group chat, share context, and hand work to each other. A manager bot can delegate to specialist bots. AIMultiple reports up to six bots per group chat and "Team Bots" on Teams/Enterprise plans (public beta since September 28).
  • Memory. Bots keep memory across conversations and may start work "before you need to ask," per SpaceXAI.
  • Interface. Work is assigned in a chat window on desktop or iOS. The bot returns a result or asks for approval.
  • Its own email address. A bot can have its own inbox on the mail.grokbot.com domain. The author verified this first-hand in October 2026: a test message to a bot's address was received, and the bot replied from that same address.

SpaceXAI's own example uses include updating a CRM from call transcripts, onboarding new hires and processing invoices in Gmail, and reproducing a bug, filing a ticket, and handing the fix to a debugging bot.

docs.title: Access, pricing, and platforms
docs.text: Item Detail Launch access (Aug 11) SuperGrok Heavy, Cursor Ultra, Cursor Teams Premium Expanded access (Aug 26) SuperGrok, SuperGrok Plus, SuperGrok Heavy, Cursor Pro, Pro+, Ultra, Teams Standard and Premium Launch prices About $300/mo (SuperGrok Heavy), $200/mo (Cursor Ultra), $120/seat/mo (Teams Premium) Entry prices (Oct 12) About $30/mo (SuperGrok), $20/mo (Cursor), $40/seat/mo (Cursor Teams) Usage Weekly allowance included; overage billed at token cost; allowance and rate card unpublished Platforms macOS, Windows, Linux (.deb), iOS; Android "coming soon" Models Not disclosed; AIMultiple reports Cursor picks a model per task Enterprise Waitlist at launch; "through sales" by October 12

docs.title: Security claims and open questions
docs.text:
SpaceXAI states that Grok Bot uses Cursor SSO and authentication, privacy mode, encryption in transit and at rest, a training opt-out, and an "Auto Review" step for sensitive actions. Enterprise admins can configure data-loss prevention, certificates, proxies, and network controls.

Open questions raised by analysts:

  • Shared logins. Isolation is per user, not per bot. All of a user's bots share one computer, including its files, browser, and logins, so one compromised bot exposes the rest.
  • Undocumented details. Retention defaults, credential handling, permission granularity, audit records, which actions need approval by default, and whether memory can be viewed or edited.
  • Reliability. Nothing documents failure handling or what happens to a saved routine when a website's interface changes.
  • Cost surprises. Cursor itself warns that an hourly routine or a busy Slack trigger "can use a week of usage in a day."

docs.title: Dots (OpenAI)
docs.text:
OpenAI introduced Dots at DevDay on September 29, 2026, as a personal agent inside ChatGPT, powered by GPT-6 Astra.

  • Always-on. A dot runs in the background with its own cloud computer and browser, pursuing goals with minimal oversight.
  • App ecosystem. It can use the 4,000+ apps already connected to ChatGPT and can delegate coding to Codex.
  • Visibility. The user can open a dot's "computer" at any time to see what it is doing, and can connect a dot to their own PC.
  • Communication. A dot can message or call the user with progress, questions, or decisions. Slack and Microsoft Teams integrations were announced; text-message support is described as coming later.
  • Safety model. Passwords used for sign-in are not exposed to the underlying model. Proactive background research uses read-only app access. Dots have built-in rules for when to act versus ask, and users can write custom approval rules. OpenAI says it is working with Microsoft to bring Dots under Agent 365 security controls.
  • No email address of its own. At launch a dot can use your connected personal email account but cannot have its own address. See Agent Email.
  • One dot for now. Each eligible user gets one primary dot they can name and customize. OpenAI says it expects "teams of Dots working together," but multi-dot control is not available at launch.
  • Availability. Launched for Pro and Business Premium users in "eligible markets"; reports differ on whether Business and Enterprise are included, and some exclude the EEA, Switzerland, and the UK for personal accounts.

Conflicting price reports

Engadget reports the first dot is free for Pro and Business Premium subscribers. AIMultiple lists a $100/mo starting price. We could not reconcile the two; check OpenAI's own announcement.

TechCrunch notes that much of what Dots do was already possible with Codex and similar agent harnesses — Dots package those capabilities around independent action.

docs.title: Muse (Meta)
docs.text:
Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026, in the U.S. for users 18 and older, as a separate app that also runs inside WhatsApp. It is aimed at everyday tasks: schedules, shopping, travel, and turning long-term goals into plans.

  • Architecture. Each user's agent runs in its own cloud virtual machine.
  • Permissions. A layer called Sentinel decides whether each connected-app action and outbound request is allowed, blocked, or sent for approval. Meta says the agent never sees your actual passwords or payment details, and each purchase needs approval showing exact details.
  • Visibility. Users can watch the agent's browser as it works and review an activity log.
  • Memory. Stored as editable text files.
  • Email address. Meta announced on September 23 that each agent will get its own address "soon"; it has not shipped. Muse can already be messaged in WhatsApp. See Agent Email.
  • Pricing. Free tier, plus $20/mo (Power) and $100/mo (Maximum) tiers with weekly token allowances.
  • Privacy. Training on user data is on by default, with an opt-out.
  • Integrations. Centered on Meta's platforms plus email, calendar, payments, and a handful of consumer categories — narrower than the developer-oriented tools.

docs.title: Claude Cowork (Anthropic)
docs.text:
Cowork launched in January 2026 and became generally available on April 9, 2026. It lives in a tab inside Claude Desktop, where Claude reads your files, runs multi-step tasks, and uses plugins and MCP connectors.

  • Platforms. macOS first, with Windows following in February 2026. Anthropic's download page also lists Linux and ChromeOS builds.
  • Scheduled tasks. Added February 25, 2026. A March 2026 source says they require the computer to be awake and Claude Desktop open, which makes Cowork the least "always-on" of the commercial products. That may have changed since.
  • Dispatch. Lets you assign a task from your phone.
  • No email address of its own. Cowork uses your Gmail or Microsoft 365 through connectors. See Agent Email.
  • Pricing. No separate SKU: it is included in Claude Pro ($20/mo), Max ($100 or $200/mo), Team, and Enterprise plans. Agentic tasks reportedly burn usage allowances five to twenty times faster than ordinary chat, and the usage pool is shared with Claude chat and Claude Code.
  • Enterprise. Role-based access control, per-group spend limits, and usage analytics. One source notes Cowork activity is not yet captured in audit logs or the Compliance API.

docs.title: Gemini Spark (Google)
docs.text:
Google announced Gemini Spark at Google I/O on May 19, 2026, as a personal agent for consumers. It is the product Google describes as running "24/7"; a separate work-oriented product, the Gemini Agent, is covered below.

  • Always-on. Spark runs on dedicated virtual machines on Google Cloud, so long tasks keep going when the user's own device is off.
  • Integrations. It has its own Gmail address that users can email like a colleague, and it reaches Gmail, Docs, Calendar, and other Workspace apps without manual setup. It browses through Chrome and supports MCP for outside services. Press lists Canva, OpenTable, and Instacart among launch partners.
  • Model and harness. The Next Web reports it is built on Gemini 3.5 and powered by the Antigravity agent harness.
  • Safety model. Press coverage says Spark asks before high-stakes actions such as spending money or sending email, that Google connectors are off until enabled, and that permissions are set per app. Autonomous purchases through the Agents Payment Protocol, within user-set limits, are described as coming later in 2026. On Android, a "Halo" overlay for live status is expected with Android 17. We found no first-party documentation of these controls.
  • Availability. A U.S. beta for Google AI Ultra subscribers aged 18 and older, plus some business users, with expansion planned over the following weeks. Reports differ on whether it was "next week" or already rolling out, so the exact launch date is unsettled; the poster uses the May 19 announcement date.

Conflicting price reports

Spark has no separate price; it comes with the Google AI Ultra tier. The Next Web reports Google cut that tier from $250 to $100 a month at I/O, while some outlets still cite $250. The poster shows $100.

docs.title: Gemini Agent (Google, for work)
docs.text: At Google's Gemini at Work 2026 event, Google introduced a separate Gemini Agent for knowledge work. It accepts high-level objectives, plans multi-step workflows, writes and runs code, and creates media. Reporting says it can route work between Google's Gemini models and Anthropic's Claude models, works across Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Salesforce, and developer command lines, and lets each agent have its own identity, corporate email address, activity log, and IT-enforced spending limits. We have not read Google's announcement directly, and the poster leaves this product out because it targets organizations rather than individuals.

docs.title: Open-source alternatives: OpenClaw and Hermes Agent
docs.text:
• OpenClaw is an MIT-licensed, self-hosted agent that lives in chat apps such as WhatsApp, Telegram, and Discord. You choose the model (Claude, GPT, Gemini, or a local model through Ollama). Model usage is the main cost — one estimate is $5–50/month. Reviews report reliability problems: runaway loops, malicious skills, and unattended deletions.

  • Hermes Agent (Nous Research, public since February 25, 2026) is also MIT-licensed. It runs on a laptop, server, or cloud sandbox, supports many model providers, and has a learning loop that writes its own skills. The trade-off is that you manage your own servers, secrets, and security.

Press describes Grok Bot as "a user friendly OpenClaw": the same idea, hosted and managed, in exchange for openness and control.

docs.title: Side-by-side comparison
docs.text: Grok Bot Dots Muse Claude Cowork Gemini Spark OpenClaw / Hermes Vendor SpaceXAI / Cursor OpenAI Meta Anthropic Google Community / Nous Research Announced Aug 11, 2026 Sep 29, 2026 Sep 8, 2026 GA Apr 9, 2026 May 19, 2026 (beta) Hermes public Feb 2026 Runs where Cloud computer shared by your bots Own cloud computer and browser Dedicated cloud VM per user Mostly local sandbox plus connectors Dedicated Google Cloud VM Your laptop, server, or cloud Model Undisclosed GPT-6 Astra Muse Spark Claude Gemini 3.5 (per The Next Web) Any Multi-agent Yes: many bots, group chats One dot now; teams planned One agent Single session Not reported Build your own Always-on Yes Yes Yes Needs computer awake (Mar 2026 source) Yes Yes, if you host it Integrations Browser/computer use, Slack, connected apps 4,000+ ChatGPT apps, Codex, Slack/Teams Email, calendar, payments, WhatsApp MCP connectors, plugins Gmail, Docs, Calendar, Chrome, MCP Chat apps, skills, your own tools Safety model Auto Review model; shared logins Read-only background access; approval rules Sentinel layer; per-purchase approval; activity log Local sandbox; enterprise RBAC Asks before high-stakes actions; connectors opt-in You manage it Price From $20/mo plus usage Conflicting reports Free, $20, $100/mo Included in $20–$200/mo plans Included in Google AI Ultra, about $100/mo Free software plus API costs Own email address Yes (author-tested) No, not at launch Announced, not shipped No Yes (press-reported) Unknown Open source No No No No No Yes (MIT)

docs.title: Contrast: what actually differs
docs.text:
• Grok Bot's differentiator is the manager/specialist bot model. OpenAI says multi-dot control is planned but not shipped; Muse is one agent per user.
  • Grok Bot is the least transparent. Models are undisclosed, usage allowances are unpublished, and the shared-login design widens the blast radius of any one failure. Dots and Muse document their approval rules more explicitly.
  • Dots lean on the ChatGPT ecosystem — its apps, Codex, and voice calls.
  • Muse targets consumers, with the strongest purchase-approval story but the narrowest work-tool integrations.
  • Cowork is session-oriented and the most mature knowledge-work tool, but the least autonomous.
  • Spark is the Workspace-native option. It lives inside Google's mail and document tools and can be emailed directly, but it is bundled with a single premium consumer tier and its safety controls are documented mostly by press.
  • OpenClaw and Hermes trade convenience for control: you pick the model and own the security.

docs.title: Caveats and gaps
docs.text:
• No independent testing. AIMultiple's comparison reports no benchmarks or controlled tests of Dots, Grok Bot, or Muse; the only first-hand evidence is the author's anecdotal use of Grok Bot, including the email test above.
  • Email status moves fast. Dots and Cowork have no address of their own, and Muse's is announced but not shipped; the poster shows all three. The evidence is secondary and some of it is vendor-written, so see Agent Email. Spark's address is press-reported, not author-tested.
  • Moving prices. Tiers and prices changed within weeks of each launch.
  • Beta status. SpaceXAI's October 12 pages checked by Kingy.ai do not say whether Grok Bot is still in beta.
  • Source bias. Many comparison blogs host or sell one of the products they rank.
  • Unread source. The Neowin article returned HTTP 403 and was not read directly.
  • Cowork currency. The newest Cowork source we found is from August 2026.

docs.title: Questions to resolve before this becomes a chapter
docs.text:
1. Which of these agents suits an EE research workflow (long simulations, licensed EDA tools, lab data) — and which cannot reach those tools at all?
  2. What is each agent's behavior on sensitive or unpublished research data (training defaults, retention, memory)?
  3. How should a research group audit what an always-on agent did overnight?
  4. Which claims can the author verify first-hand with a hands-on trial?

docs.title: Appendix: Personal Knowledge Graphs
docs.text:
Summary of prior research

This appendix summarizes the author's earlier work on personal knowledge graphs. It is based on the book-chapter version of that work (Integrating personal knowledge graphs into the enterprise, Chapter 14), which docs/pkg.md in the author's profile site states is the same content as the original blogs, reformatted for the book. The blog pages themselves could not be fetched while preparing this summary (HTTP 403), so the blogs were not compared line by line against the chapter.

docs.title: Primary reference
docs.text: Ketter, W., Batchu, A., Berosik, G., and McCreary, D. (2008). A semantic web architecture for advocate agents to determine preferences and facilitate decision making. Proceedings of the 10th International Conference on Electronic Commerce (ICEC '08), ACM, pp. 1-10. The full citation is the first entry in the book's References.

docs.title: The thesis
docs.text: High-quality personal AI agents need access to a person's notes, and the best place to keep notes is a personal knowledge graph (PKG): concepts stored as nodes, with the relationships between them stored as links. The hard part is not the single-user case. It is integrating many individual PKGs into an organization's collective knowledge, which the author calls an integrated personal knowledge graph (IPKG), without losing the speed of personal note taking or exposing knowledge to the wrong people. The research focuses on how to do that securely.

docs.title: What we mean by knowledge
docs.text:
Before a graph can hold knowledge, we need a working definition of it. The Knowledge Triangle shows three layers of increasing value. Raw data is the largest volume but has the lowest meaning. Information is isolated facts extracted from that data. Knowledge is facts connected by meaningful relationships, which is exactly what a graph stores. Hover over each layer for a description.

Run the Knowledge Triangle MicroSim fullscreen

The sim is hosted in the author's Introduction to Graph Databases book, where it has its own lesson page.

docs.title: Publications
docs.text:
Work Venue and date Focus Personal Knowledge Graphs Towards Data Science, April 6, 2022 What PKGs are and why they matter; one of the most popular of the series Integrating PKGs into the Enterprise Medium, December 5, 2022 Integration challenges and steps Integrating Siloed Personal Knowledge Graphs Medium, December 10, 2022 Bringing isolated PKGs together Controlling Access to IPKGs Medium, December 11, 2022 Role-based access control for shared graphs Personal Knowledge Graphs: Methodology, Tools and Applications, Chapter 14, abstract and PDF IET book, Amazon listing The blogs consolidated and reformatted; see References

The April 6, 2022 article as published on Medium, with 1.1K claps. The diagram shows the evolution of personal knowledge graphs from Zettelkasten and note-taking, through hypertext, HTML and Markdown, mind maps, concept graphs and cloud note-taking apps. Image by the author.

docs.title: Where PKGs came from
docs.text:
The chapter traces PKGs through a lineage of ideas for linking notes:

  1. Zettelkasten, the 1500s linked index-card system built on one concept per card and explicit links between concepts.
  2. Hypermedia and hypertext in the 1960s, then HTML and the World Wide Web.
  3. The Semantic Web in 2001, which added relationship types to links.
  4. Electronic note-taking tools such as outliners, mind maps, and Evernote.
  5. Markdown in 2004, a lightweight format that any text editor can produce.
  6. Tools such as Roam Research and Obsidian, which combine hyperlinks, Markdown, and graphs.

The author's point is that Markdown matters: it is why notes can survive changes of tool, which is the same reason this book uses Markdown for project knowledge.

docs.title: Why people use PKGs
docs.text:
The chapter lists five advantages that practitioners report:

  • Quickly organize thoughts. Typing [[ turns a phrase into a node, and autocomplete shows whether the concept already exists.
  • Lower cognitive load. Notes are linked to existing knowledge as they are taken, so the PKG acts as a "second brain" that offloads memory.
  • Non-linear thinking. Concepts connect in any order instead of in the fixed order of sections in a document.
  • Long-term persistence. Plain Markdown outlasts the tools used to edit it.
  • Breaking writer's block. Small subgraphs grow over time, like a "digital garden of ideas."

docs.title: Limits of the tools
docs.text: The chapter also names real problems at the time of writing: sharing a subgraph with others is crude import and export, graph visualization is limited, relationships are untyped, and tools have no fine-grained role-based access control. It raises an ownership question too. A "personal" graph of work knowledge overlaps with an employer's intellectual property.

docs.title: The free-form versus structured tension
docs.text:
The central design tension is between fast, free-form personal note taking and the consistent structure an organization needs to reuse knowledge.

Free form Structured No rules, quick and easy Many rules, slow but consistent Low semantics High semantics Hard to validate and query Easy to validate and query Example: Notepad Example: Wikipedia Infobox

The chapter places tools on a spectrum from Notepad and wikis, through PKGs, to ontology editors such as Protege and graph databases such as Neo4j and TigerGraph, with a not-yet-built "ML-PKG" that uses machine learning to suggest links as you type.

Two ideas follow from this tension:

  • Typed versus untyped links. A wiki links pages of a single type with a single relationship ("is related to"). A true knowledge graph gives each node and edge a type, which is what makes it queryable. The author cites Jim Hendler's hypothesis that "a little semantics goes a long way."
  • Name uniqueness and aliases. PKGs should refuse duplicate concept names, offer to merge on rename, and support aliases, which many tools do poorly.

docs.title: Making integration feel fast
docs.text:
The practical recipe is to extend the as-you-type loop with organizational knowledge instead of adding forms:

  • Trigger characters such as [[, @ (people), and # (tags), plus prefixes such as g: for a company glossary, pull suggestions from enterprise lists.
  • Monitor the acceptance rate of suggestions and aim for 30% or higher before wide rollout, or users will turn the feature off.
  • Link to permalinks (PURLs) rather than file paths, and monitor for broken links, because broken links erode trust.
  • Use bidirectional links so renaming a concept updates every reference. The author's rule of thumb is that about 60% of a knowledge graph's value is in its nodes and 40% in its relationships.
  • Run NLP in real time (entity extraction, classification), within roughly 100 ms, so suggestions do not interrupt typing.
  • Expect to write converters, because each tool extends Markdown differently.

docs.title: Steps to integrate PKGs into the enterprise
docs.text:
The chapter proposes the IPKG hypothesis: users of integrated PKGs will create more valuable knowledge than users of siloed note-taking tools. It then gives a roll-out plan:

  1. Align benefits with the organization's strategy (sharing knowledge, avoiding duplication, consistency, collaboration, productivity, search).
  2. Find an executive sponsor.
  3. Define metrics that a non-specialist can understand, starting with simple features such as shared spell-check dictionaries and automatic hyperlinking of glossary terms.
  4. Inventory existing knowledge repositories (glossaries, product catalogs, employee names, wiki pages, system lists).
  5. Draw a reference architecture diagram with sources on the left, the IPKG in the middle, and consumers on the right.

docs.title: Controlling access
docs.text:
Access control is easy for one person and hard for an organization. The chapter defines the vocabulary (vertex, subgraph, the public graph, roles, access types such as read, rename, move, update and delete, authentication, authorization) and recommends a role-based model:

  • Grant permissions to roles and named groups, not to individuals, so access does not need to change every time someone moves teams.
  • Let people create shared subgraphs with their own permissions.
  • Treat the ontology management problem carefully: low-level changes such as fixing a typo are cheap, but changes to upper ontologies ripple into downstream consumers and need version control and regression tests.
  • Expect merge conflicts. Copying a page from a private graph into a shared one breaks the links that depended on private concepts, so it is often better to create the concept in the shared context in the first place.

docs.title: How this connects to the book
docs.text:
The research supplies the concepts behind the personal knowledge graph material in Chapter 6 and Chapter 19:

Learning graph concept Where the research speaks to it Knowledge Graph, Entity and Relationship Nodes (vertices) and typed edges; graphs versus flat lists of concepts Personal Knowledge Graph The core subject of the blogs and chapter Graph Schema Typed vertices and edges; "a little semantics goes a long way" Backlinks Bidirectional links that update when a concept is renamed Entity Extraction Real-time NLP for entities and facts while typing Personal Knowledge Privacy Ownership of a "personal" graph; role-based access control Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graph Memory Not covered directly; the chapter anticipates ML-assisted PKGs, and the opening thesis ties PKGs to personal agents

docs.title: Gaps to fill
docs.text:
• Written before LLM agents. The chapter expects BERT and GPT-3 to make ML-assisted PKGs practical. Retrieval over graphs and agent memory are the natural updates, and this book's Personal Agent Software appendix covers the agent side.
  • Blogs not re-read. The four blog posts were not fetched, so details that exist only in the blogs are missing from this summary.
  • Reach and influence. Two points are documented: the work was republished as Chapter 14 of an IET book (the DOI and Amazon links are in the Publications table), and the Towards Data Science article shows 1.1K claps in a screenshot of the Medium page. One point is the author's own claim and is not independently checked: that many other projects use the blogs as a basis for personal knowledge agents. Naming a few of those projects would turn it into a citation.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 20 chapters covering 379 concepts.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator - Introduces the research workflow, the five everyday research tasks, core generative AI vocabulary, and the central idea of the researcher as an orchestrator of agent teams.
  2. How Language Models Work - Explains tokens, context windows, prompts, training data, and hallucination so researchers understand why models produce fluent but sometimes false output.
  3. Choosing Models and Writing Clear Prompts - Covers choosing among models by size, cost, and access, adding retrieval, and writing clear, constrained prompts with examples and output formats.
  4. Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting - Develops context engineering, grounding, prompt testing, and multi-step prompting, along with defenses against prompt injection and long-document problems.
  5. Markdown Project Files and Version Control - Teaches Markdown, project instruction files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, and the Git practices that keep project knowledge organized and reliable.
  6. Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill - Builds project knowledge through notes, logs, and knowledge bases, turns a researcher's notes into a personal knowledge graph that agents can query, then introduces the parts of an agent skill.
  7. Designing, Testing, and Sharing Agent Skills - Shows how to scope, test, version, share, and maintain agent skills, ending with a template for turning a repeatable research task into a skill.
  8. Agents, Tool Use, and Subagents - Describes the agent loop, tool calls, file and shell access, sandboxing, permissions, the Model Context Protocol, and subagents that work in parallel.
  9. Supervising Agents and Defining Agent Roles - Covers autonomy, supervision, logging, failure modes, and cost control for agents, then defines the planning, execution, and reviewer roles agent teams need.
  10. Orchestrating Teams of Planning and Execution Agents - Shows how to coordinate teams of planning and execution agents through task queues, handoffs, approval gates, delegation, and scaling decisions.
  11. AI-Assisted Literature Search and Synthesis - Applies agents to search strategy, paper triage, summarization, citation verification, and evidence synthesis for rigorous literature reviews.
  12. AI-Assisted Data Analysis and Scripting - Uses AI to clean, explore, visualize, and analyze measurement data with Python scripts and notebooks while keeping errors visible.
  13. Simulation, Testing, and Reproducible Code - Covers unit tests, debugging, silent errors, simulation and HDL code, parameter sweeps, and reproducible environments for AI-written research code.
  14. Brainstorming and Problem Framing - Applies AI to framing problems, generating and ranking ideas, developing hypotheses, designing experiments, and checking novelty.
  15. AI-Assisted Manuscript Preparation - Walks through paper structure, drafting, revision, author voice, LaTeX, figures, references, peer review responses, and arXiv submission with AI assistance.
  16. MicroSims and Research Communication - Uses slide decks, interactive simulations, MicroSims, learning graphs, and intelligent textbooks to communicate and teach research results.
  17. Verification and Reproducibility - Presents verification and validation methods, including independent and cross-model checks, replication, audit trails, and tracing errors to their source.
  18. Responsible and Ethical Use of AI - Addresses citation and disclosure of AI use, privacy, intellectual property, bias, institutional and journal policy, accountability, and over-reliance.
  19. Always-On Personal Agents for Research - Surveys always-on personal agents such as Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, Claude Cowork, OpenClaw, and Hermes Agent, then shows how to compare, secure, and select them and how a personal knowledge graph serves as their memory.
  20. Case Studies and Capstone Project - Applies the whole toolkit through case studies, including the MicroSims paper and intelligent textbook project, and closes with the capstone project and adoption plan.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
Work through the chapters in order. Each chapter lists the earlier chapters it builds on, and every concept appears in exactly one chapter, after the concepts it depends on. Early chapters build the foundations of models, prompts, project files, and skills; middle chapters apply agents to the five research tasks; late chapters cover verification, ethics, always-on personal agents, and the capstone.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of concepts covered. Make sure to complete prerequisites before moving to advanced chapters.

docs.title: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
Summary
docs.text: This chapter maps the pipeline of repeatable tasks that make up graduate research in electrical engineering and computer design: literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, coding, and manuscript preparation. It introduces the core vocabulary of generative AI and agents and the book's central idea, the researcher as orchestrator. After this chapter you can describe where AI helps in your own workflow and where your direct judgment is still required.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter assumes only the prerequisites listed in the course description.

Welcome, and Meet Your Guide

Hello, I'm Volt, a border collie, and I will be your guide through this book. Border collies are patient and precise, and I always want to know how a result could be checked. Trust, but verify! Here is exactly what I do in every chapter:

  1. Welcome: I open a chapter and tell you why it is worth your time.
  2. Think: I mark an idea worth pausing on, one that should change how you think.
  3. Tip: I hand you a shortcut you can use right away.
  4. Warn: I flag a trap that catches many researchers, along with the way out.
  5. Encourage: I tell you when a topic is genuinely hard and how to approach it.
  6. Celebrate: I close a chapter by naming what you can now do.

If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter.

docs.title: Research as a Workflow
docs.text:
A research career is often described in terms of insight, but the day-to-day reality of a graduate student, postdoc, or faculty member is dominated by procedure. A question is chosen, literature is read, an experiment or simulation is designed, data are collected and cleaned, results are analyzed, and a manuscript is written, revised, and submitted. Each of these activities has inputs, outputs, and recognizable quality criteria. The research workflow is this sequence of repeatable activities by which a research question is turned into a validated, communicated result. Naming it matters because anything that can be described as a procedure with checkable outputs can, at least in part, be delegated, and it is precisely this procedural layer that generative AI and agents now handle with useful competence.

Two properties of a workflow make it the right unit of analysis for this book. First, a workflow has stages, and each stage consumes the output of the stage before it. Second, a workflow has handoffs, the points at which one activity ends and another begins, and handoffs are where quality is either confirmed or silently lost. When you work alone and by hand, you carry the handoffs in your head. When part of the workflow is performed by an AI system, the handoffs become explicit artifacts: a file, a prompt, a log, a table of results. Making them explicit is the first practical skill this course teaches.

Real workflows are not straight lines. Analysis that produces a surprising number sends you back to re-examine the measurement, a reviewer's comment sends you back to the analysis, and a new paper in the literature sends you back to the question. These loops are where much of the time in research is actually spent, and they matter for AI use in a specific way: every loop is another chance for a model to introduce an error, and another place where a stale artifact can be mistaken for a current one. A workable discipline is to give every handoff artifact a name, a date, and a note of which earlier artifact it was derived from, so that when a loop is traversed the downstream artifacts known to be stale can be identified at once. In the running example, the quantity being measured is the effective number of bits (ENOB), the resolution in bits that an analog-to-digital converter actually achieves once its noise and distortion are counted, and it is at most the converter's nominal bit count. A change to the record length in the measurement procedure invalidates every ENOB value computed under the old procedure, and the naming convention is what lets you list them.

To keep the discussion concrete, this chapter uses one running example, which is illustrative and not drawn from any published study. A doctoral student is designing a low-power successive-approximation-register (SAR) analog-to-digital converter (ADC) for battery-powered sensor nodes, and must show whether the design meets a resolution target. Table 1 follows that project through the workflow.

Stage Input Output Typical handoff artifact Find what is known A topic and a gap in understanding Annotated list of relevant papers Reading list with citations Frame the question Reading list and a design goal One falsifiable research question Question statement Build and measure Question and a design Simulated and measured output records Netlists, scripts, raw data files Analyze Raw data files Quantified results with uncertainty Result tables and plots Communicate Result tables and plots A paper, thesis chapter, or talk Manuscript source and figures

Table 1. The running example's workflow, with the artifact passed between stages.

docs.title: Diagram: Research Workflow Handoffs
docs.text:
Research Workflow Handoffs

Type: microsim sim-id: research-workflow-handoffs Library: Mermaid Status: Built Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: describe Learning Objective: The learner will describe the input, output, and handoff artifact of each of the five stages of the running example's research workflow.
