Git Has a Steep First Week

If Git's vocabulary feels like a lot, that is normal, and most researchers get confused about branches at first. You already keep dated copies of files named "final" and "final2". Begin with only status, diff, add, and commit, and add branches when you first want to try something you might throw away.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
An agent is only as reliable as the project it works in. Plain-text files, a short and checkable instruction file, a predictable layout, and a version history give both you and the agent the memory, the boundaries, and the means of recovery that safe delegation needs.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Plain text is readable by agents, comparable line by line, searchable, and durable. Keep your source in it.
  • Markdown adds just enough structure with headings, lists, tables, and code blocks, and its syntax is a handful of precise rules.
  • YAML frontmatter carries machine-readable metadata, and every value containing a colon must be quoted.
  • A project instruction file (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) states goals, conventions, and constraints, in lines you could check, and contains no secrets.
  • File organization and naming conventions make a project predictable, and separating raw data from generated results gives agents a clear boundary.
  • Documentation as code keeps the explanation in the same history as the work.
  • Git commits and branches record small, named, recoverable changes, and a GitHub repository backs them up and supports review.
  • Diff review is the check on what an agent actually did, and prompt versioning ties each result to the prompt that made it.

A Project an Agent Can Work In

You can now write Markdown with correct headings, lists, tables, and code, set up a project with an AGENTS.md of goals, conventions, and constraints, and review a diff before accepting an agent's work. That is a workspace in which delegation is reversible.

The next chapter builds the reusable pieces that sit on top of this foundation: knowledge bases, personal knowledge graphs, and the anatomy of an agent skill. Round up your files, commit them, and bring the project you would like an agent to work in.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Markdown Project Files and Version Control
docs.text: Test your understanding of plain text, Markdown syntax, project instruction files, file organization, and Git version control.

docs.title: 1. What is plain text?
docs.text:
1. Any file that can be opened in a web browser
  2. A document saved as a PDF
  3. A file containing only characters, with no embedded formatting or binary structure
  4. A Microsoft Word file exported to .txt
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Plain text contains only characters, so any editor or program can read it and two versions can be compared line by line. PDFs and Word files are binary containers that need conversion, and browser readability is not the defining property.

Concept Tested: Plain Text

See: Plain Text

docs.title: 2. Why is Markdown a good shared format for humans and agents?
docs.text:
1. It is plain text that adds just enough structure for a human to scan and a model to parse.
  2. It is a binary format that preserves exact fonts and colors.
  3. It can only be read by specialized Markdown editors.
  4. It automatically runs code embedded in documents.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Markdown is plain text with lightweight syntax for headings, lists, tables, code, links, and emphasis. It stays human-readable in source form and is easy for agents to process. It is not binary, not editor-locked, and does not execute code.

Concept Tested: Markdown

See: Markdown

docs.title: 3. What is YAML frontmatter?
docs.text:
1. The main body text of a Markdown file
  2. A block of key-value metadata at the top of a Markdown file, enclosed in triple hyphens
  3. A separate file that holds all project metadata
  4. A Git command for tracking file changes
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. YAML frontmatter sits at the very top of a Markdown file between two --- lines and carries machine-readable properties such as title, status, owner, and date. Static-site generators and agents often read it, and values containing colons should be quoted.

Concept Tested: YAML Frontmatter

See: YAML Frontmatter

docs.title: 4. Which three kinds of content belong in a project instruction file such as AGENTS.md?
docs.text:
1. Project goals, project conventions, and project constraints
  2. Secrets, API keys, and passwords
  3. Yesterday's debugging notes and transient observations
  4. Vague encouragements such as "be careful" and "do excellent work"
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A useful instruction file states what the project is for, how work is done, and what must not happen. It should not contain secrets, stale notes, or uncheckable exhortations, because all of those either leak, become stale, or waste context on every turn.

Concept Tested: Project Instruction File

See: Project Instruction Files

docs.title: 5. Which of the following lines is best classified as a project constraint?
docs.text:
1. "The goal is to reach ENOB >= 9.5 bits."
  2. "Name scripts in lowercase with hyphens."
  3. "Report ENOB with one decimal place."
  4. "Never modify files under data/raw/."
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A constraint is a boundary that limits what an agent may do; it can be checked with a diff. The goal is a purpose statement, and the other two lines are conventions about how work is done.

Concept Tested: Project Constraints

See: Project Instruction Files

docs.title: 6. Which file name best follows the naming conventions in the chapter?
docs.text:
1. Final results (new) v2.xlsx
  2. results/enob-sweep-2026-10-15.csv
  3. Notes 10-15.md
  4. Script.PY
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter recommends lowercase, hyphen-separated words, descriptive names, and ISO-order dates so files sort chronologically. The other options use spaces, mixed case, ambiguous "final" labels, or non-sortable date formats.

Concept Tested: Naming Conventions

See: Organizing a Project for Agents and People

docs.title: 7. What is a Git commit?
docs.text:
1. A request to download the latest version from a remote server
  2. A copy of the repository on GitHub
  3. A saved snapshot of the project's tracked files, with a message describing the change
  4. A list of all branches in the project
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A commit records a snapshot of tracked files along with a message, making that state named and recoverable. A GitHub repository is a hosted copy, a pull or fetch downloads changes, and branches are separate lines of commits.

Concept Tested: Git Commit

See: Version Control

docs.title: 8. What is the recommended practice before asking an agent to change files in a project?
docs.text:
1. Delete all previous commits to start fresh
  2. Hide the .git directory so the agent cannot see the history
  3. Make sure the working tree has uncommitted changes
  4. Commit the current state so the agent's changes appear clearly in the diff
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Committing before delegation makes the agent's edits the only uncommitted changes, so git diff shows exactly what the agent did and a single command can discard them if needed. Deleting history or hiding Git defeats version control, and uncommitted prior changes blur the picture.

Concept Tested: Version Control

See: Version Control

docs.title: 9. The diff of an agent's edit changes a measured ENOB from 9.2 to 9.6 bits and removes the qualifier "only at the typical corner." What should you conclude?
docs.text:
1. The agent likely made a meaningful change to a reported result and its interpretation; review it carefully before accepting.
  2. The edit is purely typographic and can be accepted as-is.
  3. The diff is unreliable and should be ignored in favor of the agent's summary.
  4. The change is correct because larger ENOB values are always better.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The diff shows both a numeric change and the deletion of a qualification that turns a failing target into a passing one. Diffs reveal what summaries hide. You should not accept such changes without checking against the source data and the original wording.

Concept Tested: Diff Review

See: Version Control

docs.title: 10. Where should a note like "Yesterday's run crashed at corner ss_0p9v; likely a license server problem" live instead of AGENTS.md?
docs.text:
1. In the project goals section of AGENTS.md
  2. In a session log or notes file, because it is transient
  3. In the YAML frontmatter of the README
  4. As a project constraint
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Transient debugging notes become stale quickly and do not belong in a standing instruction file. A session log or dated notes file is the right place. Goals and constraints are durable, and frontmatter is for metadata, not narrative debugging notes.

Concept Tested: Project Instruction File

See: Project Instruction Files

docs.title: References: Markdown Project Files and Version Control
docs.text:
1. Markdown - Wikipedia - Covers the history, syntax, and variants such as CommonMark and GitHub Flavored Markdown. Relevant to the chapter's headings, lists, tables, and code blocks, and shows side-by-side source and rendered syntax examples.

  2. Git - Wikipedia - Describes Git's history, distributed design, core commands, and hosting services. Relevant to the commit, branch, and GitHub repository concepts, with a clear account of how snapshots and branches are stored.

  3. Version control - Wikipedia - Explains why systems record every change to a set of files, with terminology for commits, branches, merging, and history. Relevant to the chapter's argument that any earlier project state must be recoverable and comparable.

  4. Pro Git (2nd Edition) - Scott Chacon and Ben Straub - Apress - Teaches Git by explaining that it stores a stream of snapshots rather than file-by-file deltas, then builds commits and branches on that model with diagrams. This clarifies why commits are cheap and branches are lightweight.

  5. The Pragmatic Programmer: Your Journey to Mastery (20th Anniversary Edition) - David Thomas and Andrew Hunt - Addison-Wesley - Its "The Power of Plain Text" section argues for keeping knowledge in plain text and under version control. This supports the chapter's rule that the source is plain text and binaries are build products.

  6. What is Git? (Pro Git, Section 1.3) - Git SCM - Official free online text contrasting snapshots with delta-based version control, and describing the modified, staged, and committed states. Relevant to the working loop of status, add, and commit, with explanatory diagrams.

  7. CommonMark Specification - CommonMark - The standardized Markdown specification by John MacFarlane, with versioned releases. Relevant as the authoritative definition of heading, list, and code-block rules, and it includes executable examples showing source and output.

  8. AGENTS.md - AGENTS.md project - Introduces AGENTS.md as an open, tool-neutral "README for agents," with a sample file covering setup commands, code style, and testing steps. Directly relevant to writing project goals, conventions, and constraints.

  9. How Claude remembers your project - Anthropic Claude Code Docs - Official guidance on writing CLAUDE.md files, using an existing AGENTS.md, and keeping instructions specific and concise. Relevant to project instruction files, with examples of what to include and how files are loaded.

  10. About GitHub and Git - GitHub Docs - Official introduction to how GitHub builds on Git, covering hosted repositories, collaboration, and review. Relevant to the GitHub repository concept and the push-and-review workflow, with pointers to starter guides.

docs.title: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill
Summary
docs.text: This chapter extends project files into a working knowledge base: research notes, decision logs, session logs, specifications, glossaries, and cross references. It then shows how to turn that material into a personal knowledge graph, with entities, relationships, a schema, backlinks, agent-assisted entity extraction, and graph queries that ground a model's answers. It closes with the anatomy of an agent skill, including its name, description, instructions, and supporting files. After this chapter you can organize project memory as a queryable graph and read or draft a basic skill.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 2: How Language Models Work
  • Chapter 3: Choosing Models and Writing Clear Prompts
  • Chapter 4: Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting
  • Chapter 5: Markdown Project Files and Version Control

Memory That Outlasts the Session

A model forgets everything between sessions, so the only memory your research has is the memory you write down. This chapter turns your files into a knowledge base an agent can query, and shows you the small file format that packages a repeatable task into a skill. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: From Project Files to a Knowledge Base
docs.text:
Chapter 5 gave a project its instruction file. That file says how to work. It does not say what is known: which experiments ran, what was decided and why, what each term means, what the specification requires. Without that material every session starts from zero, and the researcher becomes the only memory the project has. A knowledge base is the organized collection of such written material for a project or group, kept in plain text so that people and agents read the same files. Project memory is the subset of it that an agent loads to continue work: the durable record of what the project is, what has been decided, and what is in progress.

A knowledge base is built from a small number of file types. Each has a distinct job, and the discipline is to keep each one doing only that job.

Research notes are the running, dated record of what you read, tried, and thought. They are informal and cheap to write, and they are the raw material for everything else. A good note records the source or experiment, what was observed, and what it suggests, in a few lines. Notes are written once and rarely rewritten; they are a log of thinking, not a polished document.

A specification file states what a piece of work must do: its inputs, outputs, constraints, and acceptance criteria, as in the ENOB specification of Chapter 4. Unlike notes, a specification is the current agreed statement and is edited in place, with its history in version control. It is the file an agent reads before it writes code or text, and the file against which the result is checked.

A glossary file defines the project's terms, one entry per term, so that every collaborator and every agent uses the words the same way. This is the file that implements the domain vocabulary of Chapter 4 once for the whole project. An entry should be short and precise: the term, a one-sentence definition, units where relevant, and the related terms.

A decision log records choices made and the reasons, one entry per decision, with the date and the alternatives rejected. Its value is that reasoning decays faster than results. Six months later you will remember that the record length is 4,096 samples, and you will not remember that 8,192 was rejected because of the capture buffer.

A session log is the record of one working session with an agent: what was asked, what was produced, what was accepted, and what remains. It is the bridge between sessions. A new session that begins by reading the last session log can continue without you re-explaining anything.

Cross references are explicit links from one file to another, such as a note that points to the specification section it affects, or a decision that points to the experiment that motivated it. They are what make a folder of files a connected body of knowledge, and they are the seed of the graph discussed below.

File type Job Edited how Typical agent use Research notes Dated record of reading and experiments Appended Searched for what was tried Specification file Current statement of what work must do Edited in place Read before writing code or text Glossary file Fixed meaning of terms Edited in place Loaded as domain vocabulary Decision log Choices and reasons Appended Consulted before revisiting a choice Session log What happened in one session Appended Read to resume work

Table 1. The file types of a research knowledge base and the job each one does.

Short worked examples show the formats. Each is illustrative and uses the running SAR ADC project. A research note is dated and records the source, the observation, and what it suggests:

## 2026-10-09: Capture buffer limit
Source: test board user guide, section 4.
Observed: the capture buffer holds at most 4,096 samples at 16 bits.
Suggests: records longer than 4,096 samples need two captures. See decision of 2026-10-12.

A glossary entry gives one precise definition per term, with units and related terms, so that an agent reading it cannot choose a different sense:

### ENOB
Effective number of bits: (SNDR_dB - 1.76) / 6.02, computed from a coherently
sampled record. Unit: bits. Related: SNDR, SFDR, nominal resolution.

A specification file states the current requirement and how it is checked, and a session log records what happened in one sitting, ending with the next step:

## Spec 3.2: Record length
Requirement: every ENOB record is 4,096 samples, coherently sampled.
Check: scripts/check-record.py exits with status 0.

## Session 2026-10-12
Asked: implement enob(). Produced: scripts/enob.py and tests. Accepted: all 5 criteria pass.
Open: window function for non-coherent records. Next: write the spec section for it.

The decision-log entry below completes the set. Notice that it names the alternative that was rejected and the evidence, so that nobody reopens the question without new information.

## 2026-10-12: Record length for ENOB measurements

Decision: use 4,096 samples per record, coherently sampled.
Rejected: 8,192 samples (exceeds the capture buffer of the test board).
Evidence: notes/2026-10-09-capture-buffer.md; spec section 3.2.
Consequence: ENOB resolution in the frequency domain is fs / 4,096.
Revisit if: the capture board is replaced.

Log the Rejected Option

When you record a decision, add one line naming what you did not choose and why. That line is what stops you, a collaborator, or an agent from re-proposing the rejected idea a month later as if it were new.

The value of a knowledge base appears at the moment of use. Instead of pasting five documents into a prompt and hoping you chose well, you tell the agent: "Read the specification, the glossary, and the last two session logs, then continue." The context is assembled from files you have already curated, and you will have applied the selection discipline of Chapter 4 once, in the structure of the files.

docs.title: From Files to a Knowledge Graph
docs.text:
A folder of linked files is a good memory for reading. It is a poor one for asking. Questions such as "which experiments used the dataset we later found to be corrupted?" require following several links in sequence, and a folder offers nothing to follow them with. A knowledge graph is a representation of knowledge as entities and typed relationships between them, so that a program can traverse the connections to answer such questions.

An entity is a distinct thing the project cares about: a paper, an experiment, a dataset, a design, a person, a concept. A relationship is a named, directed connection between two entities, such as "Experiment 07 used Dataset A" or "Paper Beta cites Paper Alpha". The word typed matters. A wiki link that means only "is related to" lets you navigate but not compute. A relationship named USED or CITES tells a program what the link means, and so it can answer questions that depend on the meaning. Dan McCreary's research on personal knowledge graphs, summarized in the Personal Knowledge Graphs appendix, puts the point as a hypothesis from Jim Hendler: a little semantics goes a long way.

A personal knowledge graph (PKG) is a knowledge graph of one person's, or one small group's, own notes, papers, experiments, people, and projects. It differs from a folder of notes in exactly two ways: its links are typed, and its entities have types with expected properties. It differs from an enterprise ontology in being built bottom-up and cheaply, usually by the person who uses it.

A graph schema is the declared list of entity types and relationship types a graph allows, and the properties each carries. A schema is what keeps the graph from decaying into a wiki. It does not need to be large. The schema for the running project fits in a table:

Entity type Typical properties Relationships it takes part in Paper title, year, DOI CITES (Paper to Paper), REPORTS (Paper to Experiment), ABOUT (Paper to Concept), AUTHORED (Person to Paper) Experiment date, settings TESTED (Experiment to Design), USED (Experiment to Dataset) Dataset name, path, checksum incoming USED Design version, process node REVISES (Design to Design) Concept name, definition incoming ABOUT Person name, role AUTHORED

Table 2. A graph schema for the research project: entity types and the relationships they take part in.

Two practical features of personal graphs deserve a name. Backlinks are the automatic reverse of a link: if Note A links to Concept ENOB, then ENOB's page shows that Note A refers to it. Backlinks are what turn one-way notes into a web, because from any concept you can see everything that mentions it, without having remembered to link back. The rule of thumb from the PKG research is that roughly 60 percent of a graph's value is in its nodes and 40 percent in its relationships, so adding links to existing notes is worth the effort.

Entity extraction is the identification of entities and relationships in free text, and it is where an agent earns its place in building the graph. Given a research note, an agent can propose "this note mentions Dataset A, Experiment 07, and the concept ENOB, and says Experiment 07 used Dataset A." You review the proposed entities and links, accept the correct ones, and fix the rest. This is the supervised pattern of Chapter 1 applied to knowledge: the agent proposes, you decide. A worked example: from the note line "Run 08 reused Dataset A and added a new capture, Dataset B, for the v3 design", an agent might propose the triples (Run 08, USED, Dataset A), (Run 08, USED, Dataset B), and (Run 08, TESTED, ADC Design v3). The first two are stated. The third is inferred from "for the v3 design" and should be confirmed against the experiment record before it is accepted. Extraction is wrong in characteristic ways. It invents plausible entities, merges two distinct things with the same name, and misses implicit relationships, so a human review of each batch is not optional.

Typed Links Make the Notes Computable

Notice the shift. A folder lets you find a note you already know exists. A typed graph lets you derive a fact no single note states, by chaining relationships. The question moves from "where did I write that?" to "what follows from what I know?"

Graph querying is the retrieval of answers from a graph by following relationships. In a graph database such as Neo4j the query language Cypher expresses a path as a pattern. Before the example, read the notation: parentheses are nodes, square brackets are relationships, and an arrow gives the direction. The query below asks for every paper that reports an experiment that used a given dataset.

MATCH (p:Paper)-[:REPORTS]->(e:Experiment)-[:USED]->(d:Dataset {name: "Dataset A"})
RETURN p.title, e.name

You do not need a graph database to benefit. A graph can live in your Markdown files as typed links in the frontmatter of each note, and a short script can read them and answer the same question. What matters is that the relationships are explicit and typed, not what stores them.

docs.title: Diagram: Personal Knowledge Graph Query Explorer
docs.text:
Personal Knowledge Graph Query Explorer

Type: graph-model sim-id: pkg-graph-query-explorer Library: vis-network Status: Built Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/infographics/tree/main/docs/sims/learning-path-explorer Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: solve Learning Objective: The learner will solve five questions about a twelve-edge personal knowledge graph by following typed, directed relationships, and give each answer as the exact set of entities, with at least 4 of 5 correct.

Prerequisites: entity, relationship, typed relationship, graph schema, backlink, and graph querying, all defined in the section "From Files to a Knowledge Graph" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of five questions the learner selects the set of entities that answer it and submits. An answer is correct when the selected set equals the answer set in Content exactly. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Hovering over edges to read their types is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A relationship can be followed in either direction with the same meaning. (2) A question that needs more than one hop cannot be answered from the graph. (3) A paper that is not directly linked to a dataset is unaffected by that dataset.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level work needs the learner to carry out the traversal procedure on a concrete graph. The questions rise from one hop to three, so the learner practices chaining relationships, which is the property that makes a graph more than a folder.

Content:

The graph is invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative" in the sim. Entities and their types:

ID Entity Type E1 Run 07 Experiment E2 Run 08 Experiment D1 Dataset A Dataset D2 Dataset B Dataset S1 ADC Design v2 Design S2 ADC Design v3 Design P1 Paper Alpha Paper P2 Paper Beta Paper C1 ENOB Concept A1 Dr. Rivera Person

Relationships, each directed from the first entity to the second:

# From Relationship To 1 Run 07 TESTED ADC Design v2 2 Run 08 TESTED ADC Design v3 3 Run 07 USED Dataset A 4 Run 08 USED Dataset A 5 Run 08 USED Dataset B 6 ADC Design v3 REVISES ADC Design v2 7 Paper Alpha REPORTS Run 07 8 Paper Beta REPORTS Run 08 9 Paper Beta CITES Paper Alpha 10 Paper Alpha ABOUT ENOB 11 Paper Beta ABOUT ENOB 12 Dr. Rivera AUTHORED Paper Beta

Questions, in this order:

# Question Answer set Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which experiments used Dataset A? Run 07, Run 08 Follow USED edges backward into Dataset A (edges 3 and 4). 2 Which designs were tested in an experiment that used Dataset B? ADC Design v3 Dataset B is used only by Run 08 (edge 5), and Run 08 tested ADC Design v3 (edge 2). 3 Which papers report an experiment that tested the design that ADC Design v3 revises? Paper Alpha ADC Design v3 REVISES ADC Design v2 (edge 6), Run 07 tested ADC Design v2 (edge 1), and Paper Alpha reports Run 07 (edge 7). 4 Which papers are cited by a paper that Dr. Rivera authored? Paper Alpha Dr. Rivera authored Paper Beta (edge 12), and Paper Beta cites Paper Alpha (edge 9). 5 If Dataset A were found to be corrupted, which papers must be rechecked? Paper Alpha, Paper Beta Dataset A is used by Run 07 and Run 08 (edges 3 and 4), which are reported by Paper Alpha and Paper Beta (edges 7 and 8).

Provenance: The traversal procedure and the schema are from the section "From Files to a Knowledge Graph" of this chapter. The entities, names, and relationships are invented for illustration.

Rules: An answer set is computed by following edges only in their stated direction, or against it where the question asks for the "from" side. Each question has exactly one answer set, given above. A selection is correct only if it equals the answer set, with no missing and no extra entities.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the graph and question 1.
  2. The learner clicks the entities that answer the question and submits.
  3. The sim highlights the path that produces the correct answer set and shows the "Why" sentence, then advances.
  4. After question 5, the sim shows the count correct. The learner should notice that question 5 needs a path of two hops and has two answers.

Feedback: Five questions, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the "Why" sentence and the highlighted path. Incorrect: the correct answer set, the highlighted path, and the "Why" sentence. The correct set is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 5 correct" is shown, with whether the mastery threshold of 4 was met.

Starting State: The full graph is shown with edge types visible on hover and question 1 posed. The question on screen is "Which entities answer this, by following the relationships?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that typed, directed relationships let a program answer multi-hop questions, and that the PKG research rule of thumb is about 60 percent of value in nodes and 40 percent in relationships.

MicroSim: Personal Knowledge Graph Query Explorer. Open it fullscreen.

docs.title: Grounding a Model With the Graph
docs.text:
Graph retrieval-augmented generation (graph RAG) is retrieval-augmented generation, as introduced in Chapter 3, where the retrieved material is a subgraph of facts selected by following relationships, not a set of text passages ranked by similarity. The question is mapped to entities in the graph, the neighbourhood of those entities is collected, and the resulting facts are placed in the prompt with an instruction to answer from them.

The advantage over passage retrieval is on multi-hop questions. A vector search for "which papers need rechecking if Dataset A is corrupted?" finds passages that mention Dataset A and misses the paper that reports an experiment that used it, because that paper never names the dataset. Following the relationships finds it. A worked example: the question is converted to the entity "Dataset A", the traversal collects two experiments and two papers, and the prompt receives four lines such as "Run 07 USED Dataset A; Paper Alpha REPORTS Run 07", with the instruction "answer only from these facts; if they are insufficient, say so". The model's answer is then both grounded and checkable against named links.

The same caution as in Chapter 4 applies. The graph is only as good as its entities and relationships, an agent-extracted link that nobody reviewed can be wrong, and a graph that exposes private results to a tool must be governed. Chapter 19 returns to the privacy of a personal knowledge graph that an always-on agent can read.

docs.title: The Anatomy of an Agent Skill
docs.text:
Everything so far organizes what is known. The remainder of the chapter concerns what is done repeatedly. An agent skill is a packaged, reusable capability for an agent: a directory containing instructions, and optionally scripts and reference files, that teaches the agent how to carry out one kind of task the same way each time. A prompt you saved is a skill's ancestor. A skill adds a name, a description the agent can use to decide when it applies, and supporting material loaded only when needed.

The skill's central file is SKILL.md, a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter followed by instructions. Its parts have specific jobs.

The skill name is a short identifier, in lowercase with hyphens, that names the capability and typically matches the directory name. It is also how you invoke the skill explicitly.

The skill description is a one- or two-sentence statement of what the skill does and when to use it. It is the most important line in the file, for a reason that comes from how skills are loaded. An agent keeps only the names and descriptions of its available skills in context. It reads the full instructions only when it decides a skill applies.

Skill triggering is that decision: the agent compares the user's request with the descriptions of the available skills and loads the matching skill's instructions. A skill with a vague description, such as "helps with data", will trigger on the wrong requests or not at all. A skill whose description names the task and the situations that call for it will trigger reliably.

Skill instructions are the body of SKILL.md: the numbered procedure, the constraints, and the output format that the agent follows once the skill is loaded. They apply the techniques of Chapters 3 and 4, written once.

Supporting files are the other files in the skill directory: scripts the agent runs, reference documents it reads when needed, and templates it fills in. Keeping them outside SKILL.md keeps the always-loaded text small, because the agent opens a supporting file only when the instructions point to it.

A complete minimal skill for the running project, with illustrative content, has this layout and main file.

enob-report/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/enob.py
├── references/targets.md
└── templates/report.md

---
name: enob-report
description: Compute ENOB from a coherently sampled ADC record and write a one-page report. Use when the user asks for ENOB, SNDR, or an ADC characterization summary.
---

# ENOB Report

1. Read the record file the user names. If none is named, ask for it.
2. Run scripts/enob.py with the sampling rate and the nominal bits.
3. Compare the result with the target in references/targets.md.
4. Write the report using templates/report.md.

Never edit files in data/raw/. Report ENOB in bits to one decimal.

Triggering is easiest to understand with examples. Given the description above, the agent compares each request with it. "What is the ENOB of capture-07.csv?" matches the named task and the cue "ENOB", so the skill loads. "Give me an ADC characterization summary for the new board" matches the cue "characterization summary", so it loads. "Plot the spectrum of capture-07.csv" mentions the same file but asks for a different task, so it should not load, and a description that read "helps with ADC data" would have loaded it wrongly. "Draft the related-work paragraph" has nothing in common with the description, so it does not load.

Read the file as a reader would. The frontmatter is between the two lines of three hyphens and contains exactly two fields. The description does both jobs, saying what the skill does and when to use it. The body is short and procedural, and it points to the script, the reference, and the template by path.

A Vague Description Never Triggers

A common trap is a well-written skill with a description such as "analysis helper". The agent sees only the description when choosing, so the skill is skipped, or fires on requests it cannot handle. State the task and the cues in the description, test it with five realistic requests, and rewrite it until it fires on the right ones.

docs.title: Diagram: Skill Anatomy Labeler
docs.text:
Skill Anatomy Labeler

Type: microsim sim-id: skill-anatomy-labeler Library: p5.js Status: Built Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify, for each of eight lines or files of a skill, whether it is the skill name, the skill description, skill instructions, or a supporting file, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: skill name, skill description, skill instructions, supporting files, and SKILL.md, all defined in the section "The Anatomy of an Agent Skill" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight items the learner commits one of four labels. A label is correct when it equals the label in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Viewing the whole SKILL.md and directory tree is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The description only says what the skill does and not when to use it. (2) Scripts and templates are part of SKILL.md. (3) The name and the description are the same thing.

Instructional Rationale: Remember-level recognition is the base for later design work. Labeling items in a single realistic skill ties each term to a concrete example.

Content:

The skill is the enob-report skill shown in the chapter. The four labels are Skill name, Skill description, Skill instructions, and Supporting file.

# Item shown Correct label Why (shown as feedback) 1 name: enob-report Skill name It is the short identifier of the capability. 2 description: Compute ENOB from a coherently sampled ADC record and write a one-page report. Use when the user asks for ENOB, SNDR, or an ADC characterization summary. Skill description It states what the skill does and when to use it, which is what the agent reads to decide to load it. 3 1. Read the record file the user names. If none is named, ask for it. Skill instructions It is a step of the procedure that is followed once the skill is loaded. 4 Never edit files in data/raw/. Skill instructions It is a constraint in the body of SKILL.md. 5 scripts/enob.py Supporting file It is a script the instructions tell the agent to run, and it lives outside SKILL.md. 6 references/targets.md Supporting file It is a reference document opened only when the instructions point to it. 7 templates/report.md Supporting file It is a template the agent fills in, kept outside SKILL.md. 8 3. Compare the result with the target in references/targets.md. Skill instructions It is a procedural step that points to a supporting file.

Provenance: The skill and its parts are from the section "The Anatomy of an Agent Skill" of this chapter. The file contents are illustrative.

Rules: Each item has exactly one correct label. A line inside SKILL.md below the frontmatter is Skill instructions. A path to a file other than SKILL.md is a Supporting file.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the skill directory tree and SKILL.md with item 1 highlighted.
  2. The learner chooses one of the four labels and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence, then highlights the next item.
  4. After item 8, the sim shows the count correct.

Feedback: Eight items, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "This is a ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct label is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown, with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: The directory tree and SKILL.md are shown with item 1 highlighted. The question on screen is "Which part of the skill is this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that SKILL.md has YAML frontmatter with a name and a description, that the description says what the skill does and when to use it, that instructions are the body, and that scripts, references, and templates are supporting files opened only when pointed to.

MicroSim: Skill Anatomy Labeler. Open it fullscreen.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
A research project that lasts needs memory that does not live in anyone's head or in a chat window. Plain files of defined types form a knowledge base. Typed links turn it into a graph that can be queried and used to ground an agent. And a skill packages one repeatable task so that it is done the same way, loaded only when it applies.

The main points to carry forward:

  • A knowledge base is built from research notes, specifications, glossaries, decision logs, and session logs, each with one job, joined by cross references.
  • Project memory is the part an agent loads to resume work, and a session log is the bridge between sessions.
  • A knowledge graph stores entities and typed, directed relationships, and a personal knowledge graph applies this to one researcher's own material, governed by a small schema.
  • Backlinks and entity extraction make the graph cheap to grow, and extracted links must be reviewed.
  • Graph querying and graph RAG answer multi-hop questions that text similarity misses.
  • An agent skill is a directory built around SKILL.md: a name, a description that drives triggering, instructions, and supporting files loaded on demand.

Your Project Can Remember

You can now sort project material into notes, specifications, glossary, decisions, and logs, answer a multi-hop question by following typed relationships, and name the four parts of a skill. That is the memory and the packaging the rest of the book builds on.

The next chapter takes the skill from a file you can read to one you can design, test, and share. Round up a task you do at least once a month, and bring it.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill
docs.text: Test your understanding of project knowledge files, personal knowledge graphs, and the parts of an agent skill.

docs.title: 1. What is a knowledge base in the context of a research project?
docs.text:
1. A web search engine specialized for academic papers
  2. A large language model trained on the project's documents
  3. An organized collection of written project material kept in plain text so people and agents can read it
  4. The set of all files in the repository, regardless of purpose
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A knowledge base is the curated set of notes, specifications, glossaries, decision logs, and session logs that capture what the project knows. It is not a trained model, not every file indiscriminately, and not an external search engine.

Concept Tested: Knowledge Base

See: From Project Files to a Knowledge Base

docs.title: 2. Which knowledge-base file type states the current agreed requirements and is read before writing code or text?
docs.text:
1. Research notes
  2. Session log
  3. Specification file
  4. Decision log
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A specification file states inputs, outputs, constraints, and acceptance criteria and is edited in place as the agreement changes. Research notes are informal and appended, session logs bridge sittings, and decision logs record choices and reasons.

Concept Tested: Specification File

See: From Project Files to a Knowledge Base

docs.title: 3. What is the main purpose of a glossary file?
docs.text:
1. To define the project's terms so everyone uses them the same way
  2. To store all session logs in one place
  3. To list every reference cited by the project
  4. To record the final results of experiments
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A glossary fixes the meaning of load-bearing terms, with units and related terms, so agents and collaborators do not silently choose different senses. It is not a session archive, bibliography, or results ledger.

Concept Tested: Glossary File

See: From Project Files to a Knowledge Base

docs.title: 4. Why does the chapter recommend keeping a decision log?
docs.text:
1. It replaces the need for a specification file.
  2. It stores API keys and passwords.
  3. It makes the project searchable by web search engines.
  4. Reasoning decays faster than results, so the reasons for choices are easily forgotten.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A decision log captures the choice, the alternatives rejected, and the evidence, so that nobody reopens the question later without new information. It complements, rather than replaces, the specification, and it must not contain secrets.

Concept Tested: Decision Log

See: From Project Files to a Knowledge Base

docs.title: 5. At the start of a new working session, which file should an agent read to continue work without re-explaining the project?
docs.text:
1. The glossary file only
  2. The most recent session log
  3. The oldest research note
  4. The project's README, ignoring earlier sessions
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The session log records what was asked, produced, accepted, and left open in the last sitting, making it the bridge between sessions. The glossary and README provide context, but they do not carry the current state of the work.

Concept Tested: Session Log

See: From Project Files to a Knowledge Base

docs.title: 6. In a knowledge graph, why are typed relationships more useful than undifferentiated wiki links?
docs.text:
1. They let a program traverse and compute with the meaning of the connection.
  2. They make the graph look nicer when rendered.
  3. They guarantee that every link is factually correct.
  4. They reduce the number of entities the graph must store.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A typed relationship such as USED or REPORTS tells a query engine what the link means, enabling multi-hop questions such as "which papers report an experiment that used this dataset?". A plain link only says "related to". Typing does not guarantee correctness or reduce entities.

Concept Tested: Entity and Relationship

See: From Files to a Knowledge Graph

docs.title: 7. In the chapter's graph example, if Dataset A is discovered to be corrupted, which papers must be rechecked?
docs.text:
1. Only Paper Beta
  2. Only Paper Alpha
  3. The paper authored by Dr. Rivera
  4. Both Paper Alpha and Paper Beta
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Dataset A is used by both Run 07 and Run 08; Paper Alpha reports Run 07 and Paper Beta reports Run 08, so both papers depend on Dataset A. This is a multi-hop question that a graph can answer but a simple text search might miss.

Concept Tested: Graph Querying

See: From Files to a Knowledge Graph

docs.title: 8. What is the main job of a skill description in SKILL.md?
docs.text:
1. To list every script the skill can run
  2. To tell the agent what the skill does and when to use it
  3. To provide the full step-by-step procedure
  4. To store the skill's version history
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The description is the only part of the skill the agent keeps in context when deciding whether to load the skill, so it must state both the task and the triggering cues. The full procedure is in the instructions, and version history lives in Git, not the description.

Concept Tested: Skill Description

See: The Anatomy of an Agent Skill

docs.title: 9. Given the skill description "Compute ENOB from a coherently sampled ADC record and write a one-page report. Use when the user asks for ENOB, SNDR, or an ADC characterization summary," which request should trigger the skill?
docs.text:
1. "What is the ENOB of capture-07.csv?"
  2. "Plot the spectrum of capture-07.csv."
  3. "Draft the related-work paragraph."
  4. "Install a new Python package for me."
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The request asks for ENOB, one of the explicit cues in the description. Plotting a spectrum is a different task, drafting related work is unrelated, and installing a package is outside the skill's scope.

Concept Tested: Skill Triggering

See: The Anatomy of an Agent Skill

docs.title: 10. Why are scripts, references, and templates kept as supporting files outside SKILL.md?
docs.text:
1. They are not needed when the skill runs.
  2. They are loaded only when the instructions point to them, keeping the always-loaded context small.
  3. The agent cannot read files with those extensions.
  4. They are hidden from the user for security reasons.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Supporting files are opened on demand, so the agent only pays their token cost when the instructions require them. They are still used, readable, and not hidden; the design simply avoids loading everything into every session.

Concept Tested: Supporting Files

See: The Anatomy of an Agent Skill

docs.title: References: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill
docs.text:
1. Knowledge graph - Wikipedia - Defines knowledge graphs as entities and typed relationships, with history, implementations, and reasoning over data. Directly supports the chapter's move from linked files to a queryable personal knowledge graph and graph schema.

  2. Knowledge base - Wikipedia - Explains what a knowledge base is, how it differs from an ordinary database, and common types and examples. Frames the chapter's notes, specifications, glossaries, and logs as project memory that people and agents share.

  3. Named-entity recognition - Wikipedia - Covers identifying entities in free text, with evaluation metrics, difficulties, and approaches. Background for the chapter's entity extraction step, including why extracted entities and relationships need human review.

  4. Designing Data-Intensive Applications (1st Edition) - Martin Kleppmann - O'Reilly Media - Chapter 2 introduces the property graph model of vertices and edges and shows the same graph in Cypher and in relational tables. This side-by-side comparison clarifies why typed relationships make multi-hop questions easy.

  5. How to Take Smart Notes (2nd Edition) - Sonke Ahrens - Sonke Ahrens (self-published) - Presents Niklas Luhmann's Zettelkasten method, with literature notes, permanent notes, and explicit links between them. Ahrens is not the originator of the method, but this book is widely praised for explaining linked notes as a thinking system, which clarifies the chapter's cross references and backlinks.

  6. Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills - Anthropic Engineering - Explains the skill as a folder built around SKILL.md with name and description frontmatter. Describes progressive disclosure, where metadata loads first and bundled files load only on demand, matching the chapter's triggering discussion.

  7. Agent Skills overview - Anthropic Documentation - Official reference for skill structure, required name and description fields and their limits, and the three loading levels, with a worked pdf-processing example. Use it to check the chapter's SKILL.md anatomy.

  8. Knowledge Graphs (Hogan et al.) - arXiv - A comprehensive survey of knowledge graph data models, query languages, construction, quality, and enterprise and open examples. Gives rigorous definitions behind the chapter's entities, relationships, schema, and graph querying.

  9. From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization - arXiv (Microsoft Research) - Introduces GraphRAG, in which a language model builds an entity graph and community summaries to answer corpus-wide questions. A research-grade example of the chapter's graph retrieval-augmented generation.

  10. Cypher Manual: Introduction - Neo4j Documentation - Official manual for Cypher, the property graph query language used in the chapter's MATCH example. Shows how node and relationship patterns express multi-hop traversals, with beginner resources and syntax references.

docs.title: Designing, Testing, and Sharing Agent Skills
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the full life of a skill: choosing a scope, writing single-purpose skills, testing and evaluating them, versioning, sharing, installing, and maintaining them. It ends with a research skill template. After this chapter you can turn a repeatable task from your own workflow into a skill that a colleague can install and trust.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 17 concepts from the learning graph:
