The correct answer is D. Go/no-go criteria make the decision to continue, pivot, or stop explicit before the data arrive, protecting the team from persisting because of effort already invested. They do not guarantee success or replace literature search.

Concept Tested: Research Roadmap

See: ./index.md#the-research-roadmap

docs.title: References: Brainstorming and Problem Framing
docs.text:
1. Brainstorming - Wikipedia - Covers Alex Osborn's group idea-generation method, its rules on deferring judgment and seeking quantity, and variations. Supports the chapter's separation of divergent generation from convergent evaluation.

  2. Hypothesis - Wikipedia - Explains what a scientific hypothesis is, working hypotheses, falsifiability, and statistical testing. Directly supports the chapter's rule that a hypothesis must name a change, effect size, and conditions that a result could contradict.

  3. Design of experiments - Wikipedia - Presents independent and dependent variables, randomization, blocking, replication, and a worked weighing example. Supports the chapter's treatment of baselines, controls, and fixing the support criterion before data are seen.

  4. The Craft of Research (4th Edition) - Wayne C. Booth, Gregory G. Colomb, Joseph M. Williams - University of Chicago Press - Moves a researcher from topic to question to significance using the "I am studying X because I want to find out Y in order to help my reader understand Z" sentence template, a concrete device for problem framing.

  5. How to Solve It (2nd Edition) - George Polya - Princeton University Press - Gives a four-phase problem-solving method and a question list ("Have you seen it before?", "Could you solve a related problem?") that made analogy and restating the problem teachable heuristics, clarifying analogical thinking.

  6. Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers - arXiv (Si, Yang, Hashimoto) - Blind study in which expert reviewers rated LLM-generated research ideas as more novel but slightly less feasible than expert ideas. Evidence for why ranking, feasibility, and novelty checks matter.

  7. Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models - arXiv (Sharma et al., Anthropic) - Shows that AI assistants tend to agree with users, partly because human preference data rewards agreement. Explains why the chapter demands explicit devil's advocate prompts rather than neutral requests for opinion.

  8. Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models - arXiv (Yao et al.) - Introduces a framework where a model explores several reasoning paths, evaluates them, and backtracks. Illustrates the generate-then-evaluate structure behind idea generation and ranking, with benchmark results.

  9. You and Your Research - Richard W. Hamming (transcript) - Bell Labs mathematician's talk on choosing important problems, asking what the important problems in your field are, and why. A practitioner's perspective on problem framing and project selection.

  10. Prompt engineering overview - Anthropic Documentation - Official guide to defining success criteria, writing prompts, and iterating, with links to best practices and an interactive tutorial. Supports the structured idea-generation prompts and explicit output formats used in this chapter.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter follows a paper from structure to submission: outlining, drafting, revision, author voice, LaTeX, figures and captions, reference formatting, venue requirements, peer review responses, and arXiv submission. It also covers authorship and co-author review. After this chapter you can draft a section from notes and revise it into your own voice.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 3: Choosing Models and Writing Clear Prompts
  • Chapter 4: Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting
  • Chapter 5: Markdown Project Files and Version Control
  • Chapter 6: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill
  • Chapter 9: Supervising Agents and Defining Agent Roles
  • Chapter 11: AI-Assisted Literature Search and Synthesis
  • Chapter 12: AI-Assisted Data Analysis and Scripting

The Paper Is Yours

A model can turn notes into prose faster than you can type, and prose that has not passed through your judgment is not your paper. This chapter shows how to let an agent draft and polish while every claim, every number, and the voice stay yours. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Structure, Outline, and Abstract
docs.text:
Paper structure is the standard arrangement of a research paper into sections that each answer one reader question. For an engineering paper the arrangement is usually an abstract, an introduction, related work, the method or design, the experiments and results, a discussion, and a conclusion. Readers rely on this: they go to the results for the numbers and to the discussion for the limits. A paper that follows the convention is read faster and judged more fairly.

Section The reader's question Typical contents Abstract Should I read this? Context, gap, contribution, headline result, significance Introduction Why does this matter? Problem, why it is hard, contribution, roadmap Related work What is already known? Grouped prior work and the remaining gap Method What exactly was done? Design, algorithm, setup, enough to reproduce Results What was found? Data, tables, figures, with conditions Discussion What does it mean, and what are the limits? Interpretation, limitations, comparison Conclusion What should I take away? Summary and future work

Table 1. The sections of a typical engineering paper and the question each answers.

Outline generation is producing the skeleton of the paper, section by section, with the claim each paragraph will make. It is the stage at which an agent saves the most effort and the one at which your control matters most, because the outline fixes the argument. A good outline is a list of claims, each tied to the evidence that supports it, such as a result file, a figure, or a reference. Give the agent your notes and results, ask for an outline in which every bullet is a claim and names its evidence, and ask it to mark any bullet for which no evidence was supplied. Those marks are the work still to be done.

Abstract writing is the compression of the whole paper into about 150 to 250 words. An abstract has a fixed anatomy, and it is useful to check a draft against it: one sentence of context, one stating the gap or problem, one stating what the paper contributes, one or two giving the key result with its numbers and conditions, and one on significance. The most common defect is a result stated without a number. Write the abstract last, from the finished paper, and make sure every number in it appears in the body.

docs.title: Drafting and Revising
docs.text:
Drafting is writing the first version of a section. A dependable method for working with an agent is to draft from claims, not from a topic. For each paragraph, supply the claim, the evidence, and the intended reader, and instruct the agent to use only the supplied material and to insert a marker such as [NO EVIDENCE] wherever it would have to assert something not supplied. The marker is what keeps a fluent draft from smuggling in claims you cannot support.

Revision is the repeated improvement of a draft, and it benefits most from a human eye on the argument and a machine's help on the sentences. The sequence that works is to revise the structure first (order of sections and paragraphs), then the argument within paragraphs, then the sentences, and last the surface. A model asked to "improve this" at the start works on the surface and leaves a structural problem in place.

Author voice is the consistent personality and phrasing of your writing, and it is what makes a paper read as written by one person. Left alone, models drift toward a generic register: long lists of three, stock transitions, and claims of significance larger than the evidence. Three practices protect your voice. Draft the sections that carry the argument yourself, such as the introduction and discussion, and use the agent for the more routine ones. When you ask for edits, supply a paragraph of your own earlier writing as a style sample and an instruction to edit and not to rewrite. And read the result aloud. If a sentence sounds like no one you know, change it.

Revision by an agent has a specific hazard, which is that numbers and claims change without notice while the prose improves. The check is mechanical and cheap. The script below, with its logic explained first, extracts every number from the text before and after an edit and reports any number that appears in only one of them. The regular expression matches optional signs, digits, decimal points, and thousands separators.

import re, sys

def numbers(text):
    return set(re.findall(r"[-+]?\d[\d,]*\.?\d*", text))

before = open(sys.argv[1]).read()
after = open(sys.argv[2]).read()
b, a = numbers(before), numbers(after)
print("only in original:", sorted(b - a))
print("only in revision:", sorted(a - b))

Run on a revised paragraph, it takes a second and flags a changed ENOB figure that no amount of reading fluent prose would have caught. A clean report does not prove that the claims are unchanged, since a qualifier could have been deleted, but a report with differences is always worth reading.

Edit, Do Not Rewrite, and Diff the Numbers

Tell the agent to preserve every number, unit, and claim, and to change only the wording. Then run the number check and read git diff on the paper source. A revision that changes a number or removes a qualifier is not a revision.

docs.title: Diagram: Paper Section Sorter
docs.text:
Paper Section Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: paper-section-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Built Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of ten sentences from an engineering paper into the section where it belongs, with at least 8 of 10 classified correctly.

Prerequisites: the sections of a paper and the reader question each answers, defined in the section "Structure, Outline, and Abstract" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of ten sentences the learner commits one of six sections. A classification is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the table of sections is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any sentence with a number is a result. (2) A contribution statement belongs only in the abstract. (3) A limitation belongs in the conclusion and not in the discussion.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level classification needs the learner to explain a sentence's function by the reader question it answers. The sentences are drawn from one invented paper so that the sections can be compared in context.

Content:

All sentences are invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative". The six sections are Abstract, Introduction, Related work, Method, Results, and Discussion.

# Sentence Correct section Why (shown as feedback) 1 Successive-approximation converters dominate low-power sensor interfaces, yet their accuracy is limited by capacitor mismatch. Introduction It states the problem and why it matters. 2 Prior calibration schemes either require a dedicated reference or converge slowly [3], [7]. Related work It positions earlier work and points to the gap. 3 The comparator offset is measured by shorting its inputs and averaging 256 decisions. Method It states what was done, in enough detail to reproduce. 4 The calibrated converter reaches an ENOB of 9.4 bits at 1 MS/s. Results It reports a measured finding. 5 The residual error is consistent with the thermal noise of the comparator, which suggests that a larger input pair would give a further gain. Discussion It interprets a result and points to a consequence. 6 Measurements were taken on 12 devices from one wafer at 25 °C with a 4,096-sample record. Method It describes the experimental setup. 7 We present a foreground offset calibration for SAR ADCs that raises measured ENOB from 8.6 to 9.4 bits at 1 MS/s in 65 nm CMOS using 45 µW. Abstract It compresses context, contribution, and key result with numbers into one sentence. 8 Table II lists the ENOB of the 12 devices before and after calibration. Results It presents the data. 9 The gain is limited to chips with an offset below 15 mV, since larger offsets saturate the correction range. Discussion It states a limitation. 10 Section III describes the calibration algorithm and Section IV the measurement setup. Introduction It is the roadmap paragraph that ends an introduction.

Provenance: The sections and their questions are from the section "Structure, Outline, and Abstract" of this chapter. The sentences and values are invented for illustration.

Rules: Each sentence has exactly one correct section. A sentence is classified by the reader question it answers.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads sentence 1.
  2. The learner chooses one of the six sections and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence.
  4. After sentence 10, the sim shows the count correct and the sentences grouped by section.

Feedback: Ten sentences, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "This belongs in ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct section is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 10 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 8 was met.

Starting State: Sentence 1 is shown with six sections and none chosen. The question on screen is "Which reader question does this sentence answer?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists the sections and the reader question each answers, states that an abstract compresses context, gap, contribution, and result, and that the introduction ends with a roadmap.

MicroSim: Paper Section Sorter. Open it fullscreen.

docs.title: Figures, LaTeX, and References
docs.text:
LaTeX is the typesetting system that most engineering venues use, and it is plain text. That makes it a good fit for the version-controlled project of Chapter 5 and for agents, which write LaTeX fluently. The cautions are practical. An agent may use packages your venue's template does not allow, produce markup that compiles with warnings, or silently alter a macro. Keep the venue's class file and template unchanged, compile after every substantial edit, and read the log for warnings, since a wrong cross-reference shows up there as ?? in the output.

Figure preparation is making the figures that carry the results, and the standards are those of Chapter 12: labeled axes with units, a legible size at the column width, visible spread, and a consistent style across figures. Generate every figure from a script that reads the processed data, so that the figure can be regenerated when the data change. A figure drawn by hand in an editor cannot be reproduced and tends to go stale.

Figure captions are the text that makes a figure readable without searching the body for its context. A good caption states what is plotted, the conditions under which the data were obtained, how to read any markers or error bars, and, where it helps, the one observation the reader should take. The standard to apply is that the figure and caption together can be understood without the body text.

docs.title: Diagram: Figure Caption Critic
docs.text:
Figure Caption Critic

Type: microsim sim-id: figure-caption-critic Library: p5.js Status: Built Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: critique Learning Objective: The learner will critique each of six figure captions by naming its main defect, or that it has none, with at least 5 of 6 judged correctly.

Prerequisites: figure caption and the four properties of a good caption (what is plotted, conditions, how to read it, no unsupported claim), all defined in the section "Figures, LaTeX, and References" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of six captions the learner commits one of five judgments. A judgment is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the checklist is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A short caption is a good caption. (2) A caption can rely on the body text for its conditions. (3) A caption should state the paper's main claim.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to apply a checklist to a caption and name the failing criterion. One item has a caption that is long but has no defect, and one has a short caption that fails, so that length is not a cue.

Content:

All captions are invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative". Judgment options: Vague, Missing conditions, Undefined symbols, Overclaims, No defect.

# Caption Correct judgment Why (shown as feedback) 1 Figure 3. ENOB results. Vague It does not say what is plotted against what, so the reader cannot tell what the figure shows. 2 Figure 4. Measured ENOB versus input frequency for 12 devices at 1 MS/s, 1.0 V, and 25 °C. Markers show the mean and error bars show one standard deviation. No defect It states the quantity, the conditions, and how to read the markers. 3 Figure 5. Measured ENOB versus input frequency. Missing conditions The sampling rate, supply, temperature, and number of devices are not stated. 4 Figure 6. SNDR versus input frequency at 1 MS/s, 1.0 V, and 25 °C, showing that our design is the best known SAR ADC. Overclaims A single figure of SNDR versus frequency cannot establish that the design is the best known. 5 Figure 7. FoM_W versus fs for ADC1 to ADC9 (measured, 65 nm). Undefined symbols FoM_W, fs, and ADC1 to ADC9 are not defined in the caption. 6 Figure 8. Power breakdown of the converter at 1 MS/s and 1.0 V (simulated, typical corner): comparator 38 percent, DAC 27 percent, logic 25 percent, clock 10 percent. No defect It states the conditions, that the data are simulated, and the breakdown, which sums to 100 percent.

Provenance: The caption properties are from the section "Figures, LaTeX, and References" of this chapter. The captions and values are invented for illustration.

Rules: Each caption has exactly one correct judgment. A caption is judged by the first failing property, in this order: Vague, Missing conditions, Undefined symbols, Overclaims. A caption with none of these defects is judged No defect.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads caption 1 and the checklist.
  2. The learner chooses one of the five judgments and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence, and offers a corrected caption where there is a defect.
  4. After caption 6, the sim shows the count correct.

Feedback: Six captions, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "The main issue is ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct judgment is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 6 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 5 was met.

Starting State: Caption 1 is shown with five judgments. The question on screen is "Could a reader understand this figure from the caption alone?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a caption says what is plotted, the conditions, how to read the markers, and the observation to take, and that figure and caption together should be understandable without the body.

MicroSim: Figure Caption Critic. Open it fullscreen.

Reference formatting is producing the reference list in the style a venue requires. With BibTeX and a venue's style file the formatting is automatic, so the job is to keep the BibTeX entries correct and complete: verified as in Chapter 11, with the venue name, year, volume, pages, and DOI present. Never let an agent retype a reference by hand into the text, since that is where fabricated and corrupted entries enter.

Venue requirements are the rules a particular journal or conference sets: the template, the page limit, whether review is anonymous, the reference style, the required statements such as data availability, ethics, and use of AI tools, and the file formats for submission. Read them before drafting, not after. A common and avoidable waste is a paper written to one length and then cut to another, and an agent can check a manuscript against a pasted copy of the requirements.

docs.title: Editing, Consistency, and Co-Authors
docs.text:
Technical editing is the line-by-line check for correctness of terminology, symbols, units, and cross-references. Style consistency is the uniform treatment of the same thing throughout the paper: one abbreviation for each term, one convention for units and number formatting, one notation for each symbol, one spelling variant. Grammar and clarity are the sentence-level correctness and readability of the prose. These three are tasks in which an agent is strong and in which you should still ask for a list of proposed changes and not a silent rewrite, so that each change can be accepted or rejected in the diff. A useful instruction is "list inconsistencies in notation and terminology and propose one resolution for each, without editing the text".

Authorship is the question of who is credited for the work and who is accountable for it. The widely used criteria require substantial contribution, drafting or critical revision, approval of the final version, and accountability for the work. Those criteria cannot be satisfied by a language model, and major publishers, including IEEE and ACM, state that AI systems may not be listed as authors and that substantive use of AI tools must be disclosed. Policies change, so read the current policy of your venue. Chapter 18 treats disclosure in detail.

Co-author review is the circulation of the draft to the people who share responsibility for it. Send them a version that is complete enough to read, with the claims, the evidence, and the open questions marked, and ask for specific things: check the numbers in Table II, confirm the description of the method, read Section 5 for fairness to prior work. Every co-author should know which parts were drafted with AI assistance.

docs.title: Submission and Response
docs.text:
arXiv submission is the posting of a manuscript to the arXiv preprint server, which makes a paper available before or alongside peer review. The practical points are these. You submit the LaTeX source and its figures, and arXiv compiles it, so the source must build cleanly from a clean directory. Include the compiled bibliography file (the .bbl), since arXiv's guidance is to submit that file and not to rely on BibTeX running during processing. Choose the subject category with care, and check the current submission guidelines, including the endorsement rules for first-time submitters. Check the compiled PDF that arXiv produces before announcing, because it is the version readers get.

A cover letter accompanies a journal submission and is short: the title and the contribution in a few sentences, why the work fits the venue, confirmation that it is not under consideration elsewhere, and any required declarations. An agent drafts it adequately from the abstract and the venue's scope statement. Check that it claims nothing the paper does not.

A peer review response is the reply to reviewers' comments, normally a point-by-point document. Each reviewer comment is quoted, followed by your response and, where the paper changed, the location of the change. An agent is useful for organizing the comments into a table and drafting a first response. Three rules apply. Never claim a change that was not made. Answer the comment actually asked, not a nearby easier one. And decide yourself where to disagree: a polite, evidenced disagreement is acceptable, and an agent will tend to accommodate every comment whether or not it is right.

Reviewer comment Response Change Location R1.2: ENOB is measured on one chip only. We now report 12 devices, with mean and standard deviation. Added Table III Section V-B R2.4: The comparison omits the work of [14]. We agree and have added it with matching conditions. Added row to Table IV Section VI R2.5: The method should be tested at 125 °C. We could not test at this temperature with our setup and state this as a limitation. Added a sentence Section VII

Table 2. A fragment of a response matrix, with illustrative content.

Accommodating Every Comment

A common trap is letting an agent draft a response that agrees with every reviewer comment. It happens because the model is inclined to please, and the draft reads as gracious. Decide your position on each comment first, then ask for wording. A reviewer who sees a claimed change that is missing from the paper will stop trusting the rest.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
A manuscript is the point where all the earlier verification meets a reader, and the practices of this chapter keep AI assistance from eroding it. Draft from evidenced claims, protect your voice and your numbers, regenerate every figure from data, verify every reference, and keep to the venue's rules.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Paper structure answers one reader question per section, and an outline of evidenced claims fixes the argument. Write the abstract last, with numbers.
  • Drafting from claims with a no-evidence marker, and revising from structure to surface, keep unsupported claims out.
  • Author voice is protected by drafting argument-bearing sections yourself, supplying style samples, and reading aloud. A number check on every revision catches silent changes.
  • LaTeX, figures, and captions are generated from source and data. A caption stands alone with its figure.
  • Reference formatting relies on verified BibTeX and never on hand-typed entries.
  • Venue requirements are read first. Technical editing, style consistency, and grammar are done through proposed changes, not silent rewrites.
  • Authorship requires accountability that a model cannot take, so AI is disclosed and is not an author.
  • arXiv submission, cover letters, and peer review responses have specific forms. Never claim an unmade change.

A Draft That Is Still Yours

You can now place a sentence in its section, build an abstract with numbers, check a revision for changed numbers, judge a figure caption against a checklist, and write a response that claims only what changed. The agent supplies speed, and you supply the claims.

The next chapter turns a result into something readers can interact with: simulations, slides, and teaching materials. Round up the one result you would most like others to understand, and bring it.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: AI-Assisted Manuscript Preparation
docs.text: Test your understanding of paper structure, outlining, drafting, revision, figures, LaTeX, references, authorship, and peer review responses with these 10 review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is the purpose of inserting a [NO EVIDENCE] marker when an agent drafts from claims?
docs.text:
1. It flags where the agent would have to assert something not supplied
  2. It indicates the section needs more figures
  3. It marks claims that should be removed from the paper
  4. It shows where LaTeX compilation failed
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The marker keeps a fluent draft from smuggling in unsupported claims. It tells the researcher exactly where evidence must be supplied before the prose can stand.

Concept Tested: Drafting

See: ./index.md#drafting-and-revising

docs.title: 2. According to major publishers such as IEEE and ACM, can a language model be listed as an author on a research paper?
docs.text:
1. Yes, if it contributed to the writing
  2. Yes, if the human authors approve
  3. Only if its use is disclosed in the acknowledgments
  4. No, because authorship requires accountability a model cannot take
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Authorship criteria require substantial contribution, approval of the final version, and accountability for the work. A model cannot take accountability, so it is not listed as an author, and substantive AI use must be disclosed.

Concept Tested: Authorship

See: ./index.md#editing-consistency-and-co-authors

docs.title: 3. Why should the abstract typically be written last?
docs.text:
1. Because it is the least important section
  2. Because it must accurately reflect the finished results and numbers
  3. Because agents cannot draft abstracts first
  4. Because it must be submitted separately from the paper
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The abstract compresses the whole paper, so it should be written once the results, methods, and numbers are final. Every number in the abstract must also appear in the body.

Concept Tested: Abstract Writing

See: ./index.md#structure-outline-and-abstract

docs.title: 4. What is the main danger of asking an agent to "improve this" on an early draft?
docs.text:
1. The agent will change the paper structure
  2. The agent will add too many references
  3. The agent works on surface wording and may leave structural problems in place
  4. The agent will refuse to make changes
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Without specific instructions, an agent tends to polish sentences rather than fix the order of sections or the argument within paragraphs. Revision should move from structure to argument to sentences to surface.

Concept Tested: Revision

See: ./index.md#drafting-and-revising

docs.title: 5. Why is it important to generate figures from scripts rather than drawing them by hand?
docs.text:
1. So they can be regenerated when the data change
  2. Because hand-drawn figures are always less accurate
  3. Because agents cannot draw figures
  4. Because journals require script-generated figures
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Script-generated figures are reproducible: when the processed data or analysis change, the figure updates automatically. Hand-drawn figures tend to go stale and cannot be reproduced.

Concept Tested: Figure Preparation

See: ./index.md#figures-latex-and-references

docs.title: 6. A caption reads: "Figure 4. Measured ENOB versus input frequency for 12 devices at 1 MS/s, 1.0 V, and 25 °C. Markers show the mean and error bars show one standard deviation." How should this caption be judged?
docs.text:
1. Vague
  2. No defect
  3. Missing conditions
  4. Overclaims
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The caption states what is plotted, the conditions, and how to read the markers and error bars, so a reader can understand the figure without the body text. It does not overclaim.

Concept Tested: Figure Captions

See: ./index.md#figures-latex-and-references

docs.title: 7. A reviewer asks why a method was not tested at 125 °C, but the researcher could not do so with the available setup. Which response is best?
docs.text:
1. Add a fabricated measurement at 125 °C
  2. Ignore the comment because it is inconvenient
  3. State the limitation and explain why the test could not be performed
  4. Promise to test at 125 °C in a future paper without evidence
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An honest, evidenced response that acknowledges a limitation is acceptable. Fabricating data, ignoring the comment, or making unsupported promises all damage trust in the response.

Concept Tested: Peer Review Response

See: ./index.md#submission-and-response

docs.title: 8. Before drafting a paper, what should the researcher do first regarding venue requirements?
docs.text:
1. Write the paper and then adapt it to whatever venue is chosen
  2. Let the agent choose the venue automatically
  3. Read the requirements only after drafting is complete
  4. Read the venue requirements before drafting
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Venue rules on length, template, reference style, and required statements shape the draft. Reading them first avoids wasted rewriting. The researcher, not the agent, chooses the venue.

Concept Tested: Venue Requirements

See: ./index.md#figures-latex-and-references

docs.title: 9. A researcher runs a number-extraction script before and after an agent's revision and finds that an ENOB value changed. What should the researcher conclude?
docs.text:
1. The revision silently altered a result and must not be accepted without checking
  2. The revision improved the accuracy of the result
  3. The number check is wrong because the prose reads better
  4. Such changes are normal and should be ignored
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A number check catches silent changes to values, units, and qualifiers during editing. A revision that changes a reported result without explicit instruction is a defect, not an improvement, until verified.

Concept Tested: Technical Editing

See: ./index.md#drafting-and-revising

docs.title: 10. A peer review response drafted by an agent agrees with every comment and claims changes throughout the paper. What is the main risk?
docs.text:
1. The response will be too long
  2. The reviewers will be offended by the tone
  3. The agent has misunderstood the paper's contribution
  4. The response may claim changes that were not actually made
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Models tend to accommodate, so an agent may agree with comments and claim changes that do not exist. The researcher must decide the position on each comment first and ensure every claimed change is actually in the paper.

Concept Tested: Peer Review Response

See: ./index.md#submission-and-response

docs.title: References: AI-Assisted Manuscript Preparation
docs.text:
1. IMRAD - Wikipedia - Explains the Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion layout of research papers. It grounds the chapter's paper-structure table and the idea that each section answers one reader question, with history and discipline variants.

  2. LaTeX - Wikipedia - Describes the LaTeX document-preparation system built on TeX, covering its markup model, packages, and bibliography tooling. Useful background for why plain-text source suits version control and agent-assisted editing of manuscripts.

  3. Abstract (summary) - Wikipedia - Covers the purpose, types, structure, and limits of academic abstracts. It supports the chapter's guidance that an abstract compresses context, gap, contribution, and result, and is written from the finished paper.

  4. Writing Science: How to Write Papers That Get Cited and Proposals That Get Funded (1st Edition) - Joshua Schimel - Oxford University Press - Schimel's distinctive contribution is the Opening-Challenge-Action-Resolution story structure, which turns an introduction into a narrative argument. It sharpens the outline-as-claims approach and the drafting of the introduction and abstract.

  5. Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace (12th Edition) - Joseph M. Williams and Joseph Bizup - Pearson - Teaches clarity by making characters the subjects and actions the verbs of sentences, with before-and-after revision exercises. It directly supports the grammar-and-clarity and revision-from-structure-to-surface practices of this chapter.

  6. Submitting TeX/LaTeX to arXiv - arXiv - Official guidance on preparing LaTeX source, figure formats, and the compiled bibliography (.bbl) file for arXiv submission. Essential checklist for the chapter's advice that source must build cleanly from a clean directory.

  7. arXiv Endorsement - arXiv - Explains why first-time submitters or new categories need endorsement, how to obtain it, and who may endorse. Directly relevant to the chapter's arXiv submission cautions for new authors.

  8. Learn LaTeX in 30 Minutes - Overleaf - Hands-on beginner tutorial covering document structure, sections, figures, tables, math, and packages with runnable examples. Gives students enough LaTeX to review and compile agent-generated manuscript source.

  9. Bibliography management with BibTeX - Overleaf - Shows how .bib databases, \cite commands, and bibliography styles work, with entry types and author-name formatting examples. Supports the chapter's rule to keep BibTeX entries verified and never retype references.

  10. Defining the Role of Authors and Contributors - ICMJE - States the four authorship criteria, including accountability, and that AI tools cannot be listed as authors and their use must be disclosed. Grounds the chapter's authorship and co-author review sections.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the ways research results are communicated and taught: slide decks, interactive simulations, MicroSims, embedded simulations, learning graphs, and intelligent textbooks. It introduces generating a MicroSim with an agent. After this chapter you can create an interactive simulation that illustrates a concept from your research.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 11 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Research Communication 15 Slide Deck 2 Interactive Simulation 10 p5.js 10 MicroSim 9 Concept Dependency 7 Learning Graph 6 Intelligent Textbook 5 Embedding Simulations 1 Teaching From Research 2 MicroSim Generation 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 5: Markdown Project Files and Version Control
  • Chapter 6: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill
  • Chapter 9: Supervising Agents and Defining Agent Roles
  • Chapter 13: Simulation, Testing, and Reproducible Code
  • Chapter 15: AI-Assisted Manuscript Preparation

Let Readers Turn the Knob

A figure shows one setting of a result, and a reader who can move the slider understands the whole relationship. You are looking at a book built this way: every interactive on these pages began as a written specification. By the end you will be able to write one for your own result. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Communicating Research
docs.text:
Research communication is the transfer of a result and its reasoning to a particular audience for a particular purpose. The same result is communicated differently to a reviewer, who wants evidence and limits, to a colleague who wants the method, to a student who wants the idea, and to a funder who wants significance. The medium follows from the audience, and agents can help with several of them.

A slide deck is the standard medium for a talk. An agent drafts a deck quickly from a paper, and the common failure is a deck that mirrors the paper's structure instead of a talk's. A talk has one message, a few supporting points, and few words per slide. Ask for the deck from a stated audience, time, and single message, and require that each slide state its point as a sentence in the title. Reuse figures from the paper's source scripts and not screenshots, and run the number check of Chapter 15 on every slide, since figures in slides are copied and changed more often than anywhere else.

A static figure shows a result at the parameter values the author chose. An interactive simulation is a program that lets the viewer change parameters and see the response, and so lets the viewer explore the relationship the result describes. It is the right medium when the point of the result is a dependence: how ENOB falls as noise rises, how leakage changes with window choice, how a search converges. It is the wrong medium for a fact that has no parameter.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
A MicroSim is a small, single-concept, interactive simulation that runs in a web browser, is embedded in a page, has open and readable source code, and is built from a short specification. The idea, developed in the author's MicroSims project, is that a simulation small enough to specify in a page can be generated by an AI model, checked by a person, and embedded anywhere that displays web pages. This book contains many, each in its own directory under docs/sims/ with a main.html that is embedded in the chapter and an index.md lesson page.

The library most often used is p5.js, a JavaScript library for drawing and interaction in the browser. It needs no installation, runs everywhere, and has built-in controls such as sliders, buttons, and drop-downs. The rule in this book is to use the library's own controls and not to draw them by hand, since the built-in ones are accessible and consistent. Two further conventions keep sims embeddable: the first statement in setup() reads the container width so that the canvas fits the page, and the canvas is attached to the page's main element.

Before the code, here is the relationship it shows. When Gaussian noise of standard deviation \( \sigma \), measured in least-significant bits, is added to an ideal \( N \)-bit quantizer whose own quantization noise has standard deviation \( 1/\sqrt{12} \) LSB, the effective number of bits becomes

\[ \text{ENOB} = N - \tfrac{1}{2}\log_2\!\left(1 + 12\,\sigma^2\right). \]

For \( N = 10 \) and \( \sigma = 2 \) the value is 7.19 bits, the number used in Chapter 13. The sketch below draws one bar for ENOB and one for the nominal bits, and a slider changes \( \sigma \). It uses createSlider(min, max, value, step), which creates a slider with a minimum, a maximum, a starting value, and a step size.

let sigmaSlider;
let canvasWidth = 400;

function updateCanvasSize() {
  canvasWidth = document.querySelector('main').offsetWidth;
}

function setup() {
  updateCanvasSize();
  const canvas = createCanvas(canvasWidth, 220);
  canvas.parent(document.querySelector('main'));
  sigmaSlider = createSlider(0, 4, 1, 0.25);   // noise in LSB
  sigmaSlider.parent(document.querySelector('main'));
}

function draw() {
  background('aliceblue');
  const sigma = sigmaSlider.value();
  const enob = 10 - 0.5 * Math.log2(1 + 12 * sigma * sigma);
  const scale = (canvasWidth - 40) / 10;             // pixels per bit
  fill('lightgray'); rect(20, 40, 10 * scale, 40);   // nominal 10 bits
  fill('steelblue'); rect(20, 110, enob * scale, 40);
  fill(0); noStroke();
  text('Nominal: 10 bits', 20, 30);
  text('ENOB: ' + enob.toFixed(2) + ' bits at sigma = ' + sigma + ' LSB', 20, 100);
}

Slide the control to 0 and the bar reaches about 10 bits; slide it to 2 and it falls to about 7.2. A reader who has seen this does not need the formula explained. The same sketch, with labels and a lesson page, is a complete MicroSim.

The Interactive Is the Result in Motion

Notice that the sketch has no data in it, only the relationship. A paper's table gives you the points the authors measured, and a sim gives you the function that the points came from. That is why a good MicroSim teaches in a minute what a page of text takes ten to explain.

docs.title: Generating a MicroSim With an Agent
docs.text:
MicroSim generation is the use of an agent to build a MicroSim from a specification. The workflow of this book is specification first. A specification states what the learner must be able to do afterward, the evidence that shows it, the full content, the rules the model must obey, the activity, and the feedback. It deliberately leaves out layout and code, which the generating agent decides. You have already seen the form: each interactive in the chapters of this book has such a specification in a collapsed block above it, with a Bloom level and verb, an objective, evidence of mastery, content, rules, learner activity, feedback, and chapter anchors.

The workflow has five steps, and the checks matter more than the generation.

  1. Specify. Write the objective with one verb, the evidence of mastery, and every item of content with its correct answer. If you cannot write the evidence, the sim has no purpose yet.
  2. Search before building. Look for an existing MicroSim that already teaches the concept. Reuse is cheaper than generation.
  3. Generate. Give the specification to the agent, with the conventions above. Ask for the code in the standard directory layout.
  4. Verify. Run it. Check each rule in the specification against the behavior: the formulas, the thresholds, the feedback texts, the boundary cases. A sim that looks right and computes a slightly wrong number is the worst outcome, and the checks of Chapter 13 apply.
  5. Approve. A person tests the controls and decides that it is ready for learners. In this repository a lesson page carries a status value that shows in the navigation: scaffold for a specification with no implementation, built for an implementation awaiting review, instrumented for one that records learner events, and approved for one the author has tested. Agents may set the first three. Only the human author sets approved.

Write the Evidence of Mastery First

Before you describe the sim, write one sentence that begins "The learner shows they understand by...". If the sentence names something the sim can check, such as a number entered, a prediction committed, or an item sorted, you have the spine of the activity. If it says "explores", the sim will be a toy.

The following reused MicroSim, from the author's instructional design project, supports the first step of the workflow. It matches each of the six levels of Bloom's taxonomy to the kind of interaction that fits it, which is the guidance behind the "Bloom level" and "verb" lines of every specification in this book.

docs.title: Diagram: Bloom's Taxonomy MicroSim Matcher
docs.text:
Run the Bloom's Taxonomy MicroSim Matcher fullscreen

Bloom's Taxonomy MicroSim Matcher (reused MicroSim)

Type: microsim sim-id: blooms-microsim-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/infographics/sims/blooms-microsim-matcher/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/infographics/tree/main/docs/sims/blooms-microsim-matcher Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each Bloom's taxonomy level with the kind of MicroSim interaction pattern that suits it.

Reused from the MicroSim catalog (WHAT match score 0.85).

The five-step workflow has a prerequisite that is easy to overlook: the sim must be the right medium. The following specification practices the judgment of when a MicroSim earns its place.

docs.title: Diagram: MicroSim Suitability Judge
docs.text:
MicroSim Suitability Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: microsim-suitability-judge Library: p5.js Status: Built Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge, for each of eight pieces of research content, whether an interactive MicroSim or a static figure or text is the better medium, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: interactive simulation, MicroSim, and the criterion that a MicroSim suits a dependence or process the learner can manipulate or predict, all defined in the sections "Communicating Research" and "MicroSims" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight items the learner commits "MicroSim" or "static figure or text". A judgment is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the criterion is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Interactive is always better than static. (2) Any technical content should become a simulation. (3) A table of values is equivalent to a sim of the function.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to apply a criterion and decline to build when the criterion is not met, which saves the effort of building sims that add nothing.

Content:

All items are invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative". The criterion shown is: "A MicroSim suits content with a parameter the learner can change, or a process the learner can step through or predict, where seeing the response builds understanding."

# Content Correct medium Why (shown as feedback) 1 How the ENOB of an ADC falls as added noise increases. MicroSim It is a dependence on a parameter, and moving the noise slider shows the relationship. 2 A die photograph of the fabricated converter. Static figure or text It is a single image with no parameter or process. 3 How a successive-approximation search converges, bit by bit, to the digital code of an input voltage. MicroSim It is a process the learner can step through and predict. 4 The bill of materials for the test board. Static figure or text It is a reference table with no parameter or process. 5 How the choice of window changes spectral leakage when the signal frequency moves away from an exact FFT bin. MicroSim It is a dependence on two parameters, and the response is visual. 6 The author list and affiliations of the paper. Static figure or text It is a fact with no parameter or process. 7 The derivation of the Walden figure of merit from its definition. Static figure or text It is a short derivation with no parameter, and text with an equation serves it. 8 How the spread of residual offset across devices changes as the number of calibration bits increases. MicroSim It is a dependence on a parameter, and the distribution changes visibly.

Provenance: The criterion is from the sections "Communicating Research" and "MicroSims" of this chapter. The items are invented for illustration.

Rules: An item is a MicroSim when it has a parameter the learner can change, or a process the learner can step through or predict, and the response aids understanding. Otherwise it is static figure or text. Each item has exactly one correct answer.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads item 1 and the criterion.
  2. The learner chooses "MicroSim" or "static figure or text" and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence, naming the parameter or process where there is one.
  4. After item 8, the sim shows the count correct.

Feedback: Eight items, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "The better medium is ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct answer is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: Item 1 is shown with two choices. The question on screen is "Would a learner understand this better by changing something?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that an interactive simulation is the right medium when the point of the result is a dependence, and the wrong medium for a fact that has no parameter.

MicroSim: MicroSim Suitability Judge. Open it fullscreen.

docs.title: Embedding, Concept Dependencies, and Intelligent Textbooks
docs.text:
Embedding simulations is placing a MicroSim in a page, normally with an HTML iframe element that points at the sim's main.html. An iframe isolates the sim from the page, which is also a safety property: the sim's code cannot reach the rest of the page. The chapter pages of this book embed their sims with a relative path such as ../../sims/<sim-id>/main.html and add a link to open the sim fullscreen. The same sim can be embedded in a slide deck, a course page, or a paper's supplementary website without change. When you cite a sim in a paper, give its published address, and include the repository name in the address so that it can be found.

A concept dependency is the relation that one concept must be understood before another can be. A learning graph is a directed acyclic graph of concepts in which each edge is a concept dependency. It is the structure that decides the order of a course and, with the chapter's concept impact scores, how much space each concept deserves. This book is organized by one, and its chapters are the groupings of the graph's concepts in dependency order. The reused sim below lets you explore a graph of concept dependencies, including the difference between hard prerequisites and supporting ones.

docs.title: Diagram: Concept Dependencies Graph
docs.text:
Run the Concept Dependencies Graph MicroSim fullscreen

Concept Dependencies Graph (reused MicroSim)

Type: graph-model sim-id: concept-dependencies Library: vis-network Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/automating-instructional-design/sims/concept-dependencies/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/automating-instructional-design/tree/main/docs/sims/concept-dependencies Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: interpret Learning Objective: The learner will interpret a directed acyclic graph of concept dependencies, distinguishing hard prerequisites from supporting ones and tracing upstream and downstream concepts.

Reused from the MicroSim catalog (WHAT match score 0.86).

An intelligent textbook is a textbook whose content is interactive and, at higher levels, responsive to the reader. The author's classification of intelligent textbooks distinguishes five levels: static text (level 1), interactive content with MicroSims and learning graphs (level 2), adaptive content driven by student goals and progress (level 3), conversational tutoring (level 4), and autonomous generation of personalized instruction (level 5). This book sits at level 2, and it is organized so that the skills and records needed for level 3 could be added. Level 3 and above require storing student records, which raises privacy questions that the classification flags as a threshold.

Teaching from research is turning a result into instruction. The procedure follows the structure of this chapter. Choose one concept from your paper that a newcomer needs. Write the objective and the evidence of mastery. Check the catalog for an existing sim. Specify the one you need, build and verify it, and write a short lesson page that states the prerequisite, the activity, and what the learner should notice. The same sim then serves your talk, your group's onboarding, and your supplementary materials, and a result that others can manipulate is a result that others can build on.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Communicating a result well is choosing the medium that matches the point. When the point is a dependence, an interactive that lets the reader move the parameter does what a static figure cannot, and an agent can build it quickly from a precise specification that you check.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Research communication is shaped by the audience. A slide deck carries one message and needs a number check.
  • An interactive simulation suits a dependence or a process, and not a fact.
  • A MicroSim is small, single-concept, embeddable, and readable. p5.js with built-in controls is the usual library.
  • MicroSim generation is specification first: evidence of mastery, content, and rules, then search, generate, verify, and approve. Only a human marks a sim approved.
  • Embedding is an iframe with a relative path, and the sim is reusable across decks, pages, and papers.
  • Concept dependencies and learning graphs order a course, and intelligent textbooks range from static to autonomous, with student data privacy rising at the adaptive level.
  • Teaching from research turns one concept of a paper into an objective, a sim, and a lesson page.

From a Result to a Lesson

You can now say when a result deserves a simulation, read a p5.js sketch that shows a dependence, and write the specification, evidence, and checks from which an agent builds one. That gives a result a form that others can handle, not only read.

The next chapter returns to the question that runs under all of these: how do you know an AI-assisted result is right. Round up one result you are about to rely on, and bring it.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: MicroSims and Research Communication
docs.text: Test your understanding of research communication, slide decks, interactive simulations, MicroSims, p5.js, learning graphs, and intelligent textbooks with these 10 review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is the standard JavaScript library used in this book for building MicroSims?
docs.text:
1. p5.js
  2. D3.js
  3. React
  4. Three.js
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. p5.js is the library chosen for MicroSims in this book because it runs in the browser, needs no installation, and provides built-in controls. The other libraries are useful for other purposes but are not the standard here.

Concept Tested: p5.js

See: ./index.md#microsims

docs.title: 2. What is the term for placing a MicroSim in a web page using an HTML iframe that points at the sim's main.html?
docs.text:
1. Concept dependency
  2. Parameter sweep
  3. Handoff protocol
  4. Embedding simulations
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Embedding simulations means placing the sim in a page with an iframe, which isolates the sim from the surrounding page and lets the same sim be reused in decks, course pages, and papers.

Concept Tested: Embedding Simulations

See: ./index.md#embedding-concept-dependencies-and-intelligent-textbooks

docs.title: 3. Why is an interactive simulation a better choice than a static figure when showing how ENOB changes with added noise?
docs.text:
1. Because static figures cannot include numbers
  2. Because the relationship depends on a parameter the viewer can manipulate
  3. Because static figures cannot be included in papers
  4. Because interactive simulations are always easier to create
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A MicroSim suits a dependence: moving the noise slider shows the whole relationship. Static figures are fine for facts without parameters, and interactivity is not always easier to build.

Concept Tested: Interactive Simulation

See: ./index.md#communicating-research

docs.title: 4. Why should a MicroSim specification include evidence of mastery before any code is written?
docs.text:
1. Because the agent needs it to choose colors
  2. Because the evidence determines the file name
  3. Because the evidence defines what the sim must check to be useful
  4. Because the specification cannot be written without code
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Evidence of mastery states what the learner must be able to do and how the sim will detect it. Without that, the sim has no purpose and may become a toy. Colors and file names are secondary, and the specification precedes code.

Concept Tested: MicroSim Generation

See: ./index.md#generating-a-microsim-with-an-agent

docs.title: 5. What is the role of a learning graph in organizing an intelligent textbook?
docs.text:
1. It orders concepts by their dependencies
  2. It generates the MicroSim code automatically
  3. It replaces the need for written chapters
  4. It stores student data for adaptive content
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A learning graph is a directed acyclic graph of concepts in which edges are dependencies; it helps decide teaching order and how much space each concept deserves. It does not generate code, replace chapters, or store student data.

Concept Tested: Learning Graph

See: ./index.md#embedding-concept-dependencies-and-intelligent-textbooks

docs.title: 6. A slide deck is being prepared from a paper. What is the most important check to perform on the figures copied into the slides?
docs.text:
1. Make the slides mirror the paper's section order
  2. Run the number check on every figure to catch changed values
  3. Use screenshots instead of source figures
  4. Add as many words as possible to each slide
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Figures in slides are often copied and edited, so numbers can change silently. The number check of Chapter 15 should be run on every slide. Slides should carry one message with few words, and source figures are preferred over screenshots.

Concept Tested: Slide Deck

See: ./index.md#communicating-research

docs.title: 7. A researcher wants to teach how a SAR ADC's successive-approximation search converges bit by bit. Which medium is most appropriate?
docs.text:
1. A static table of digital codes
  2. A reference list
  3. A MicroSim that lets the learner step through the conversion
  4. A cover letter
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Bit-by-bit convergence is a process the learner can step through and predict, which is exactly what a MicroSim can make interactive. A static table, reference list, or cover letter does not show the process.

Concept Tested: MicroSim

See: ./index.md#microsims

docs.title: 8. An agent has implemented a MicroSim from a specification. What is the final step before learners use it?
docs.text:
1. Set the status to approved automatically
  2. Add the sim to the learning graph
  3. Skip verification if the sim looks right
  4. A person tests it and sets the status to approved
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Only a human author may mark a sim approved after testing the controls and behavior. Agents may set scaffold, built, or instrumented, but approval is a human gate.

Concept Tested: MicroSim Generation

See: ./index.md#generating-a-microsim-with-an-agent

docs.title: 9. A paper includes a die photograph of a fabricated converter. Why is this content not a good candidate for a MicroSim?
docs.text:
1. It is a single image with no parameter or process for the learner to manipulate
  2. Die photographs are too large to embed
  3. p5.js cannot display images
  4. MicroSims are only for electrical measurements
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A die photograph is a static fact with no parameter or process. A MicroSim earns its place when the viewer can change something or step through a process. Size and display capability are not the issues.

Concept Tested: Interactive Simulation

See: ./index.md#communicating-research

docs.title: 10. A researcher is deciding whether to build a MicroSim for the derivation of the Walden figure of merit. Why might a static figure or text be better?
docs.text:
1. The derivation is too complex for a simulation
  2. Students prefer reading equations
  3. The Walden figure of merit is not a real concept
  4. The derivation has no parameter to vary, so a short derivation in text serves it better
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A MicroSim suits dependencies or processes. A derivation with no variable parameter is better explained by text and equations. Complexity and student preference are not the deciding factors, and the Walden figure of merit is a real metric.

Concept Tested: MicroSim

See: ./index.md#microsims

docs.title: References: MicroSims and Research Communication
docs.text:
1. Scholarly communication - Wikipedia - Overview of how researchers produce, share, and evaluate results through journals, books, and open access. Relevant to the chapter's framing of research communication by audience, including peer review and publishing channels.

  2. Simulation - Wikipedia - Broad article on imitating real-world processes and systems with models, surveying types and uses in computing and education. Supports the chapter's case for interactive simulations that expose how a result depends on its parameters.

  3. Directed acyclic graph - Wikipedia - Explains graphs with directed edges and no cycles, with topological ordering and scheduling uses. Directly underpins the chapter's definition of a learning graph, where concept dependencies fix the order of a course.

  4. The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (2nd Edition) - Edward R. Tufte - Graphics Press - Introduces the data-ink ratio and small multiples as principles for honest, dense graphics. Useful for judging when a static figure suffices and when a result needs an interactive display.

  5. slide:ology: The Art and Science of Creating Great Presentations - Nancy Duarte - O'Reilly Media - Treats the slide deck as visual communication, with worked redesigns of cluttered slides. Chosen as a widely praised, clear guide to the one-message talk discussed here; no single originator is claimed.

  6. createSlider() reference - p5.js - Official documentation for the built-in slider control, with its min, max, value, and step parameters. The same function drives the ENOB sketch in this chapter, so it is the exact reference needed.

  7. p5.js Get Started tutorial - p5.js - Beginner walkthrough of the web editor, setup() and draw(), shapes, colors, and mouse interaction. Gives the minimum p5.js background for reading and checking agent-generated MicroSim code.

  8. iframe: The Inline Frame element - MDN Web Docs - Reference for embedding one HTML page in another, including sizing, title accessibility, and the sandbox attribute. Explains the mechanism and the safety property behind embedding simulations.

  9. MicroSims for Education - Dan McCreary - Project site defining MicroSims as small AI-generated, embeddable, open-source p5.js simulations, with sample sims and a metadata schema. The primary source for the chapter's MicroSim concept and generation workflow.

  10. Building Intelligent Textbooks With AI - Dan McCreary - Step-by-step guide to building MkDocs textbooks with MicroSims, glossaries, quizzes, and concept graphs, including the levels of intelligent textbooks. Supports the chapter's treatment of learning graphs and teaching from research.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers verification and validation as habits: independent checks, primary source checks, cross-model checks, test-driven research, and result replication. It addresses overconfidence and sycophancy in model output and builds audit trails and reproducibility packages. After this chapter you can decide whether an AI-assisted result meets the standard of your field.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 16 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Verification 56 Validation 1 Independent Check 8 Primary Source Check 1 Cross Model Check 1 Test Driven Research 1 Result Replication 1 Uncertainty Awareness 5 Overconfidence 1 Sycophancy 3 Output Bias 3 Audit Trail 10 Reproducibility Package 1 Peer Verification 1 Acceptance Review 1 Error Tracing 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 2: How Language Models Work
  • Chapter 3: Choosing Models and Writing Clear Prompts
  • Chapter 4: Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting
  • Chapter 6: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill
  • Chapter 10: Orchestrating Teams of Planning and Execution Agents
  • Chapter 11: AI-Assisted Literature Search and Synthesis
  • Chapter 13: Simulation, Testing, and Reproducible Code

Round Up the Evidence

Every earlier chapter had a check in it, and this chapter is where the checks become a standard you can state. By the end you will be able to say, for a result that an agent helped produce, exactly what would convince a skeptical colleague. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Verification and Validation
docs.text:
Two words that people often use interchangeably name different questions, and engineers already know the difference. Verification asks whether the work was done right: whether the code implements the formula, whether the computation matches the specification, whether the numbers in the paper are the numbers the script produced. Validation asks whether the right thing was done: whether the specification itself matches reality, whether the simulated circuit behaves as the fabricated one does, whether the result answers the research question. A design can be fully verified against a specification that was wrong, and it will be wrong in exactly the way the specification was.

Both matter for AI-assisted work, and they fail differently. Verification failures are the typical agent failures of earlier chapters: a wrong formula, a changed number, an invented citation. Validation failures are quieter. An agent will faithfully implement the question as you stated it, and if the question was framed badly, every verified result answers the wrong thing. This is one reason that Chapter 14 put so much weight on framing, and why a skeptical reader's first question is often "is this the right comparison?"

Verified Against What?

Notice that a verification always has an object: the specification, the standard, the primary source. When someone says "it was verified", ask against what. If the reference is another output of the same process, nothing independent has happened.

docs.title: Kinds of Checks
docs.text:
An independent check is a check whose failure causes are different from those of the thing being checked. That condition is what gives a check its power. Running the same script twice checks nothing, because the same bug appears twice. Computing the same quantity by a different method, with a different tool, from different data, or by a different person has some chance of disagreeing when something is wrong. Four kinds of independent check are especially useful with agents.

A primary source check is going to the original source to confirm a claim: the paper itself and not a summary of it, the datasheet and not a model's recollection of its limits, the standard and not a paraphrase of its requirement. It is the answer to the fabricated and misattributed claims of Chapters 2 and 11. It takes minutes when the agent supplied the location of every claim.

A cross-model check asks a different model, or a fresh session of the same one with none of the earlier context, to answer the same question or review the same output independently, and compares the answers. It is cheap and a good screen. Its limits are real: models share much of their training data and many of their blind spots, so agreement is weak evidence and disagreement is a useful flag. Use it to decide what to look at, and not to decide what is true.

A known-answer test, from Chapter 13, runs a method on an input whose answer you know independently. And a result replication, taken up below, reruns or repeats the work from the beginning.

A worked example, with illustrative numbers. An agent's script reports an ENOB of 9.4 bits for capture-07. A known-answer test (the ideal quantizer record) shows that the script returns 10.0 for a known 10-bit record, which verifies the implementation. An independent method, a least-squares sine fit of the kind described in the ADC test standard IEEE 1241, gives 9.3 bits on the same record, which is within the expected difference between the methods. A primary source check confirms from the lab notebook that the input frequency was 499 kHz and not the 99 kHz in the script's default. Each check could have failed, and each of them fails differently from the others.

Check What it guards against Cost Weakness Known-answer test Implementation errors Low once the test exists Only covers the input you tried Independent method Method-specific errors and shared assumptions Medium The two methods may share an input error Primary source check Misquotation, fabrication, outdated facts Low per claim Only as good as the source Cross-model check Gross errors, a screening aid Very low Shared blind spots Replication Non-reproducible results Medium to high Does not catch a wrong question

Table 1. Kinds of verification checks and what each one buys.

docs.title: Diagram: Verification Method Matcher
docs.text:
Verification Method Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: verification-method-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Built Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: recommend Learning Objective: The learner will recommend which of five verification methods best fits each of eight AI-assisted claims, with at least 7 of 8 matching the answer in Content.

Prerequisites: known-answer test, independent method, primary source check, cross-model check, and replication, all defined in the section "Kinds of Checks" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight claims the learner commits one of five methods. A method is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the table of methods is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Asking the same model again is an independent check. (2) A cross-model check proves a claim. (3) A single check method suits every claim.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to choose a method by what it guards against. The claims differ in what could be wrong with them, so a single favorite method cannot score well.

Content:

All claims are invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative". Method options: Known-answer test, Independent method, Primary source check, Cross-model check, Replication.

# Claim or situation Correct method Why (shown as feedback) 1 A script reports ENOB = 9.4 for capture-07, and you have never validated the script. Known-answer test Run it on a record whose ENOB you know, to check the implementation before trusting any real result. 2 A model's summary says Paper P reports 9.2 bits of ENOB at 1 MS/s. Primary source check The claim is about what a paper says, and only the paper can settle it. 3 The FFT-based ENOB is 9.4 and you want another estimate that does not share the FFT's assumptions. Independent method A different method, such as a sine fit, can disagree for different reasons. 4 An agent labeled 300 abstracts relevant or not, and you want a cheap screen for likely mislabels before sampling by hand. Cross-model check A second model's disagreement points to items worth reading, at very low cost. 5 A colleague wants to reuse your figure, and you must confirm it regenerates from raw data on a clean machine. Replication The question is whether the result can be reproduced from the raw inputs and code. 6 A model states "the standard requires jitter below 10 ps in section 4.3". Primary source check A requirement is quoted from a document, and the document must be read. 7 You doubt a simulation result because a model-written netlist might misstate a component value. Independent method A hand calculation of the expected value is a different route to the same quantity. 8 A result must hold for a different batch of devices before you publish a claim. Replication The claim is that the result recurs, which only another run can show.

Provenance: The five methods are from the section "Kinds of Checks" of this chapter. The claims are invented for illustration.

Rules: Each claim has exactly one correct method, chosen by what the claim could be wrong about: an implementation, a method, a quotation, a screening question, or recurrence.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads claim 1.
  2. The learner chooses one of the five methods and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence.
  4. After claim 8, the sim shows the count correct and groups the claims by method.

Feedback: Eight claims, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "The better fit is ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct method is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: Claim 1 is shown with five methods and none chosen. The question on screen is "What could be wrong with this claim, and which check would reveal it?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that an independent check has different failure causes from the thing checked, that cross-model agreement is weak evidence while disagreement is a useful flag, and that a primary source check is made against the original document.

MicroSim: Verification Method Matcher. Open it fullscreen.

docs.title: Working Test-First and Replicating
docs.text:
Test-driven research is the practice, borrowed from software, of deciding in advance what result would count as success or failure and writing it down before the experiment or analysis is run. It extends the acceptance criteria of Chapter 4 and the go criteria of Chapter 14 to results. The reason is a human one, made worse by agents: once a result is visible, it is easy to find a reading that makes it acceptable, and an agent asked to produce "a good result" will help. A criterion written first cannot be adjusted to fit.

Result replication is obtaining the result again. There are two levels, and both are worth distinguishing. Computational replication reruns your own analysis from the raw data in a clean environment, to confirm that the result is a property of the code and data and not of a leftover file or an unrecorded setting. Independent replication has another person, another instrument, or another dataset produce the result from the description, which also tests the description. The first is cheap and should be routine. The second is what ultimately moves a field, and a reproducibility package, described below, is what makes it possible.

docs.title: Behaviors of Models That Undermine Checks
docs.text:
Three tendencies of language models weaken verification when they are not recognized. They are properties of the models, not of any one product.

Uncertainty awareness is the discipline of stating how sure a result is, and asking for it. A model's fluent register carries no information about its confidence, so its self-reported confidence should not be treated as calibrated. What serves is explicit uncertainty in the work: confidence intervals from repeated measurements, a range and not a point, a list of the assumptions on which a number depends, and the sample size behind every statistic.

Overconfidence is the model's tendency to state conclusions with a certainty that its evidence does not support, including stating a specific figure where "unknown" would be correct. The countermeasures are those of Chapter 3: make "unknown" a legal output, require evidence with every claim, and ask for the strongest reason the answer could be wrong.

Sycophancy is the tendency to agree with the user, to tell them what they appear to want to hear, and to change an answer under pushback even when no new evidence has been given. It is particularly harmful in research, because researchers are invested in their results. A worked example: asked "I measured an ENOB of 9.5 bits, which looks great, doesn't it?", a model is likely to agree and elaborate. Asked "Here are the measurement conditions and the ENOB value. What are the three most likely reasons this number could be wrong?", the same model will produce something useful. The difference is in the framing. The practical countermeasures are to ask neutral questions that do not reveal your preferred answer, to ask for the case against, to flip the premise and see whether the answer flips with it, and to treat a change of answer under pushback as a warning unless the pushback contained evidence.

Output bias is a systematic tilt in what a model produces. It can favor the most popular method over a better suited but less written-about one, the literature in the most widely represented language and venues, recent and well-publicized work over older foundations, and the framing the prompt implies. It is hard to see from one answer. Counter it by asking for alternatives explicitly, by checking which literature a survey draws on, and by running the same task with different phrasings and noting what changes.

Flip the Premise

To test whether an answer reflects the evidence or your framing, ask the question again with the opposite premise: "I suspect this result is wrong. What supports that?" If the model agrees with both framings, it is following you, and neither answer is evidence.

docs.title: Diagram: Sycophancy Spotter
docs.text:
Sycophancy Spotter

Type: microsim sim-id: sycophancy-spotter Library: p5.js Status: Built Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish, among six exchanges between a researcher and a model, the replies that are sycophantic from those that are calibrated, with at least 5 of 6 classified correctly.
