docs.text: Course: AI for EE Research Analyzer: Course Description Analyzer v0.05 Source: Course Description

docs.title: Overall Score: 97/100
docs.text: Quality Rating: Excellent - Ready for learning graph generation

docs.title: Detailed Scoring Breakdown
docs.text: Element Points Possible Points Earned Notes Title 5 5 Clear title with subtitle Target Audience 5 5 Graduate students in EE, computer engineering and computer design; postdocs and faculty Prerequisites 5 5 Five concrete prerequisites; no ML background assumed Main Topics Covered 10 9 16 topics; above the 5-10 ideal, and topics 7 and 8 overlap Topics Excluded 5 5 Eight explicit boundaries Learning Outcomes Header 5 5 "After completing this course, students will be able to:" Remember Level 10 10 Six specific outcomes Understand Level 10 10 Six specific outcomes Apply Level 10 9 Outcomes are concrete but few name EE-specific tasks or tools (for example SPICE, HDL or MATLAB) Analyze Level 10 9 Five outcomes; the case-study analysis outcome does not yet name which case studies Evaluate Level 10 10 Five outcomes with clear criteria Create Level 10 10 Four outcomes plus a capstone project Descriptive Context 5 5 Three-paragraph overview with the orchestration vision Total 100 97

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
1. Topic count and overlap (-1). Topics 7 (planning and execution agents) and 8 (orchestration) cover closely related ground. They can stay separate for concept generation, but consider grouping the 16 topics under four or five themes for chapter planning.
  2. EE specificity in Apply (-1). The outcomes read as generally applicable to any research field. Adding two or three EE and computer-design tasks (for example generating a testbench, scripting a parameter sweep, or cleaning measurement data) would anchor the learning graph in the audience's domain.
  3. Named case studies in Analyze (-1). The case-study outcome refers to case studies generically. Naming them (for example the MicroSims arXiv paper and a specific intelligent textbook) would let the graph include concrete case-study concepts.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
Prioritized by their effect on concept generation:

  1. Add two or three EE or computer-design examples to the Apply level.
  2. Name the specific case studies once the talk content is final.
  3. Optionally add a short "Course Format" section (duration, hands-on versus lecture, expected tools). The rubric does not score it, but it helps chapter design.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
Estimated concepts: about 220-260.

  • 16 topics at an average of 12-16 concepts each gives roughly 190-260 concepts.
  • Six Bloom's levels with 4-6 outcomes each suggest a healthy mix of vocabulary, procedural, and evaluative concepts.
  • Topics 4 and 5 (Markdown and skills) and topic 14 (verification) are the densest and are likely to produce the most concepts.
  • Likely to fall short only if the case-study chapter stays generic.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Score is at or above 85, so the course description is ready for learning graph generation. Recommended next skill: learning-graph-generator.

docs.title: LinkedIn Announcement
docs.text:
This Friday, Oct 23, I’m speaking at the University of Minnesota in the monthly departmental workshop on AI for Research Productivity, organized by [Gang Qiu] and [Prof. Katie Zhao].

My talk: “From Researcher to Orchestrator: Managing a Team of AI Agents for Research.”

What if every researcher managed a team of 30 AI agents? About 20 planning agents that explore the literature and draft specifications, and 10 execution agents that write code, run analyses, and build simulations. The researcher’s job shifts from doing every task to setting direction, supplying domain judgment, and reviewing results.

I’ll cover:

  • Meet Volt, our guide, and the many kinds of “chat” agents
  • Task-completion time horizons, a Moore’s Law for agentic capability
  • Agent skills that turn a repeatable task into a one-line command
  • A personal knowledge graph that keeps every agent aligned
  • The security, ethics, and legal questions we can’t skip

This presentation is backed by a free, open, interactive textbook with 20 chapters, MicroSims, and infographic posters. And yes, the first draft of the textbook was built with AI agents. The human stays accountable for the science.

  • Akerman Hall, Room 319, University of Minnesota (110 Union St SE, Minneapolis)
  • The talk starts at 11:00 AM CT and it will be followed with a discussion

Please DM me if you want a draft of my slides and a link to the new textbook on agents for research. Feedback appreciated!

docs.title: Instructor's Guide
docs.text:
Welcome to the instructor's guide for AI for EE Research: From Researcher to Orchestrator. This guide explains every part of the textbook, how to use each part in a graduate course, seminar, or workshop series, and how to adapt the book for your own students. No prior knowledge of web publishing or learning analytics is assumed. Each technical term is defined before it is used.

The book is written for graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, and for postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research. You may be teaching it as a for-credit course, running it as a lab-group reading series, or working through it yourself before you introduce it to your group. The guide covers all three.

docs.title: What Is an Intelligent Textbook?
docs.text: An intelligent textbook is a digital textbook that goes beyond static text and images. It includes interactive simulations, self-check quizzes, a searchable glossary, and a structured map of how concepts depend on each other. The aim is to let students practice the judgments a subject requires, not only read about them.

docs.title: The Five Levels of Intelligent Textbooks
docs.text:
Intelligent textbooks are grouped into five levels by how interactive and adaptive they are:

Level Name Description Example Features Level 1 Static Digital A PDF or basic web version of a print textbook Text and images only, no interactivity Level 2 Interactive Adds simulations, quizzes, and searchable glossaries MicroSims, self-check quizzes, concept search Level 3 Adaptive Adjusts content based on student performance Personalized learning paths, difficulty adjustment Level 4 AI-Assisted Includes an AI tutor that answers student questions Chatbot integration, automated feedback Level 5 Fully Adaptive AI Learns from student interactions and optimizes the experience Real-time content generation, predictive analytics

This textbook is a Level 2 intelligent textbook. It has 50 MicroSims, 20 chapter quizzes, a 379-term glossary, and an interactive learning graph. It also lays groundwork for Level 3: 47 of its MicroSims are instrumented to record learning events in a standard format (see Analytics and Learning Records), although the book does not yet adapt itself to each learner.

docs.title: What Makes This Textbook Different
docs.text:
• The researcher as orchestrator. The book is organized around one idea: the researcher's job is shifting from doing every task personally to directing a team of roughly 20 planning agents and 10 execution agents, while staying accountable for the science.
  • Verification on every page. Every chapter trains students to check AI output before trusting it: citations against primary sources, numbers against sanity checks, code against tests. The book's catchphrase is "Trust, but verify!"
  • Two concrete building blocks. Students learn to capture project knowledge in plain Markdown files and to turn repeatable research tasks into tested agent skills, which are packaged instructions an AI agent can load and follow as a single command.
  • Practice, not only reading. 50 MicroSims and 25 interactive infographic posters let students sort, judge, calculate, and explore. Most of them train decisions, such as whether a citation is real or whether an agent should be allowed to act without approval.
  • A learning graph maps all 379 concepts and the 670 dependencies between them, so every concept is introduced after its prerequisites.
  • Volt the Border Collie, a mascot character (a "pedagogical agent"), guides students through each chapter with insights, tips, warnings, and encouragement.
  • Free and open. The book is licensed under Creative Commons for non-commercial use. There are no paywalls or access codes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The course description assumes students have:

  • Graduate standing, or equivalent research experience, in electrical engineering, computer engineering, or a related field
  • Working knowledge of at least one programming language, preferably Python
  • Basic comfort with a command line, a text editor, and Git
  • Experience writing a technical paper or report

No prior machine learning, prompt engineering, or agent experience is required. The book does not teach model training, machine learning theory, or EE domain theory. It assumes students bring their own research problems and domain knowledge.

If some students are new to Git or the command line, schedule a short lab session before Chapter 5. Chapter 5 teaches the Git practices the rest of the book relies on, but it moves quickly for someone who has never opened a terminal.

docs.title: Tools and Accounts Students Will Need
docs.text:
The tools students need grow as the book progresses.

Chapters What students need 1–4 A chat interface to at least one large language model. API access (programmatic access to a model from a script) is useful from Chapter 3 onward, where students price a batch job. 5–7 Git, a GitHub account, a text editor, and an AI coding agent: a tool that reads project files and runs commands on the student's behalf, such as Claude Code or OpenAI Codex. Agents read the project instruction files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) taught in Chapter 5. 8–15 The same coding agent, plus Python with the usual scientific libraries for Chapters 12–13. 16–20 A browser for MicroSims. Chapter 19's always-on personal agents are best demonstrated by the instructor rather than required of every student.

Before the term starts, decide three things:

  1. Which tools are approved. Many universities license specific AI tools with data-protection terms that consumer accounts lack. Check what your institution provides before you ask students to sign up for anything.
  2. Who pays. Paid subscriptions and API usage cost money. Chapter 3 shows how to estimate the cost of a batch from token counts. Set a per-student budget, or provide shared credits, so that no student is disadvantaged by the tool they can afford.
  3. What data may go where. See the next section.

docs.title: Setting a Course AI-Use and Data Policy
docs.text:
A course that teaches AI use needs its own written policy on day one. Base it on Chapter 18: Responsible and Ethical Use of AI and your institution's rules, and cover at least:

  • Data classes. Which kinds of data students may send to which tools. Unpublished results, collaborators' data, data under a non-disclosure agreement, export-controlled designs, and personal data about human subjects usually belong in the most restricted class. The Data Sensitivity Sorter MicroSim is a good first-week exercise for this.
  • Disclosure. Ask for a short AI-use disclosure statement on every assignment, in the form Chapter 18 teaches.
  • Evidence of verification. Ask students to keep agent logs or a decision log, and to show at least one independent check for each AI-assisted result they submit.
  • Authorship. The researcher stays accountable. AI output a student submits is the student's responsibility, including any fabricated citation it contains.

docs.title: Suggested Pacing
docs.text:
The book has 20 chapters in five parts:

Part Chapters Topic Area 1. Foundations 1–4 Research workflows and the orchestrator idea, how language models work, choosing models and writing prompts, context engineering 2. Memory and skills 5–7 Markdown project files and Git, knowledge bases and personal knowledge graphs, designing and testing agent skills 3. Agents and teams 8–10 Agents and tool use, supervising agents and defining roles, orchestrating planning and execution agents 4. Research tasks 11–15 Literature search, data analysis, simulation and testing, brainstorming and problem framing, manuscript preparation 5. Communicate and trust 16–20 MicroSims and research communication, verification and reproducibility, responsible use, always-on personal agents, case studies and capstone

Most chapters run 4,000 to 5,000 words including their MicroSim specifications. Chapter 1 is about twice that length, because it introduces the vocabulary the rest of the book uses.

A 15-week semester fits the book well, with capstone milestones placed so that each one uses what the class has just learned:

Week Chapters Capstone milestone 1 1 Each student picks a small, real research task from their own work 2 2–3 3 4 Research question with a metric, a threshold, and acceptance criteria 4 5 Version-controlled repository with a project instruction file 5 6 Knowledge base and decision log 6 7 One tested agent skill 7 8 8 9–10 One-page agent team design with roles, autonomy levels, and review points 9 11 Annotated reading list with verified citations 10 12–13 Analysis or simulation code with tests 11 14 12 15 Draft paper section in the student's own voice 13 16–17 Reproducibility package checked on a clean machine 14 18–19 Data classification and disclosure statement 15 20 Capstone presentations

For a 10-week quarter, cover one part every two weeks and drop Chapter 19 or assign it as reading. For a five-session workshop, give one session to each part, demonstrate the MicroSims live, and replace the capstone with a single skill that each participant builds for their own work.

docs.title: What Each Chapter Contains
docs.text:
Every chapter follows the same structure:

  1. Front matter. Metadata at the top of the file (title, description, version). Students don't see it; the website builder and search engines use it.
  2. Summary. A short overview of what the chapter covers and what students will be able to do afterward.
  3. Concepts Covered. A table of the learning-graph concepts the chapter teaches, each with a Concept Impact Score. The score measures how much of the rest of the learning graph builds on that concept, directly or through other concepts. A high score marks a foundational concept that deserves extra class time.
  4. Prerequisites. Links to the earlier chapters the chapter depends on.
  5. Welcome from Volt. A short opening that tells students why the chapter matters to their research.
  6. Main content. The instruction itself, with worked examples drawn from EE research, tables, equations, and embedded MicroSims.
  7. Volt's admonitions. Colored callout boxes that highlight key ideas, practical tips, common mistakes, and encouragement on harder passages.
  8. Summary and Key Takeaways. A bulleted list of the points to carry forward, followed by a closing celebration from Volt.
  9. Annotated References and Quiz. Each chapter has a separate references page and a separate quiz page, listed under the chapter in the left navigation.

The chapters do not include end-of-chapter exercises. The MicroSims, the quizzes, and the capstone milestones fill that role. Add your own discussion questions where your students need them.

docs.title: Suggested Class Use
docs.text:
• Before class. Assign the chapter and ask students to run its MicroSims, which are interleaved with the reading. Ask them to bring one question and one place where they would want to verify the chapter's advice on their own work.
  • During class. Do live demonstrations with a real agent on a real task from the chapter. The most useful demonstrations include a failure: a fabricated citation, a script that runs but gives the wrong answer, or a prompt that the model misreads. Then have students apply the chapter to their own research task in pairs.
  • After class. Assign the quiz as a self-check and the week's capstone milestone as the graded work.

docs.title: What Is a MicroSim?
docs.text:
A MicroSim (short for "micro-simulation") is a small, interactive program that runs directly in a web browser. Students install nothing; any modern browser (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) will do.

Most MicroSims in this book train judgment rather than simulate physics. They present a realistic research scenario, ask the student to make a decision, and then explain the right answer and why. The list of all 50 is on the MicroSims page.

docs.title: How MicroSims Are Embedded
docs.text:
MicroSims appear inside chapter pages as rectangular interactive areas. They are embedded with an iframe, a web feature that displays one web page inside another. Below each one is a link to open it fullscreen, which is the better choice on a projector.

Just above each MicroSim in a chapter is a collapsible block labeled with the MicroSim's name. Click it to see the full specification: the learning objective, the scenario content and where it came from, the rules, the learner activity, the feedback, and the starting state. These specifications are useful for lesson planning and for understanding why the MicroSim asks what it asks.

docs.title: Kinds of MicroSims
docs.text:
Kind What students do Examples Sorters Place items into categories Research Task Sorter, Prompt Component Sorter, Falsifiable Hypothesis Sorter Judges and spotters Decide whether something is acceptable, and why Citation Verification Judge, Agent Permission Boundary Judge, Sycophancy Spotter Calculators Change inputs and watch a budget or load respond Context Window Budget Calculator, Orchestrator Review Load Calculator Explorers Adjust a parameter and observe a model's behavior Temperature Next-Token Explorer, Search Precision and Recall Explorer Builders and steppers Assemble a plan or step through a process Research Task Decomposition Builder, Agent Loop Stepper Graphs Explore connected entities Learning Graph Viewer, Citation Chaining Explorer, Personal Knowledge Graph Query Explorer

The MicroSims are built with four JavaScript libraries. 41 use p5.js, a library for interactive drawings with sliders and buttons. 7 use vis-network, a library for network diagrams. One uses Chart.js for charts (Projecting AI Task Completion to 2030) and one uses Mermaid for flow diagrams (Research Workflow Handoffs). You don't need to know any of these libraries to use the MicroSims in class.

docs.title: Lesson Plans
docs.text: Each MicroSim's own page (reach it from the MicroSims list) has a Lesson Plan section with a learning objective, the Bloom's Taxonomy level it targets, the intended audience, a suggested duration, prerequisites, activities, and an assessment. Most of the lesson plans that state a Bloom level target Analyze or Evaluate, the levels the quizzes cover least.

docs.title: Tips for Using MicroSims in Class
docs.text:
1. Ask for predictions first. Before revealing an answer, have students commit to theirs and say why. The explanations are more useful to a student who has just been wrong.
  2. Argue the hard items. In the judge and sorter MicroSims, some items are deliberately borderline. Pause on an item the class splits on and have each side make its case before you reveal the answer.
  3. Connect to the student's own work. After a MicroSim, ask students to find one example of the same judgment in their own research.
  4. Let students explore on their own. After a demonstration, give students five to ten minutes on their own devices. Use the MicroSim's restart control, or reload the page, to run it again.
  5. Plan for an internet connection. MicroSims load from the published website. If your room has unreliable internet, build a local copy of the site (see Customizing Your Own Copy).

Embed MicroSims in Your LMS or Course Page

You can add any MicroSim to any web page you control, such as a Canvas or Moodle page, a Google Site, or a plain HTML file, by pasting one iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-for-ee-research/sims/YOUR-MICROSIM-NAME/main.html"
    width="100%" height="600px" scrolling="no">
</iframe>

Replace YOUR-MICROSIM-NAME with the folder name of any MicroSim from the MicroSims list, such as citation-verification-judge. MicroSims differ in height, so copy the exact code from the Iframe Embed Code section on the MicroSim's own page.

docs.title: Using the Infographic Posters
docs.text:
The Posters section has 25 full-width interactive infographics. Most set a risky way of working beside a controlled one, so the difference is visible at a glance: "The Real Citation and the Fluent Fake", "Verified Is Not Validated", "Where Does Your Data Go?". Students hover over or click a region to read what it shows, then switch to Quiz mode to test themselves.

Posters work well as the first slide of a class, as a prompt for a five-minute discussion, or as a review before a quiz. Several posters, such as "Meet Your Agent Team" and "Five Personal Agents, Side by Side", summarize material from the appendices.

docs.title: Using the Slide Decks
docs.text:
The Slides section has two decks built with MARP, a tool that turns Markdown files into presentations:

  • Overview (Static) is a 20-slide tour of the whole book: the orchestrator idea, the five parts, and the key takeaways of all 20 chapters. Use it on the first day of class.
  • Overview (MicroSims) is a talk on AI for research productivity that embeds live MicroSims and posters. Use it to introduce the course to a department or a lab group.

docs.title: Using the Glossary
docs.text:
The Glossary defines all 379 concepts in the learning graph, one term per concept, in alphabetical order. Definitions follow the ISO 11179 standard for good definitions: precise, concise, distinct from one another, and never circular. Every entry includes a short example, and most include "See also" links to related terms.

Students can find a term by clicking Glossary in the left navigation and using the browser's find command (Ctrl+F on Windows and Linux, Cmd+F on Mac), or by using the search bar at the top of any page.

Ways to use the glossary in class:

  • Vocabulary preview. Before a chapter, have students read the glossary entries for the concepts in its Concepts Covered table.
  • Definitions in their own words. After a chapter, have students write their own definitions and compare them with the glossary. Differences often expose a misunderstanding.
  • Shared language for a lab. Research groups adopting agents often use the same words for different things. The glossary gives the group a common vocabulary for terms such as subagent, skill, and approval gate.

docs.title: How the Quizzes Work
docs.text:
Each chapter has a quiz page with 10 multiple-choice questions, 200 in all. Students open a quiz from the Quiz link under each chapter in the left navigation. Each question has a collapsible Show Answer block that reveals the correct answer, an explanation of the choices, the concept being tested, and a link back to the section of the chapter that teaches it.

The quizzes are self-check tools. They are not graded automatically and do not record scores. Use them for formative assessment, meaning feedback during learning, rather than for grades.

Ways to use the quizzes:

  • Exit ticket. Use a few questions at the end of class as a quick check for understanding.
  • Diagnostic. Give the quiz before the chapter to find out what students already know.
  • Re-teaching guide. The "See" link in each answer points to the section to revisit.
  • Question bank. All 200 questions are also in one machine-readable file, quiz-bank.json, which is a convenient starting point for building your own exams or importing questions into your learning management system. The questions are openly licensed (see Understanding the License).

docs.title: Bloom's Taxonomy Levels
docs.text:
Bloom's Taxonomy is a framework that classifies thinking skills from simple to complex. The 2001 revision, which this book uses, has six levels:

Level Name What It Means Example Verbs L1 Remember Recall facts and definitions Define, list, name L2 Understand Explain ideas in your own words Explain, describe, summarize L3 Apply Use a procedure in a new situation Calculate, write, use L4 Analyze Break material into parts and see how they relate Distinguish, compare, trace L5 Evaluate Make judgments against criteria Verify, judge, critique L6 Create Put parts together into something new Design, build, develop

The quiz generation report shows the quiz questions spread across the first four levels: 31.5% Remember, 31.5% Understand, 27% Apply, and 10% Analyze. The higher levels are assessed elsewhere. The judge MicroSims target Evaluate, and the capstone project targets Create. A complete assessment plan uses all three: quizzes for vocabulary and mechanics, MicroSims for judgment, and the capstone for synthesis.

docs.title: Using the Annotated References
docs.text: Each chapter has an Annotated References page with 10 curated sources, 200 in all. Each entry gives the title, a link where one exists, and a short note on why the source is useful and how it connects to the chapter. The sources mix Wikipedia articles (stable and accessible), textbooks known for clear explanations, foundational research papers on arXiv, and official documentation from AI tool vendors.

docs.title: A Note About Link Rot
docs.text:
Link rot is when a web link stops working because the page has been moved, renamed, or deleted. Wikipedia and arXiv links are very stable. Vendor documentation is not: AI companies reorganize their documentation sites often. If you or your students find a broken link:

  1. Search for the article title on the source website.
  2. Look for an archived copy on the Wayback Machine.
  3. Report the broken link (see Feedback).

docs.title: Using the Appendices
docs.text:
The Appendices hold reference material that supports several chapters:

  • Agent Personas describes seven sample agents a researcher might direct, from Ada the chief of staff to specialists for grant writing, budgets, and conferences. Use them as models when students write the team design for their capstone.
  • Personal Agent Software collects research notes on the always-on personal agents surveyed in Chapter 19.
  • Agent Email collects research notes on whether personal agents can have their own email address or text-messaging channel.
  • Personal Knowledge Graphs summarizes the author's earlier research on personal knowledge graphs and on integrating them into an organization, background for Chapters 6 and 19.

The two personal-agent appendices are dated research notes, built mostly from vendor announcements and press coverage rather than independent tests. Present them to students that way.

Check Chapter 19 Before You Teach It

Personal agent products change monthly. Chapter 19 teaches durable criteria for choosing and supervising any personal agent: where it runs, what it can reach, how approvals work, what it costs, and what happens to research data. The product details are a snapshot. Before teaching the chapter, check the current state of each product and tell students which details have changed.

docs.title: The Capstone Project
docs.text:
The capstone, described in Chapter 20, asks each student to plan and run a real research task from their own work with a coordinated team of agents, then present the verified results with an honest account of where human judgment was needed. Its eight deliverables are a question with acceptance criteria, a version-controlled project with memory, a team design, at least one tested skill, verified results, a reproducibility package, a responsible-use statement, and an account of judgment.

Chapter 20 includes a rubric with seven criteria and leaves the weights to you. Three suggestions from teaching this kind of project:

  • Keep the task small. A good capstone task is one the student could finish by hand in about a week. The point is the process, not the size of the result.
  • Stage it across the term. Each deliverable maps to earlier chapters. The milestones in the pacing table let students build the capstone one piece at a time instead of all at the end.
  • Require a rejected output. Ask each student to show at least one agent output they rejected and explain why. It is the most direct evidence that the student is judging the work rather than accepting it.

docs.title: A Sample Skill-Creation Prompt
docs.text: Sample Skill Creation Prompt shows a prompt the author used to have an agent build a skill that produces an arXiv paper as LaTeX source with a PDF build process. The prompt points the agent at sample papers, tells it to keep asking clarifying questions until it has enough material, and asks it to create a 1-to-100 scoring rubric for judging whether a paper is ready. Show it alongside Chapter 7, then have students write a prompt of the same shape for a repeatable task from their own research.

docs.title: What Is a Learning Graph?
docs.text:
A learning graph is a map of how the concepts in a book depend on each other. It is a directed acyclic graph (DAG): a network in which each arrow points from a concept to a concept it depends on, and in which no chain of arrows ever loops back to where it started. This book's graph has 379 concepts, 670 dependencies, and 17 taxonomy categories, such as Prompting and Context Engineering, Agent Skills, and Verification and Reproducibility.

The Learning Graph Viewer shows the whole graph. You can search for a concept, filter by category, and see how each concept connects to the others. The Learning Graph introduction explains how the graph was built from the course description.

docs.title: How Instructors Can Use the Learning Graph
docs.text:
• Check prerequisites. Before teaching a concept, confirm that students have covered the concepts it depends on.
  • Diagnose gaps. When a student struggles with a concept, follow its dependencies back to find the missing foundation.
  • Map your curriculum. Compare the concept list with your existing syllabus to find what each covers that the other does not.
  • Reorder with care. If you teach chapters in a different order, use the graph to check that you haven't moved a concept ahead of one of its prerequisites.

docs.title: What Is a Pedagogical Agent?
docs.text:
A pedagogical agent is a character that appears throughout a textbook to guide students. Research on pedagogical agents finds that a well-used character can raise student engagement and students' sense of how much they learned, an effect known as the persona effect.

This book's agent is Volt, a black-and-white Border Collie with a maroon bandana and a gold whistle. Border Collies herd, and Volt treats AI agents the same way: as a flock to be directed and checked, never trusted blindly. Volt is patient, precise, curious, and dry-witted, and often closes with a concrete question such as "How would you check that?" Volt has no gender; the book refers to Volt by name or as they.

docs.title: How Volt Appears
docs.text:
Volt appears in colored callout boxes, called admonitions, inside the chapters. There are seven kinds:

Kind Color Purpose How often Welcome Maroon Tells students why the chapter matters Once, at the start of every chapter Thinking Gold Highlights a key idea or mental model 1 to 4 per chapter Tip Teal Shares a practical shortcut Where the material calls for one Warning Red Flags a common mistake Where the material calls for one Encourage Blue Supports students on a hard passage Where students may struggle Celebration Purple Marks what students can now do At most once, at the end of a chapter Neutral Gray A general aside Rarely

The number of Volt admonitions in a chapter scales with the number of concepts it covers, and two admonitions never appear back to back. Each one carries a message the surrounding text does not, so none of them are decorative. The Mascot Rendering Test page shows every kind.

This instructor's guide and other instructor-facing pages do not use Volt.

docs.title: Tips for Instructors
docs.text:
• Use the thinking admonitions as discussion prompts. They mark the ideas the chapter considers most important.
  • Point students to the warning admonitions before assignments. They name the mistakes students are most likely to make.
  • Use "Trust, but verify!" as a class norm. When a student reports an AI result, ask Volt's question: "Who checked the output?"

docs.title: Reporting Problems and Suggestions
docs.text:
This book is an open-source project hosted on GitHub, a website where software and writing projects are developed in the open. You don't need to know programming to report a problem.

A GitHub Issue is like a support ticket: a numbered, public report of a problem or a suggestion that the author and others can discuss. To submit one:

  1. Go to the book's repository at github.com/dmccreary/ai-for-ee-research.
  2. Click the Issues tab, then the green New issue button.
  3. Give the issue a clear title, such as "Broken link in Chapter 11 references" or "Suggestion: MicroSim for parameter sweeps".
  4. In the description, say which page has the problem, what you expected to see, what you saw instead, and your browser and device if they matter.
  5. Click Submit new issue.

You need a free GitHub account to submit an issue. If you would rather not create one, use the Contact page.

Feedback that helps most:

  • Errors. Factual mistakes, typos, and broken formatting
  • Broken links
  • MicroSim bugs. Simulations that don't load or that behave unexpectedly
  • Outdated tool details. AI products change quickly, and reports of what has changed are especially welcome
  • Accessibility problems. Content that is hard to read or navigate for students with disabilities
  • Teaching reports. What worked and what didn't when you taught a chapter

docs.title: What Is a Creative Commons License?
docs.text: A license is a legal document that says what others may do with a work. A Creative Commons (CC) license is a standard, widely used license for educational and creative work that states those permissions in plain terms.

docs.title: This Textbook's License
docs.text:
This textbook uses the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license:

Code Full Name What It Means CC Creative Commons A standard open license BY Attribution You must credit the original author NC NonCommercial You may not use the material for commercial purposes SA ShareAlike If you adapt the material, you must share your version under the same license 4.0 Version 4.0 The current version of the license

docs.title: What You Can Do
docs.text:
• Copy the whole book or individual chapters for your students
  • Share the book with colleagues, students, and lab members
  • Print chapters for classroom use
  • Adapt the content: add your own examples, remove sections, or reorder chapters
  • Translate the content into other languages
  • Build a derivative course, such as a version focused on your own subfield

docs.title: What You Cannot Do
docs.text:
• Sell the book or charge students for access to it
  • Remove the attribution to the original author, Dan McCreary
  • Change the license of a version you adapt and share: it must stay CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
  • Present it as your own work

For the full terms, see the License page. Commercial rights are reserved by the author; the License page explains how to ask about commercial use.

docs.title: Customizing Your Own Copy
docs.text: You can publish your own version of the book, for example with examples from your subfield, a different chapter order, or your institution's AI-use policy added. This section walks through the steps.

docs.title: Key Technical Terms
docs.text:
• Repository (repo). A folder on GitHub that holds all of a project's files and their history.
  • Git. A version-control tool that tracks every change to a set of files. Chapter 5 of this book teaches it.
  • Fork. A complete copy of someone else's repository in your own GitHub account.
  • Clone. A complete copy of a repository on your own computer.
  • Markdown. A plain-text formatting language. **bold** makes bold, # Heading makes a heading, and - starts a bullet point. Every page of this book is a Markdown file.
  • MkDocs. The program that turns the book's Markdown files into a website. The book uses the Material for MkDocs theme.
  • mkdocs.yml. The main configuration file for the website. It sets the title, the navigation menu, and which features are on.

docs.title: Step 1: Fork or Clone the Repository
docs.text:
If you don't have a GitHub account, create a free one at github.com.

Option A: Fork (stays on GitHub). Go to github.com/dmccreary/ai-for-ee-research and click Fork in the upper-right corner. This puts a copy in your account that you can edit in the browser.

Option B: Clone (works on your computer). Install Git from git-scm.com, open a terminal, and run:

git clone https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-for-ee-research.git

docs.title: Step 2: Make Your Changes
docs.text:
All content is in the docs/ folder as Markdown (.md) files, which you can edit in any text editor. Chapters are in docs/chapters/, one folder per chapter. MicroSims are in docs/sims/, one folder per MicroSim.

If you use an AI agent to help edit, have it read AGENTS.md and CONTENT-GENERATION-GUIDE.md in the repository first. They hold the rules the book was written to, including the formatting rules that keep pages from breaking.

Title and author. Edit these lines near the top of mkdocs.yml:

site_name: 'Your Course Title'
site_description: 'Your description here'
site_author: 'Your Name'
site_url: 'https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/ai-for-ee-research/'

Colors. The book uses University of Minnesota maroon and gold. Material for MkDocs has no built-in maroon or gold, so mkdocs.yml sets the palette to custom and the actual colors live at the top of docs/css/extra.css:

[data-md-color-primary="custom"] {
  --md-primary-fg-color:        #7A0019;   /* change to your primary color */
  --md-primary-fg-color--light: #9E2A3F;
  --md-primary-fg-color--dark:  #5B0013;
}

The accent color is set in the same block, and Volt's callout colors are in docs/css/mascot.css.

Logo. The header logo is Volt's neutral pose, set by logo: img/mascot/neutral.png in the theme: section of mkdocs.yml. Point it at your own image, about 128 by 128 pixels in PNG format.

Navigation. The left-hand menu is the nav: section of mkdocs.yml. A page that is not listed there does not appear in the menu.

docs.title: Step 3: Preview Your Changes
docs.text:
1. Install Python 3.8 or newer from python.org.

  2. Install MkDocs and the Material theme:

    pip install mkdocs mkdocs-material

  3. In the project folder, start the preview server:

    mkdocs serve

  4. Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ai-for-ee-research/ in your browser.

The preview server watches for changes. When you save a Markdown file, the page refreshes in the browser. A local preview also serves the MicroSims, which is useful in a room with unreliable internet.

docs.title: Step 4: Publish Your Version
docs.text:
To publish your version as a free website on GitHub Pages, run:

mkdocs gh-deploy

This builds the site and publishes it at https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/ai-for-ee-research/. It usually takes a minute or two to appear.

docs.title: Web Analytics
docs.text:
Web analytics measures how visitors use a website: which pages they visit, how long they stay, and where they come from. For a course, it shows which chapters students actually read and which MicroSims they open.

The published book does not currently include web analytics. To add Google Analytics, Google's free analytics service, to your own copy:

  1. Sign in at analytics.google.com and create a new property, Google's term for a tracked website.
  2. Copy the Measurement ID Google gives you. It looks like G-XXXXXXXXXX.

  3. At the bottom of mkdocs.yml, uncomment the analytics block and add your ID:

    extra:
  analytics:
    provider: google
    property: G-XXXXXXXXXX

  4. Rebuild and publish the site. Data usually starts to appear within a day or two.

What you can learn from it:

  • Which chapters and MicroSims get the most and least use, which shows where students may be skipping content
  • Time on page, where a long time can mean engagement or confusion
  • Devices, such as how many students read on phones
  • Site searches, which show the terms students look for

docs.title: xAPI Learning Records
docs.text:
xAPI (the Experience API, also called Tin Can) is a standard format for recording specific learning activities, not just page views. An xAPI record is a short statement of the form actor, verb, object, such as "a learner answered item 3 of the Prompt Component Sorter correctly". A Learning Record Store (LRS) is a database that collects and stores these statements.

47 of this book's 50 MicroSims are instrumented to produce xAPI statements. By default each MicroSim produces one compact summary statement per session rather than a statement for every click. As published, the book is not connected to an LRS, so the statements are built in the student's browser and go nowhere else. Connecting an LRS is a step for a technical team, and the settings for the whole book live in docs/js/lrs-config.js.

You can see what a MicroSim records without any of that setup. Add ?xapi=teaching to the end of a MicroSim's address, for example:

https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-for-ee-research/sims/prompt-component-sorter/?xapi=teaching

The MicroSim then shows a panel with each statement as it is produced. This makes a good live demonstration for Chapter 18's discussion of what data tools collect about their users.

docs.title: Privacy and Regulatory Considerations
docs.text:
Before collecting learning data that identifies individual students, check the rules that apply to you:

  • FERPA (Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act) is the U.S. federal law that protects student education records. It applies to graduate students as well as undergraduates.
  • GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) is the European Union's data-protection law. It applies if any of your students are in the EU.
  • State and institutional rules. Many U.S. states and most universities add their own student-privacy requirements.
  • Research ethics review. If you plan to publish findings based on your students' learning data, you will usually need approval from your Institutional Review Board (IRB) before you collect it.

The safest default is aggregate, anonymous measurement: Google Analytics counts page views, not named students. If you want records for individual students through xAPI, talk to your institution's data privacy officer first.

docs.title: Building a Progress Dashboard
docs.text: With an LRS connected, it becomes possible to build a dashboard of student progress: which chapters each student has completed, MicroSim results over time, and which concepts need re-teaching. Building one takes programming and careful attention to privacy, and it is beyond the scope of this guide. Because the book and its learning graph are open, all the data structures needed for such a dashboard are available to build on.

docs.title: Sample Skill Creation Prompt
docs.text:
Prompt

Use the /skill-creator skill to create a new skill for generating a paper in the ArXiV format. The skill will create a new folder in a github repo project "papers" (plural) directory to store the paper. The paper will consist the proper LeTeX files and a build process to create a high quality PDF file of the paper. Use the following samples:

/Users/dan/projects/microsims/paper

/Users/dan/projects/intelligent-textbooks/papers/five-levels

/Users/dan/projects/intelligent-textbooks/papers/self-improving-textbooks

If the user does not provide you with sufficient information, continue to ask clarifying questions until you are confident you have enough content to generate a high quality paper.

Create a scoring rubric of 1 to 100 to judge if the paper has enough content to be consider a high quality paper. Include things like a clear tile, abstract, references, figures and other sections required by an ArXiV paper.

docs.title: Interactive Infographic Posters
docs.text:
These posters turn the book's biggest ideas into full-width, classroom-ready pictures. Most set a risky way of working beside a controlled one, so the difference is visible at a glance. Open a poster, hover over or click a region to read what it shows, then switch to Quiz mode to test yourself.

The original concepts and their sources are in Infographic Poster Ideas.

  • From Doing Everything to Directing Everything

    The researcher's job moves from doing every task by hand to directing a team of agents, while accountability for the science stays with the researcher. Grid overlay, 7 regions.

  • The Window That Fills Up

    A context window is one shared token budget, and when it overflows the oldest content can fall off silently, so subtract before you paste. Callout overlay, 11 markers.

  • The Real Citation and the Fluent Fake

    A model writes a fabricated reference as fluently as a real one, so every citation needs three checks the model cannot perform on itself. Grid overlay, 9 regions.

  • Vague Prompt, Engineered Context

    The same model with the same input file gives a vague answer from a one-line prompt and a checkable answer from an engineered context. Grid overlay, 9 regions.

  • The Chat That Forgets, the Project That Remembers

    An agent starts every session with no memory, so a plain-text project file and a version history are what it reads first and what you can undo. Grid overlay, 7 regions.

  • A Folder of Files, a Graph of Knowledge

    Files are for reading and a typed graph is for asking, and whoever can query the graph can see it, so an agent should get only the views its job needs. Grid overlay, 7 regions.

  • Inside an Agent Skill

    A skill is a folder with a front door, and only the name and description at that door are always in the agent's context. Callout overlay, 9 markers.

  • The Agent Loop Inside Its Sandbox

    An agent is a loop of deciding, calling a tool, and observing the result, and its permissions decide how far one wrong turn can reach. Callout overlay, 12 markers.

  • The Autonomy Dial

    How much an agent may do on its own depends on whether the task is reversible, whether the result leaves your control, and whether it can be checked quickly. Grid overlay, 9 regions.

  • Twenty Planners, Ten Doers, One Researcher

    A team of about 20 planning agents and 10 execution agents needs queues, handoffs, and gates, and the scarcest thing on the stage is the researcher's attention. Callout overlay, 12 markers.

  • The Literature Funnel

    Agents make breadth cheap at every stage of a literature review, and verification is where the pipeline earns its keep. Grid overlay, 8 regions.

  • Cleaning Without Hiding

    A clean-looking dataset is not the same as a trustworthy one, so show what you removed and why. Grid overlay, 7 regions.

  • Code That Runs, Code That Is Right

    A script that finishes without an error can still return a wrong number, so check its answer against something you can compute independently. Grid overlay, 7 regions.

  • From Hunch to Falsifiable Hypothesis

    An idea only becomes research when a stated result could show it wrong, and the climb from a loose brainstorm to that claim has recognizable steps. Grid overlay, 7 regions.

  • The Manuscript Line: Where the Human Stays

    An agent can draft and format a paper, but the claims, the interpretation, and the signature stay with the author. Grid overlay, 6 regions.

  • A Figure You Read, a Simulation You Explore

    A figure shows one case of a result, while a simulation built from the same result lets a reader ask what happens at other settings. Grid overlay, 7 regions.

  • Verified Is Not Validated

    A design can pass every check against its specification and still be wrong, because verification asks whether it was built right and validation asks whether it was the right thing. Grid overlay, 8 regions.

  • Where Does Your Data Go?

    Before you paste anything into an AI tool, decide what may leave the lab and where it goes, then write that decision into a one-page lab policy. Grid overlay, 8 regions.

  • Day Shift, Night Shift

    An agent that works while you are away needs a morning review as much as a night shift needs a supervisor, and eight durable criteria tell you how to judge it. Grid overlay, 7 regions.

  • The Paper Behind the Book

    The skill pipeline that wrote this book and a paper about MicroSims shows that the pipeline is the documentation, because every stage leaves a file and every file has a check. Callout overlay, 12 markers.

  • Dan's Desktop

    Five AI desktop apps side by side, with the plan and monthly cost of each, whether it can generate images, and a total of $186 per month. Grid overlay, 6 regions.

  • Meet Your Agent Team

    Seven agent personas side by side, from Ada the chief of staff to six specialists, with each one's role, title, and detailed task list. Grid overlay, 7 regions.

  • Five Personal Agents, Side by Side

    Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, Claude Cowork, and Gemini Spark compared on launch date, where each runs, whether it is always on, its safety model, and its price. Grid overlay, 5 regions.

  • Many Types of “Chat” Agents

    Eight ways an agent like Volt can differ, from a one-shot prompt and response to an always-on cloud agent with its own browser access, credentials, and email address. Callout overlay, 8 markers.

  • Hub and Spoke: How Your Agents Communicate

    You talk to Ada, the chief of staff, and Ada talks to six specialist agents and to the agents at the University of Minnesota, so one hub replaces a tangle of agent-to-agent links. Callout overlay, 9 markers.

docs.title: Infographic Poster Ideas
docs.text:
This page proposes 20 infographic posters for AI for EE Research. Each is a large, full-screen picture that a student can open, explore with hover and click, and then use to quiz themselves. They follow the poster family in The Science of the Built Environment, with two changes of emphasis requested for this book:

  • Side-by-side comparison first. Twelve of the twenty posters are a split screen that sets two ways of working next to each other (the same task, done carelessly and done well). Another five are a full-width left-to-right bar, pipeline, or timeline. The remaining three are a dial, a ring diagram, and an exploded diagram.
  • Full screen width. Every poster is designed for a wide 16:9 canvas so it fills a laptop or classroom projector with no wasted margins. Stories run left to right.

Where the built-environment posters taught physics, these posters teach judgment. Almost every comparison here has the same shape: one side shows an AI-assisted workflow that looks fine, and the other shows the same work with the check that makes it trustworthy. That is the book's thesis, and it is Volt's catchphrase: Trust, but verify!

docs.title: How This List Was Built
docs.text:
I read the course description, the chapter outlines and summaries for all twenty chapters, the worked examples (the ENOB measurement, the lab AI policy, the MicroSims paper), and the mascot guide. I also studied the 20 posters and the poster-ideas page in science-of-the-built-environment/docs/posters to match their structure: a text-free illustration, a data.json of regions or markers, an Explore mode, and a Quiz mode.

Three honest caveats:

  • These are original designs. Every poster is drawn fresh. Where a poster uses a framework from a chapter, the footer should credit that chapter.
  • No number appears here that is not already in a chapter. Numbers such as the 20 planning agents, 10 execution agents, and the 2.8-bit ENOB drop come from the book. Do not add a figure to a poster that the chapter does not support.
  • Product names age quickly. Poster 19 touches always-on agents. Keep product logos and prices out of the picture, and follow Chapter 19's rule of teaching criteria, not rankings.

docs.title: Common Design Standards
docs.text:
Use these for every poster so the set reads as one family.

Element Standard Canvas Landscape 16:9 (generate at 1920 × 1080 or the widest ratio the image model supports; print at 36 × 20.25 in). Crop to 16:9 rather than letterboxing. Image style High-quality, polished illustration with soft lighting and rich detail: real-looking oscilloscope benches, probe stations, server racks, lab notebooks, and laptops. Semi-realistic is welcome. No stock-photo clichés and no glowing brain or robot hands. Text in the image None. No title, no labels, no numerals, no code that can be read. All words come from the interactive overlay in data.json. Screens, notebooks, and terminals show unreadable abstract marks only. Palette Maroon #7A0019 for the researcher and human judgment, gold #FFCC33 for focal points, deep teal #1F7A8C for agents and automation, signal green #3C8D5A for verified or passed, brick red #C0392B for failures and risks, charcoal for structure, warm off-white #FAF7F2 for backgrounds Comparison rule In every split poster, left is the risky or naive version, right is the controlled version. Use the same camera angle, same scale, and same objects on both sides so students can compare at a glance. Never color alone Pair every color with an icon, a pattern, or a label so the meaning survives grayscale printing Mascot Volt the Border Collie appears once per student-facing poster, in the pose that matches the job (thinking, warning, tip, celebration). Instructor-facing versions omit Volt. Volt has no gender: use they/them. Footer The chapter links, the source credit, and the line "AI for EE Research" Overlay type Use the grid overlay (rectangular regions) for split-screen and pipeline posters. Use the callout overlay (numbered markers) for exploded and radial diagrams.

docs.title: The Top 20 at a Glance
docs.text:
# Poster Format Core idea Chapters 1 From Doing Everything to Directing Everything Side-by-side The researcher's job changes from doing tasks to orchestrating a team 1, 10 2 The Window That Fills Up Full-width bar A context window is a budget you must subtract from before you paste 2, 4 3 The Real Citation and the Fluent Fake Side-by-side A model writes a plausible reference as easily as a real one 2, 11 4 Vague Prompt, Engineered Context Side-by-side The same task with a loose prompt and with a full specification 3, 4 5 The Chat That Forgets, the Project That Remembers Side-by-side Project files and version control give an agent a durable memory 5 6 A Folder of Files, a Graph of Knowledge Side-by-side The same notes as a pile and as linked entities an agent can query 6, 19 7 Inside an Agent Skill Exploded callout Metadata, instructions, and supporting files load in layers 6, 7 8 The Agent Loop Inside Its Sandbox Loop plus rings An agent acts in a loop, and permissions decide how far it can reach 8 9 The Autonomy Dial Four columns How much autonomy a task earns depends on reversibility, reach, and verifiability 9 10 Twenty Planners, Ten Doers, One Researcher Full-width org The orchestra, its handoffs, its gates, and the one scarce resource 10 11 The Literature Funnel Full-width pipeline Search, triage, claims, citations, verification, synthesis 11 12 Cleaning Without Hiding Side-by-side Silent cleanup versus a cleanup that logs every change 12 13 Code That Runs, Code That Is Right Side-by-side A script can run clean and still be wrong; a sanity check catches it 13, 17 14 From Hunch to Falsifiable Hypothesis Side-by-side ladder An idea earns a place in the roadmap by becoming testable 14 15 The Manuscript Line: Where the Human Stays Full-width pipeline Which steps of paper preparation an agent can draft and which stay yours 15 16 A Figure You Read, a Simulation You Explore Side-by-side A static plot beside the MicroSim built from the same result 16, 20 17 Verified Is Not Validated Side-by-side Built right versus built the right thing 17 18 Where Does Your Data Go? Side-by-side Hosted model versus a model you run, and what each one sees 18, 19 19 Day Shift, Night Shift Side-by-side An always-on agent works while you sleep, so you audit it in the morning 19 20 The Paper Behind the Book Full-width timeline The MicroSims paper as a worked case: where each chapter's control fired 20

If only a few are produced, start with 1, 10, 13, 17, and 19. Together they state the book's whole argument: direct a team, keep your attention scarce, check the work, check the question, and audit what ran while you were away.

docs.title: Poster 1: From Doing Everything to Directing Everything
docs.text:
Format: Side-by-side, equal halves, with a bold vertical divider. Grid overlay.

Influence: The central idea of the course description and Chapter 1: the researcher's role moves from doing every task personally to orchestrating a team of agents while staying accountable for the science.

Core message: The work does not disappear. The role changes from doing to directing and deciding what is true.

Chapters: 1, 10

Image description:

  • Left half, "The Soloist": One researcher at a cluttered bench at night: oscilloscope, a stack of printed papers, three half-written scripts on a laptop, a coffee gone cold, a calendar with everything crossed out. Five thin arrows leave the person toward five task icons (literature, data, brainstorming, code, manuscript), each drawn as a small task on the desk that the person must reach in turn. The overall mood is warm but overloaded.
  • Right half, "The Orchestrator": The same bench, tidier, but now a wide wall display behind the researcher shows a fan of small agent workstations. Roughly twenty small teal figures on the upper tier are drawn as planners with maps and checklists. Ten sturdier teal figures on the lower tier are drawn as builders at benches. The researcher stands in front holding a single clipboard and a pen, reviewing one item.
  • Role strip: Along the bottom of the right half, four gold icons: set direction, supply domain judgment, resolve conflicts, decide what is true.
  • Constant: A single maroon thread of accountability runs from the researcher on the left, continues unbroken across the divider, and ends at a signature line on the right. It signals that the person remains responsible on both sides.
  • Volt: Thinking pose at the divider, one paw on the maroon thread.

docs.title: Poster 2: The Window That Fills Up
docs.text:
Format: One very wide horizontal bar spanning the full canvas, with three stacked rows. Callout overlay.

Influence: Chapter 2's context window arithmetic and Chapter 4's context management. A window is a budget in tokens, and the dangerous failure is silent: old content falls off the front.

Core message: Subtract before you paste. A document that fits is not a document that was read with equal care.

Chapters: 2, 4

Image description:

  • Layout: Three horizontal "window" bars, one above another, each a long glass tube filled with colored blocks from left to right. The tube's right end is open for the answer.
  • Top row, "Comfortable": Blocks in order: a thin system-prompt block, a medium conversation-history block, one large paper block, a small question block. Plenty of empty tube remains for the completion. Use the book's 32,000-token worked example for proportions.
  • Middle row, "The second paste": A second paper block of the same size is added. The tube is nearly full, and only a short empty gap remains for the answer. A drawn answer bubble is cut off partway.
  • Bottom row, "Silent overflow": The oldest blocks, the system prompt and the first instructions, are drawn as ghosted blocks that have slid off the left end of the tube and are falling into a drain. The model figure at the right is working happily without them.
  • Middle-of-the-document effect: On the paper block, a faint heat-map gradient is brightest at the start and end and dim in the middle.
  • Cost sidebar: A small token-meter icon shows that equation-heavy and code-heavy text uses more tokens per word than prose.
  • Volt: Tip pose with a ruler laid across the tube.

docs.title: Poster 3: The Real Citation and the Fluent Fake
docs.text:
Format: Side-by-side, two identical reference cards in two matching library scenes. Grid overlay.

Influence: Chapter 2's hallucination and fabricated citations, Chapter 11's reference verification, and Chapter 17's primary-source check.

Core message: A model produces a plausible reference as fluently as a real one. Fluency is not evidence.

Chapters: 2, 11, 17

Image description:

  • Left half, "Looks right": A reference card on a clean desk, with a model-generated bibliography entry. A friendly checkmark hovers over it, drawn in gray because nobody has checked. Behind the card, the library shelf is painted as a flat, unreadable backdrop of spines with nothing behind it.
  • Right half, "Looks right, and is": The same card with the same typography, but a gold thread leads from it to a real paper in a real stack, then to a DOI-style resolver lookup on a laptop, then to a green verified stamp. A magnifier hovers over the title, author list, and year.
  • Difference marks: Three small tag-shaped icons appear only on the right: a link, a date, and a person. They represent the three things you verify (the paper exists, the claim is in the paper, the authors match).
  • Failure strip: A narrow band across the bottom shows the four ways a reference fails: does not exist, exists but says something different, exists but wrong details, exists but retracted. Each is a tiny card with its own broken icon.
  • Volt: Warning pose beside the left card.

docs.title: Poster 4: Vague Prompt, Engineered Context
docs.text:
Format: Side-by-side. Same task, same model, same input file. Grid overlay.

Influence: Chapter 3's prompt engineering and Chapter 4's task specification and acceptance criteria. The idea is the same one the case study in Chapter 20 repeats: a prompt is a specification with a test.

Core message: The model did not get smarter on the right. The context did.

Chapters: 3, 4

Image description:

  • Layout: A researcher's laptop in the center of each half, with a single measurement-data file icon feeding in.
  • Left half: A short, unreadable one-line prompt. Out of the laptop comes a wobbly, sprawling answer cloud with a vague gray chart, a sloppy paragraph, and a speech bubble full of question marks.
  • Right half: The prompt is built as stacked, labeled-by-icon blocks: a role (a badge), the task (a target), the input (the file), the constraints (a fence), the acceptance criteria (a checklist with ticks), and the output format (a tidy template). Out of the laptop comes a clean chart, a short result table, and a "limits and assumptions" note.
  • Test plate: On the right only, a small test fixture is attached: three input samples go through the prompt, and each returns a green tick.
  • Shared object: The same coffee cup, same desk lamp, and same laptop sit on both sides.
  • Volt: Tip pose, holding the checklist.

docs.title: Poster 5: The Chat That Forgets, the Project That Remembers
docs.text:
Format: Side-by-side, with a calendar running across both halves to show time passing. Grid overlay.

Influence: Chapter 5's project instruction files (AGENTS.md style), plain-text Markdown conventions, and version control.

Core message: An agent starts every session with no memory. A project file is what it reads first.

Chapters: 5

Image description:

  • Left half, "Session 1, Session 2, Session 3": Three speech-bubble conversations in a row, each ending in a puff of smoke. Between them the same question is asked again and the same wrong assumption is made again (a sticky note says nothing readable but is crossed out each time).
  • Right half, "The project folder": A tidy repository tree drawn as a physical filing cabinet. One gold-edged document at the top of the cabinet is the instruction file, with four tabs for goal, conventions, constraints, and next steps. Each session opens the cabinet, reads the top document first, and works.
  • Time ribbon: Along the bottom, a branching git history in gold nodes, with one commit marked as a rollback point and one branch where an agent experiment was merged after review.
  • Plain-text cue: A Markdown file icon, a notebook icon, and a script icon sit in the cabinet, all as plain documents that both a person and an agent can read.
  • Volt: Welcome pose pointing at the top document.

docs.title: Poster 6: A Folder of Files, a Graph of Knowledge
docs.text:
Format: Side-by-side. Left is a messy directory, right is a linked network of the same items. Grid overlay.

Influence: The personal knowledge graph material in Chapter 6, and Chapter 19's discussion of memory, grounding, and what an agent may see.

Core message: Files are for reading. A graph is for asking. And whoever can query it can see it.

Chapters: 6, 19

Image description:

  • Left half, "The folder": A cluttered desktop: PDFs, notebook pages, simulation results, meeting notes, and a half-built bibliography, all stacked with no visible relationships. A search box finds only keyword matches.
  • Right half, "The graph": The same objects now appear as five kinds of node shapes: paper, experiment, person, project, and idea. They are joined by labeled-by-icon edges: cites, produced by, wrote, supports, contradicts. One question mark bubble asks something that spans three hops, and a highlighted path answers it.
  • Grounding strip: At the bottom of the right half, an agent figure holds a small card with a trail back to the node it used, to show that an answer cites its source.
  • Privacy ring: A dashed boundary around part of the graph marks nodes the agent may not read, with a lock icon.
  • Volt: Thinking pose near the highlighted path.

docs.title: Poster 7: Inside an Agent Skill
docs.text:
Format: One large exploded diagram across the center of the screen. Callout overlay with eight markers.

Influence: The anatomy of a skill from Chapter 6 and the progressive-disclosure and testing guidance of Chapter 7.

Core message: A skill is a folder with a front door. Only the front door is always in the agent's context.

Chapters: 6, 7

Image description:

  • Layout: A folder in the middle, lifted open like a hangar door. Three nested layers rise out of it from left to right.
  • Layer 1, always loaded: A small badge with the skill's name and a one-line description. A tiny scale shows its cost in context as small.
  • Layer 2, loaded on trigger: A single-sheet instruction document unfolds when a task arrow matches the badge.
  • Layer 3, loaded on demand: A shelf of supporting files: a reference table, a template, and a tested script. Only the file the current step needs slides off the shelf.
  • Test bench: A small bench on the right with two inboxes: requests that should trigger the skill (green) and near-miss requests that should not (red outline). Each is a stack of tiny request cards.
  • Contrast corner: A bloated "does everything" skill drawn as an overstuffed binder with an unclear label.
  • Volt: Tip pose beside the near-miss inbox.

docs.title: Poster 8: The Agent Loop Inside Its Sandbox
docs.text:
Format: A loop on the left two-thirds and nested permission rings on the right third. Callout overlay.

Influence: Chapter 8's tool use and the agent loop, file, shell, and code access, sandboxing, permissions, MCP, subagents, and hooks.

Core message: An agent is a loop, and its permissions decide how far one wrong turn can reach.

Chapters: 8, 9

Image description:

  • Left, the loop: A circular track of five stations with an agent figure walking it: read the goal, plan, call a tool, observe the result, decide whether to continue. A small gate on the track labeled by icon only is a hook that can pause or veto.
  • Tools around the loop: A file cabinet, a terminal, a web browser, a code runner, and an external data port with a plug for outside connectors.
  • Right, the rings: Concentric rings viewed from above, like a target: the innermost is a scratch folder, then the project directory, then the whole machine, then the network and other people's accounts. Each ring has a padlock; the inner rings are open and the outer rings are locked unless approved.
  • Subagent: A small second figure branches off the loop to work in its own small ring and returns a summary card.
  • Runaway cue: A tiny meter that shows steps and cost climbing, with a stop button.
  • Volt: Warning pose at the outer ring.

docs.title: Poster 9: The Autonomy Dial
docs.text:
Format: Four equal vertical columns, each a rung on the dial, with a large dial across the top. Grid overlay.

Influence: The four autonomy levels from 0 to 3 in Chapter 9, set by a task's reversibility, reach, and verifiability.

Core message: Autonomy is earned task by task. It is not a setting for the whole project.

Chapters: 9

Image description:

  • Top strip: A big semicircular dial with four notches from 0 on the left to 3 on the right, with the needle drawn in a neutral position so that the overlay can highlight each level.
  • Column per level: Each column shows the same agent working on a different research task in a scene appropriate to the level. Level 0, the agent only suggests while the researcher types. Level 1, the agent proposes an action and waits behind an approval gate. Level 2, the agent acts inside a boundary and reports afterward. Level 3, the agent runs on a schedule with a log and a budget limit.
  • Three gauges: Under each column, three small gauges for reversibility, reach, and verifiability, set differently in each column.
  • Task examples: One illustrative task icon per column: rename a variable, run a parameter sweep, edit the shared project file, send an email to a collaborator.
  • Log cue: In the right-hand column, a long scroll of log entries trailing off the page.
  • Volt: Neutral pose beside the dial.

docs.title: Poster 10: Twenty Planners, Ten Doers, One Researcher
docs.text:
Format: Full-width organization view, like a theater stage seen from the audience. Callout overlay with twelve markers.

Influence: The 20-planning-agent, 10-execution-agent model of the course description and Chapter 10's task queue, dependencies, handoffs, review checkpoints, human approval gates, and span of control.

Core message: The most scarce resource on the stage is the researcher's attention, and the design should spend it only where it counts.

Chapters: 10

Image description:

  • Layout: Three horizontal tiers. At the top, a wide bank of about twenty small teal planning agents at desks with maps, outlines, and specs. In the middle, a flowing conveyor belt of task cards, with a task queue on the left and dependency arrows between some cards. At the bottom, a row of ten sturdier execution agents at benches: code, analysis, simulation, figures, manuscript.
  • Orchestrator: At the center of the lower edge, a maroon figure with a baton, in front of a podium with a small status board.
  • Gates: Gold review-checkpoint gates cross the conveyor. Two taller gates are labeled by icon as human approval gates, with a person-and-pen symbol.
  • Shared workspace: A single table in the middle where agents place files, with a conflict flag on one file that two agents both touched.
  • Attention meter: A tall gauge on the far right shows researcher attention draining as the number of review items rises, with a warning band.
  • Volt: Thinking pose near the attention meter.

docs.title: Poster 11: The Literature Funnel
docs.text:
Format: Full-width left-to-right pipeline, drawn as a funnel that narrows into a clean synthesis. Grid overlay with six regions.

Influence: Chapter 11's search strategy, triage, claim extraction, citation chaining, verification, and synthesis, with the claim-to-source table.

Core message: Breadth is cheap with agents. Verification is where the pipeline earns its keep.

Chapters: 11

Image description:

  • Layout: A wide funnel runs from the left edge to the right edge. Each region is a stage with its own small workshop scene.
  • Stages, left to right: Search (keyword and source strategy, a map of databases), Triage (a pile of papers sorted into three bins), Claim extraction (each paper reduced to small claim cards), Citation chasing (a web of references forward and backward), Verification (a checklist and magnifier), Synthesis (a woven summary with a source thread behind each claim).
  • Leak points: Between stages, small drips fall off the funnel: missed papers, misread claims, fabricated references. Each drip has a small matching catch-basin icon on the verification stage.
  • Table at the end: A claim-to-source table drawn as a grid with three columns: claim, source, and a status tag of measured, cited, or expected.
  • Volt: Tip pose at the verification stage.

docs.title: Poster 12: Cleaning Without Hiding
docs.text:
Format: Side-by-side, two identical raw datasets going through two different cleaning paths. Grid overlay.

Influence: Chapter 12's cleaning, data formats, and exploration, with the principle that a cleaning step should never hide what it removed.

Core message: A clean-looking dataset is not the same as a trustworthy one. Show what you removed and why.

Chapters: 12

Image description:

  • Layout: Both halves begin on the left with the same raw capture: a noisy scatter of points with a few obvious outliers and a block of missing values.
  • Left half, "Silent cleanup": The data passes through a black box and emerges as a smooth, handsome plot. A trail of discarded points disappears down a drain. The final plot has a gold medal-style ribbon drawn on it that nobody earned.
  • Right half, "Logged cleanup": The data passes through a glass pipe in which each step is visible: drop missing rows, flag outliers by a stated rule, convert units. Each step drops its removed points into a labeled-by-icon tray. A cleaning-log scroll hangs beside the pipe.
  • Comparison: The final plot looks similar on both sides, but the right side's plot has a small gray ghost of the removed points and a count bubble.
  • Raw preserved: On the right, a locked box labeled by a raw icon holds the untouched original file.
  • Volt: Warning pose at the drain.

docs.title: Poster 13: Code That Runs, Code That Is Right
docs.text:
Format: Side-by-side, one script, one input, two outcomes. Grid overlay.

Influence: Chapter 13's tests and numerical sanity checks and Chapter 17's independent checks. It uses the book's own ENOB example: an acceptance criterion was wrong by a plausible-looking amount, and a hand calculation caught it.

Core message: No error message does not mean no error. Check the answer against something you can compute independently.

Chapters: 13, 17

Image description:

  • Layout: A short script in the middle of each half, in an editor window with unreadable marks, and an ADC-style waveform going in from the left.
  • Left half: A terminal window with a green "completed" glow and a neat number emerging. A plausible-looking result is displayed on a large meter. A small unseen crack runs under the meter.
  • Right half: The same script, but with a bench beside it where a person with a calculator and a notebook works out the expected value by hand. A comparison balance shows the script's number and the hand number side by side, and they disagree. A red tag appears on the script, and a test case has been added.
  • Seeded bug cue: A small inset shows a deliberately planted bug in a test file and a test that fails when it is present, which proves the test can catch it.
  • Example note: In the worked example from the chapter, adding 2 LSB of noise to an ideal 10-bit record lowers the effective bits by about 2.8, to near 7.2. Keep this number out of the image and put it in the overlay.
  • Volt: Tip pose holding the calculator.

docs.title: Poster 14: From Hunch to Falsifiable Hypothesis
docs.text:
Format: Two staircases side by side climbing toward the same summit. Grid overlay.

Influence: Chapter 14's framing, idea generation and challenge, hypothesis and experiment design, feasibility, ranking, novelty, and the research roadmap.

Core message: An idea only becomes research when it can be shown wrong.

Chapters: 14

Image description:

  • Left staircase, "Brainstorm": A wide, loose, cloudy staircase with many sticky-note ideas floating around it. The steps are labeled by icon only: topic, general interest, "could be better", "might work". The top step ends at a cloud with no summit marker.
  • Right staircase, "Hypothesis": A narrower, sharper staircase: problem framed, claim stated, prediction written down, measurement chosen, result that would refute it identified. The top step ends at a flag at the summit labeled by a magnifier icon.
  • Challenger: On the right staircase, a devil's-advocate agent figure stands at the third step holding a "what would make this wrong" card.
  • Ranking mat: Below, a simple matrix of three or four candidate ideas laid out on a table with columns for feasibility, novelty, and cost, with a gold marker on the top one.
  • Roadmap ribbon: A final ribbon extends right from the summit as a short research roadmap with three milestones.
  • Volt: Thinking pose on the right staircase.

docs.title: Poster 15: The Manuscript Line: Where the Human Stays
docs.text:
Format: Full-width assembly line with a clearly drawn handrail marking what stays human. Grid overlay with six regions.

Influence: Chapter 15's structure, outline, abstract, drafting, revising, figures, LaTeX, references, co-author consistency, submission, and response to reviewers, with the disclosure rules of Chapter 18.

Core message: An agent can draft and format. The claims, the interpretation, and the signature are yours.

Chapters: 15

Image description:

  • Layout: A long left-to-right conveyor with a manuscript growing from a bare outline to a printed paper.
  • Stations: Outline and structure, drafting from claims, figures and LaTeX, references and citation check, consistency across co-authors, submission and reviewer response. At each, an agent figure in teal works the belt.
  • Human line: A gold handrail runs along the top. At four stations, a maroon person reaches down and stamps a decision: the claim, the interpretation, the limits, and the final read.
  • Hazards: Small red tags on the belt show three typical agent errors: a changed number, an invented reference, and an overconfident sentence. Each is caught by a different station.
  • End: A submission box with an unreadable cover letter and a disclosure note attached.
  • Volt: Celebration pose at the end of the line.

docs.title: Poster 16: A Figure You Read, a Simulation You Explore
docs.text:
Format: Side-by-side. A printed page on the left and a screen on the right, built from the same result. Grid overlay.

Influence: Chapter 16's communication of research, MicroSims, agent generation of MicroSims, and embedding. Chapter 20's MicroSims paper is the worked example.

Core message: A reader can look at one case in a figure, or ask "what if" in a simulation.

Chapters: 16, 20

Image description:

  • Left half, "The paper": A journal page with a single clean plot of a result, with two curves. A reader at a desk traces one curve with a finger and wonders what happens at a different parameter value. A marginal note says nothing readable.
