  • Right half, "The MicroSim": The same plot appears on a wide screen with real slider handles beneath it. The reader's hand pulls a slider and the curves move. A second slider changes a parameter, and a small readout shows a number shifting.
  • Shared source: A gold thread runs from both outputs back to one data file and one script in the center bottom, to show they are the same result.
  • Embedding strip: A small browser-frame icon shows the simulation embedded on a lab website and in a paper's supplementary material.
  • Agent hand: A teal agent figure at the back of the right half builds the simulation from a specification card.
  • Volt: Welcome pose beside the sliders.

docs.title: Poster 17: Verified Is Not Validated
docs.text:
Format: Side-by-side, two inspectors at two checkpoints. Grid overlay.

Influence: Chapter 17's distinction between verification (was it done right) and validation (was the right thing done).

Core message: A design can be fully verified against a specification that was wrong, and it will be wrong in exactly the way the specification was.

Chapters: 17

Image description:

  • Left half, "Verification: built right?": An inspector compares a finished circuit board and its code against a blueprint (the specification). Every item on a checklist is ticked green. The scene is clean and calm.
  • Right half, "Validation: right thing?": The same board is placed on a real bench with a probe, a measured waveform, and the real problem the research question asks about (a drawn sensor in the field). The measured waveform and the simulated waveform disagree, and a red question mark appears over the blueprint itself.
  • The trap: A narrow band across the center shows a green-ticked blueprint that has a small flaw printed on it, with an arrow carrying that flaw all the way through the verified build.
  • Methods: Small icons at the bottom list three kinds of check: independent, primary source, and cross-model.
  • Volt: Thinking pose at the question mark.

docs.title: Poster 18: Where Does Your Data Go?
docs.text:
Format: Side-by-side. A hosted model on the left and a model you run on the right. Grid overlay.

Influence: Chapter 18's privacy, confidentiality, governance, ownership, and open resources, and Chapter 19's data exposure and self-hosted agents. The lab AI use policy is the take-home.

Core message: Before you paste, decide what may leave the lab and where it goes.

Chapters: 18, 19

Image description:

  • Left half, "Hosted": A researcher's laptop with a line running out of the lab through a window, up to a distant cloud data center. Along the line, small document icons travel in a pipe: a public paper, a draft manuscript, unpublished measurements, a collaborator's confidential spec. A retention clock and a log icon sit at the cloud end.
  • Right half, "Self-hosted": A server rack in the corner of the same lab, with the line running only to the rack. The documents stay in a lab boundary drawn as a dashed rectangle. A fan, a power meter, and a small "you maintain this" wrench icon sit beside the rack.
  • Traffic light sorter: A three-lane sorter across the bottom shows document types going to green (public), yellow (needs a decision), or red (never leaves).
  • Policy sheet: A page icon at the center bottom with six numbered checkbox rows stands for the lab policy.
  • Volt: Warning pose at the open window.

docs.title: Poster 19: Day Shift, Night Shift
docs.text:
Format: Side-by-side, one lab in daylight and the same lab at night. Grid overlay.

Influence: Chapter 19's always-on personal agents, blast radius, usage metering, and the overnight activity audit. It teaches durable criteria and avoids ranking products.

Core message: An agent that works while you are away needs a morning review as much as a night shift needs a supervisor.

Chapters: 19

Image description:

  • Left half, "Day shift": A bright lab with the researcher at a desk, three agents on screen, and every action visible as it happens. A small hand-and-clipboard icon shows approval requests coming in.
  • Right half, "Night shift": The same lab at night with the lights off. The researcher's chair is empty. A single cloud computer glows teal in the corner, and small agent figures move through it: reading email, running a sweep, filing a ticket, drafting a summary. A moon and a clock sit in the corner.
  • Morning audit: A strip across the bottom of the right half shows the next morning: the researcher with coffee, scanning a long activity log, with some entries marked as approved, some as unexpected, and one circled in red.
  • Criteria ring: Eight small dots around the right half stand for the eight comparison criteria: where it runs, blast radius, approval model, usage metering, data exposure, memory, claim verification, and activity audit.
  • Volt: Warning pose beside the audit log, holding the whistle.

docs.title: Poster 20: The Paper Behind the Book
docs.text:
Format: Full-width timeline with a lower strip of failure cases. Callout overlay with twelve markers.

Influence: Chapter 20's case study of the MicroSims paper and the intelligent-textbook skill pipeline, including the book's own failure cases and the capstone project.

Core message: The pipeline is the documentation. Every stage leaves a file, and every file has a check.

Chapters: 20

Image description:

  • Layout: A long road across the canvas, from a pile of source documents on the left to an arXiv-style submission box on the right.
  • Milestones: Source material first, structure before prose (abstract, introduction, related work, conclusion), sections filled from existing documentation, build script producing a PDF, figures with a stated policy, and a submission package.
  • Skill pipeline strip: Above the road, six small stations drawn as workshops: course description, learning graph, chapter structure, chapter content, MicroSims, and supporting pages. Arrows carry a file from each to the next.
  • Failure-case strip: Below the road, four small scenes: a wrong number in a criterion caught by a hand calculation, stray markup caught by a tag-counting script, short chapters accepted rather than padded, and unbuilt simulations left honestly marked as specifications.
  • Claim table: Over the abstract milestone, a small table with three tags (measured, cited, expected) beside a number.
  • Volt: Celebration pose at the finish.

docs.title: Bench of Extra Ideas
docs.text:
These did not make the top 20, but each would work as a poster if a chapter needs more visual weight.

Idea Format Core idea Chapter Chatbot vs. Agent Side-by-side A chatbot answers once. An agent plans, acts with tools, observes, and repeats. (Pairs with the Generative AI to Agent MicroSim.) 1, 8 The Poisoned PDF Side-by-side The same paper with and without an injected instruction, and the trust boundary that stops it 4, 9 One Prompt, Three Temperatures Three columns The same prompt at low, medium, and high temperature, showing the spread of next-token choices 2 Tokens Are Not Words Full-width strip A sentence cut into tokens, with acronyms, numbers, and equations costing more 2 The Sycophancy Mirror Side-by-side A model that agrees with a wrong claim versus one asked to argue against it 17 Planner or Doer? docs.title: Suggested Production Order
docs.text:
1. Posters 1, 10, 13, 17, 19: the five that carry the argument of the whole book.
  2. Posters 2, 3, 4, 5: the foundation cluster for Chapters 2 to 5, where students form their first habits.
  3. Posters 7, 8, 9, 11, 12: the skills, agents, and research-task cluster.
  4. Posters 6, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20: the knowledge, communication, ethics, and case-study cluster.

docs.title: How Each Poster Becomes an Interactive Page
docs.text:
Each poster follows the same recipe used in the built-environment book, so the production work is repeatable.

  1. Create docs/posters/<poster-id>/ with a kebab-case id.
  2. Write image-prompt.md from the image description above. Repeat the no text of any kind rule at the top.
  3. Generate the 16:9 image and save it as <poster-id>.png.
  4. Fill in data.json with regions (grid) or markers (callout). Each region carries a label, a student-friendly description, and a hint for Quiz mode.
  5. Add main.html and an index.md with status: scaffold in the frontmatter. Move to built when the image and overlay work. Only the author sets approved.
  6. Open main.html?edit=true, drag each region onto its place in the image, and copy the coordinates back into data.json.
  7. Generate a thumbnail and add the poster to a docs/posters/index.md gallery.
  8. Add the page to the nav: block of mkdocs.yml and run mkdocs build --strict.

Let the pictures argue

A poster that says "check the output" is a slogan. A poster that shows the same script with and without the check, side by side, is an argument. Draw the argument.

docs.title: The Agent Loop Inside Its Sandbox
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over a numbered marker or its label and read what that part of the loop or the sandbox does. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the marker that matches. The marker numbers are hidden in Quiz mode, so you must find the matching part of the picture. The loop is on the left. The permission rings are on the right.

The twelve callouts are:

  1. Repeat or Stop — The loop goes around again, or ends when the task is done, an error occurs, or a limit is reached.
  2. Decide — The model reads the task, the context, and the tool definitions, and picks an action.
  3. Call — The model writes a structured tool call. Nothing has run yet.
  4. Subagent Side Loop — A separate agent with its own context takes one part of the job and returns a summary.
  5. Network and Other Accounts — Remotes, outbound data, installs, and downloaded code.
  6. Rest of Your Machine — Credentials, other projects, and everything outside the project directory.
  7. Observe — The result goes into the context, and the model reads it.
  8. Tool Bench — Files, a shell, code execution, the web, and MCP connectors.
  9. Run — The harness executes the call after checking the permission rules.
  10. Step and Cost Meter — Step, time, and spending limits against a runaway loop.
  11. Hook Gate — A script that always runs at a set moment and can pause or veto a call.
  12. Inside the Project — The directory where the agent may work, with raw data protected.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Chapter 8 explains that a language model only emits text. Tool use turns that text into actions: the model writes a tool call, a program called the harness runs it, and the result returns to the model. That cycle is the agent loop. Sandboxing limits what a running process can reach, permissions decide which calls are allowed, need approval, or are denied, and hooks enforce rules that must never be skipped.

The permission rules on the poster follow the chapter's illustrative policy. They are an example, not a recommended configuration, and each tool uses its own syntax. The poster does not say that a sandbox or a permission list makes an agent safe. Each catches different mistakes, and version control, logs, and step limits still matter. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: The Chat That Forgets, the Project That Remembers
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read what it shows about working without memory and working with a project. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes.

A calendar runs across the top of both halves to show time passing. The left half keeps nothing between sessions. The right half keeps the goals, the files, and the history.

The seven regions are:

  1. Days Go By — Time passes across both halves while sessions end and models change.
  2. Three Chats, Three Resets — Each new conversation starts from nothing, and the same wrong assumption returns every time.
  3. Nothing to Roll Back To — A timeline with no snapshots to compare or restore.
  4. The Instruction File — The first document an agent reads: goals, conventions, constraints.
  5. Project Layout — A predictable folder structure with read-only raw data.
  6. Plain Text Files — Markdown, notebooks, and scripts that people and agents both read.
  7. Commit History — Small saved snapshots, a rollback point, and a reviewed merge.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Chapter 2 explains that a model has no memory of earlier conversations beyond what is in the prompt it is sent. A chat that seems to remember is resending its earlier turns. Chapter 5 builds the remedy from ordinary tools: a short instruction file the agent reads at the start of every session, plain-text files it can read directly, a predictable layout, and Git so that any change an agent makes can be reviewed and undone. The idea is not new. It is context engineering done once and reused every time.

The poster does not say chat is bad. Chapter 2 treats a chat interface as the right way to start and to explore, and the move to a project is for work that recurs or touches files. A file helps only if you keep it short, checkable, and free of secrets, and it does not replace reading the diff before accepting an agent's changes. The three tabs on the document are goals, conventions, and constraints, the three kinds of content Chapter 5 lists.

docs.title: Cleaning Without Hiding
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read what it shows. One raw capture at the top feeds two paths. The left half is a silent cleanup. The right half is a logged cleanup. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes.

The seven regions are:

  1. The Raw Capture — The measured data, shared by both paths, that a prompt cannot regenerate.
  2. Silent Cleanup — A black box that returns tidy data and records nothing.
  3. The Unearned Polish — A handsome plot with no way to check what was removed.
  4. Original Overwritten — A raw file edited in place, so no untouched original remains.
  5. Logged Cleanup — Named, visible steps that log the rows, the count, and the reason.
  6. A Plot With Its Ghosts — A similar plot that keeps the removed points visible.
  7. Raw File, Locked — The untouched original, read-only, with its sidecar.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Cleaning is the quietest source of wrong results in research. Every choice changes the answer, and nothing marks that a choice was made. An agent asked for a clean result has an incentive to remove what hurts it. Three rules keep it honest. Cleaning is a script and not an edit. Every change is logged. A point is removed only for a documented cause, and an undocumented outlier is kept, reported, and investigated.

The two final plots in the poster look alike on purpose, because a clean plot tells you nothing about whether the cleaning was honest. The difference is in what you can audit. The ghost points and the count bubble are a teaching device of the poster. The chapter asks for a log and for results reported with and without a step that changes a headline number, and it does not prescribe any particular plot style. The measurements quoted are the chapter's illustrative ones.

docs.title: Code That Runs, Code That Is Right
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read what it shows about trusting code an agent wrote. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes. The left half is the trusting version, where the code ran and the number was believed. The right half is the checked version, where the same script was tested against an independent answer.

The seven regions are:

  1. Run Finished, No Error — The script completes with no exception and no warning.
  2. A Plausible Number — A clean, reasonable-looking result that happens to be wrong.
  3. The Silent Error — The hidden defect, and the test that shares the code's misreading.
  4. Hand Calculation — An expected value worked out independently of the script.
  5. The Numbers Disagree — The script's number and the hand number do not match, so the script is tagged.
  6. Seeded Bug — A bug planted on purpose to show whether a test can catch it.
  7. Test Case Added — A new known-answer test whose range comes from the hand calculation.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
An agent's code almost always runs. The danger is code that runs and returns a plausible, wrong number, because research code usually has no known answer to flag a mistake. The book's worked example uses the voltage formula on a power ratio. The script prints a clean figure that makes a 10-bit converter look like an 18-bit one, and only someone who knows a converter cannot exceed its resolution would notice. The remedy is to compare every result with something outside the code that produced it: a known answer, a physical limit, or a hand calculation (Chapter 13).

The checks have limits. A sanity check can show that a number is wrong, but it cannot prove that a number is right. A passing test only shows that the cases it covers pass. The numbers in the worked example are the book's own, and the code in them is a teaching case, not a statement about any particular tool. Chapter 17 explains why the check must be independent: a check that shares the failure causes of the thing it checks proves little.

docs.title: Hub and Spoke: How Your Agents Communicate
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

The question is how to get all of your agents to communicate with each other, with the agents in your department, and with the agents at the University of Minnesota. One answer is a hub and spoke: you sit at the left, Ada the chief of staff sits in the middle, and every other agent has one spoke to Ada. Use Explore mode to hover over a numbered marker or its label and read what travels along that spoke. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the matching circle.

Seven agents that all message each other directly need 21 separate links. With a hub they need six, and you only watch one of them. The dashed spoke on the right crosses a boundary: it connects Ada to agents outside your own team.

The nine callouts are:

  1. Marisol: Events and Speakers — Seminar calendar and speaker pipeline, reported through Ada.
  2. Scout: Novelty and Prior-Art Search — The closest prior art, merged into your briefing.
  3. You — One channel to watch, and the person who sends, submits, signs, and pays.
  4. Kai: Conferences and Proposals — Deadlines and drafts that Ada checks against your calendar.
  5. Penny: Lab Budgets and Finance — Balances and warnings, with paperwork ready for your signature.
  6. Ada: Chief of Staff (the Hub) — Every agent reports to Ada, who decides what reaches you.
  7. University of Minnesota Agents — The spoke to agents in your department and across the university.
  8. Rosa: Grant Writing — Funding calls, outlines, and a skeptical review of your draft.
  9. Pixel: Presentations and Web — Decks, figures, and your web page, built from the shared record.

The University of Minnesota badge in this picture is a generic maroon-and-gold placeholder, not the official logo.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: A research workflow rarely lives in one AI app. Each subscription looks small on its own, but five of them add up to $186 a month, or $2,232 a year, and the most expensive plan alone costs more than the other four together. Putting the plans in one row shows what each dollar buys. Only three of the five apps can generate images, so a figure or diagram request has to go to the right one. Compare the plans against the work you actually do, not against the feature lists.

docs.title: Where the Numbers Come From
docs.text: Every value on this poster, including the plan names, the monthly prices, and the image-generation answers, was supplied by the author for the plans he currently uses. Nothing was checked against a vendor page. Plan names, prices, and features change often, so confirm them with each vendor before you budget. The yearly costs and percentages in the hover panels are simple arithmetic on those monthly prices. The app icons are cropped from a screenshot of the author's dock and belong to their respective owners.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
An always-on personal agent keeps its own cloud computer, signs in to tools as you, and works while you are away. That gives it standing access and no one watching, so the same questions as for any agent must hold for months and not minutes. Chapter 19 turns them into eight criteria: where it runs, blast radius, approval model, usage metering, data exposure, memory, claim verification, and activity audit. The last is a habit as much as a feature. Each morning, compare the log with the task the agent was given.

The poster teaches criteria and names no product, price, or ranking. The product facts in Chapter 19 are a snapshot of October 2026, almost all vendor-stated or reported in the press, and the research notes found no independent benchmarks or controlled tests. Prices, tiers, and features changed within weeks of launch. Check a vendor's own pages before relying on any detail, and test the claims that matter with synthetic data and a throwaway account.

docs.title: A Figure You Read, a Simulation You Explore
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read how the printed figure and the simulation differ and how they relate. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes. The left half is the page, which shows one case. The right half is the screen, where a reader can change the parameter. The bottom row shows how both come from one source and how an agent helps build the simulation.

The seven regions are:

  1. A Figure on a Page — One plot at the parameter values the author chose.
  2. The Reader's Question — A reader wonders what happens at a different value.
  3. A MicroSim With Sliders — The same plot with built-in controls the reader can move.
  4. Moving the Parameter — The ENOB falls from about 10 bits to about 7.2 as added noise rises to 2 LSB.
  5. One Source, Two Outputs — The page and the screen come from one data file and one script.
  6. Specification to MicroSim — An agent builds the sim from a specification, and a person verifies and approves it.
  7. Embedded Anywhere — The same sim in a lab website and a paper's supplementary material.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
A static figure shows a result at the settings the author chose. A reader who can move the slider understands the whole relationship. A MicroSim suits a result whose point is a dependence, such as how ENOB falls as noise rises. It does not suit a fact with no parameter, such as a die photograph or an author list (Chapter 16). Because an agent can build a small sim from a precise specification, a result can be given a form that others can handle and not only read.

The poster has limits. Interactivity is not always better, and a sim that looks right but computes a slightly wrong number is worse than no sim, so its formulas and boundary cases must be checked as in Chapter 13. The gold thread shows the ideal, where figure and sim come from one script and one data file. It does not mean a MicroSim is generated automatically from a paper. In the MicroSims paper of Chapter 20, claims about effect still have to be labeled measured, cited, or expected.

docs.title: A Folder of Files, a Graph of Knowledge
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read what it shows. The left half is the folder of files. The right half is the same material as a graph. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes.

The seven regions are:

  1. The Folder — Papers, notes, results, and drafts with no recorded relationships.
  2. Keyword Search Only — A search that finds the words you typed and misses the rest.
  3. Links That Mean Nothing — Untyped links that let you navigate but not compute.
  4. Typed Nodes and Edges — Entities with types, joined by named, directed relationships.
  5. A Three-Hop Question — A path of three links that answers what no single note states.
  6. A Grounded Answer — Facts from followed links placed in the prompt, so the answer can be checked.
  7. The Privacy Ring — The part of the graph an agent may not read.

docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
A model forgets everything between sessions, so the only memory a research project has is what you write down. A folder of linked files is a good memory for reading. It is a poor one for asking, because a question such as which papers depend on a corrupted dataset needs several links followed in order. Typed links turn the notes into a graph a program can traverse. The same graph can ground an agent's answer in facts you can check.

The same property has a cost. Whoever can query the graph can see it. Chapter 19 treats this as personal knowledge privacy: partition the graph by data class, give each agent a view of only what its job needs, and review what an agent writes back. The poster does not claim that a graph is always better than a folder. It claims that a graph is better for questions that follow relationships, and that the graph is only as good as its entities and links, which a human must review. The example graph is invented for illustration.

docs.title: From Hunch to Falsifiable Hypothesis
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read what happens at that stage of turning a topic into a testable claim. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes. Two staircases climb toward the same summit. The left one is loose and cloudy and ends in nothing. The right one is sharp and ends in a claim that a result could contradict.

The seven regions are:

  1. Loose Brainstorm — Many cheap ideas, produced without judgment, none yet testable.
  2. Hypothesis Staircase — Problem framed, claim stated, prediction written, measurement chosen, refuting result named.
  3. Ranking Mat — Candidate ideas scored on weighted criteria, where the weights are the decision.
  4. Devil's Advocate — A challenger prompt that asks what would make the idea wrong.
  5. Criterion Set in Advance — The refuting result is decided before any data arrive.
  6. Novelty Check — A search, and not a model's say-so, shows whether the idea is new.
  7. Research Roadmap — A plan with decision points that say continue, change direction, or stop.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
A language model will produce dozens of ideas in a minute, and it tends to agree with the person it is talking to. What it cannot do is decide which idea is worth months of your time. Chapter 14 keeps the volume with the agent and the choice with you. A statement counts as a hypothesis when it names a measurable quantity, a threshold, and conditions, so that some possible observation would contradict it. "Calibration makes the ADC better" cannot be wrong, so it cannot yet be tested.

The poster simplifies. The ranking example uses invented scores, and the scores change when the weights change. The roadmap numbers are illustrative. A falsifiable claim is necessary for research but not sufficient, because it must also be feasible, novel, and worth doing. The matrix on the poster uses the chapter's four criteria of impact, feasibility, novelty, and risk. Cost is part of feasibility in practice but is not a separate column in the chapter.

  4. Layer 2: The Instruction Sheet — The body of SKILL.md, loaded when the skill triggers.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
An agent keeps only the names and descriptions of its skills in context. It reads the full instructions when it decides a skill applies, and it opens a supporting file only when the instructions point to it. This is progressive disclosure. It is why the description is the most important line in the file, and why a vague one means the skill is skipped or fires on the wrong request.

A skill also needs tests in two directions. Trigger tests check that it loads when it should. Near-miss tests check that it stays quiet when it should. The poster teaches the structure and the testing habit. It does not claim that a well-structured skill is correct: you still run behavior tests with known answers. The enob-report skill used here is an illustrative example from the chapters.

docs.title: Many Types of “Chat” Agents
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Everything called a "chat" agent looks the same on screen: a box where you type. What differs is what sits behind the box. Use Explore mode to hover over a numbered marker or its label and read what that kind of agent can do and what it costs you in risk. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the matching tile. Volt, the border collie in the middle, stands for the agent itself; the tiles on the left describe how it runs and the tiles on the right describe what it can reach.

The eight callouts, in order from simplest to most capable, are:

  1. Simple Prompt/Response — One prompt in, one response out, like the original ChatGPT.
  2. Multiple Questions — Session management keeps earlier turns so follow-ups make sense.
  3. Always On — The agent keeps working when your laptop is closed.
  4. Disconnected from Desktop — The agent runs in a virtual machine in the cloud, not on your computer.
  5. Browser Takeover — The agent can use your browser and the sites where you are already signed in.
  6. More Credential Access — The agent holds passwords, keys, or tokens of its own.
  7. Email — The agent can add drafts to your mailbox for you to review and send.
  8. Agent Email — Each agent has its own email address.

Each step down the list gives the agent more reach, and each one needs a matching control: a fresh session, a sandbox, a separate account, a human who presses send.

docs.title: Five Personal Agents, Side by Side
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a column and read what that agent does, how it is kept in check, and what it costs. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the agent it describes.

The five columns are:

  1. Grok Bot (SpaceXAI) — A hosted agent whose bots share one cloud computer and one set of logins.
  2. Dots (OpenAI) — A personal agent inside ChatGPT with its own cloud computer, read-only background access, and approval rules you can write.
  3. Muse (Meta) — A consumer agent in a dedicated cloud VM, with a Sentinel permission layer and approval for each purchase.
  4. Claude Cowork (Anthropic) — A tab in Claude Desktop that works in a local sandbox and is the least always-on of the five.
  5. Gemini Spark (Google) — A consumer agent on dedicated Google Cloud VMs with its own Gmail address, built into Workspace and bundled with the Google AI Ultra tier.

docs.text: All five products arrived within about six months of each other in 2026, and they make the same promise: an agent that carries out multi-step work while you do something else. They differ in where the agent runs, who can see its logins, and how much it can do without asking. For a research group, those differences decide whether an agent can be trusted near unpublished data or a licensed tool chain. Read the Safety Model row before the Price row.

docs.title: The Real Citation and the Fluent Fake
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read what it shows about unchecked and checked references. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes.

The left half shows the careless version and the right half shows the same reference after it has been checked. The strip along the bottom shows the three ways a reference fails.

The nine regions are:

  1. Fluent Reference — A well-formed card that looks right and has not been looked up.
  2. Asking the Model Again — The trap of letting the model certify its own citations.
  3. Same Card, Checked — The identical reference after a lookup you ran yourself.
  4. Does It Exist — The DOI resolves and the exact title is in a database.
  5. Do Details Match — Authors, venue, and year agree with the record.
  6. Does It Support the Claim — The paper says what the citation says it says.
  7. Fabricated — No such paper exists.
  8. Wrong Details — The paper exists, but year, venue, volume, or an author is wrong.
  9. Unsupported Claim — The paper exists and the details are right, but it does not say that.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
A citation has a regular structure, and a model can write a well-formed one about any topic without looking anything up. Chapter 2 names four outcomes for a model-written reference: fabricated, wrong details, unsupported claim, or verified. Chapter 11 adds the tools: a DOI lookup, a script that resolves every DOI in a BibTeX file, and a rule to ask the agent for the location of every claim. Chapter 17 adds the principle behind the left half of the poster: a check must be independent of what it checks, so asking the same model to confirm its own output tells you almost nothing.

The poster does not say that models are usually wrong about references, and it does not give an error rate, because the chapters do not either. The three cards in the failure strip use the chapters' own invented examples. A script can resolve identifiers and compare fields, but only a person who opens the paper can confirm that it supports the sentence it is cited for.

  4. Level 1: Approve Each Step — The agent acts only after each action is approved.

docs.title: The Literature Funnel
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read what happens at that stage and what can go wrong there. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes.

The eight regions are:

  1. Search Strategy — The written procedure of questions, terms, databases, and filters.
  2. Paper Triage — A rubric-based sort into read closely, skim, and set aside.
  3. Claim Extraction — Checkable claims, each with its conditions and location.
  4. Citation Chaining — Following references backward and citations forward.
  5. Citation Verification — Looking up every reference to confirm it exists and matches.
  6. Evidence Synthesis — Combining sources by comparing like with like.
  7. Where the Funnel Leaks — The missed paper, the misread claim, and the fabricated reference.
  8. Claims Tied to Sources — A table of claims with locations and the kind of evidence.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
AI assistance changes the speed of every stage of the literature workflow and none of the standards. An agent can generate search terms, run queries, sort results against your rubric, and pull claims out of papers faster than you can read them. That is breadth, and it is cheap. What the agent cannot do for you is vouch for the result. It can write a well-formatted reference to a paper that does not exist, and it can summarize a paper from its abstract and its expectations.

So each stage has a check you keep: a logged search strategy, a rubric with reasons, a location for every claim, a lookup for every reference, and a table that compares like with like. The poster shows citation chaining as its own stage between extraction and verification. The chapter's numbered pipeline does not list it as a step, and presents chaining as a second way of finding papers that keyword searches miss. The poster does not claim that the pipeline finds every relevant paper. It claims that the pipeline makes its losses visible. The example claims and values are illustrative.

docs.title: The Manuscript Line: Where the Human Stays
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a station and read what the agent does there and what the person keeps. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the station it describes. The line reads left to right across the top row (outline, drafting, co-author review), then left to right across the bottom row (figures, references, submission), as a paper grows from an outline to a submission. A gold handrail marks what stays human, and four stations carry a human stamp.

The six regions are:

  1. Outline From Claims — An outline of claims, each tied to its evidence, with unsupported bullets marked.
  2. Drafting From Evidence — The agent drafts only from supplied claims, and a number check follows each edit.
  3. Co-Author Consistency — Co-author review, with agent-proposed consistency fixes as a list.
  4. Figures and LaTeX — Figures regenerated from scripts, and LaTeX compiled after every substantial edit.
  5. References Checked — Verified BibTeX entries, never retyped by hand.
  6. Submit and Respond — The cover letter, the disclosure note, and a reviewer response that claims only real changes.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
A model can turn notes into prose faster than you can type, and prose that has not passed through your judgment is not your paper. Chapter 15 lets the agent draft and polish while every claim, every number, and the voice stay yours. It names three typical hazards: numbers that change during a revision, references that are fabricated or corrupted, and a drift toward claims larger than the evidence. Authorship carries accountability that a language model cannot take, so AI use is disclosed and an AI system is not listed as an author (Chapters 15 and 18).

The poster simplifies in three ways. It shows four human stamps, but a person should read every station, and the stamps mark the decisions that cannot be delegated. Pairing each hazard with one station is a teaching device, since several checks can catch the same error. And policies on disclosure differ and change, so read the current rules of your venue and institution at submission time.

docs.title: The Window That Fills Up
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over a numbered marker or its label and read what that part of the window does. Use Quiz mode to read the name in the prompt, then click the marker that matches. The marker numbers are hidden, so you must find the matching part of the three tubes.

Read the poster from top to bottom. The top tube is comfortable. The middle tube is crowded after a second paste. The bottom tube has lost its oldest content without any warning.

The eleven callouts are:

  1. Budget Ruler — The subtraction that tells you what is left.
  2. System Prompt — Standing instructions that spend budget on every turn.
  3. The Paper Block — A pasted document, counted in tokens.
  4. Token Meter — Equations and code cost more tokens per word than prose.
  5. Middle Gets Overlooked — Material in the middle of a long prompt is used less well.
  6. Room for the Answer — The space the completion draws from the same pool.
  7. Silent Overflow — The oldest content slides off and nothing looks wrong.
  8. Conversation History — Earlier turns, resent each time, that pile up.
  9. The Second Paste — The step that fills the window.
  10. Cut-Off Answer — A reply that stops partway because the window is full.
  11. Model Working Unaware — The model carries on without what it lost.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
A model can only use what is in its window, and the completion draws from the same pool as the prompt. Chapter 2 gives the arithmetic: the window minus the system prompt, history, attachments, and your message is what remains for the answer. In the chapter's worked example a 32,000-token window handles one 11,000-token paper comfortably and cannot finish a 6,000-token summary after a second paper. The dangerous case is the quiet one, where many tools drop the oldest content instead of reporting an error.

The poster is a schematic. The block widths are roughly to scale for the chapter's illustrative numbers, and the glow across the papers shows the chapter's point that the middle of a very long prompt is used less well, not a measurement. Real window sizes differ by model and change with each release, so look up the current figure in the provider's documentation. Chapter 4 covers what to do about it: select, summarize, compress, and restart with a short summary.

docs.title: Twenty Planners, Ten Doers, One Researcher
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over a numbered marker or its label and read what that part of the team does. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the marker that matches. The marker numbers are hidden in Quiz mode, so you must find the matching part of the stage. Planners are on the top tier, the task belt is in the middle, and the doers are at the bottom.

The twelve callouts are:

  1. Task Queue — The ordered list of waiting tasks, kept as a plain file everyone reads.
  2. Handoff Card — The goal, inputs, constraints, criteria, and status that pass from one agent to the next.
  3. Planning Agent Bank — About twenty agents that explore, decompose, and specify.
  4. Review Checkpoint — A point where output is examined before the next step uses it, often automated.
  5. Human Approval Gate — A checkpoint where a person must say yes.
  6. Attention Meter — The review budget that sets how big a team can usefully be.
  7. Execution Agent Bank — About ten agents that carry out specified tasks.
  8. Shared Workspace — The common area for files, with separate outputs and reviewed merges.
  9. Critical Path — The longest chain of dependent tasks, which extra agents cannot shorten.
  10. Status Board — The morning report: finished, blocked, needs a decision, and spent.
  11. The Orchestrator — The researcher, who coordinates the work and stays accountable.
  12. Conflict Flag — Two agents with incompatible results, traced to the first point of divergence.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Chapter 10 describes an agent team as planning agents plus execution agents with explicit handoffs. Planning output is cheap and reversible, so many plans can run in parallel. Execution output changes files and costs more attention to check, so that side stays smaller. The chapter's arithmetic makes the point: 20 planners, 10 executors, and 30 minutes of conflict resolution need 300 minutes of review, which is more than a 4-hour budget unless you sample, automate checks, or shrink the team.

The numbers on the poster are the chapter's illustrative figures. The 20-to-10 ratio is a design target, not a law, and the right team size depends on how checkable your tasks are and how much attention you have. The poster does not claim that more agents get more done. Dependencies, review cost, and coordination all cap the benefit.

docs.title: Vague Prompt, Engineered Context
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read what it adds to the prompt and why. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes.

The left half is the vague prompt and what it leaves to chance. The right half is the same task with the context engineered. The model, the laptop, and the input file are the same on both sides.

The nine regions are:

  1. One-Line Prompt — A short request with everything else left in the researcher's head.
  2. Guessed Gaps — The choices the model makes wherever the prompt is silent.
  3. Vague Result — A fluent answer that cannot be checked or used.
  4. Task and Inputs — The goal, a role, the source material, and the definitions of terms.
  5. Constraints — Limits on sources and scope, plus a sanctioned way to say not stated.
  6. Acceptance Criteria — Testable conditions written before the prompt is run.
  7. Output Format — A known shape that a script or a glance can validate.
  8. Prompt Test Plate — A fixed set of samples run through the prompt after every change.
  9. Checked Result — A grounded answer with its limits and assumptions stated.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Chapter 3 treats a prompt as a specification and Chapter 4 widens that to the whole input: what is present, what is absent, and how you will know the result is acceptable. The idea is that a weak result is often the apparatus, not the instrument. In Chapter 4's worked example, the same model and the same request gave a different and useful answer once the procedure section, a definition, and a standing instruction were added. Nothing about the model changed. Only the input did.

The poster does not promise that an engineered context makes a model correct. Source grounding, chain of thought, and self critique help but do not replace an external check, which is the subject of Chapter 17. The ENOB criteria and the paper-summary example are the chapters' own illustrative cases, not measured results.

docs.title: Verified Is Not Validated
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read what it shows about verification, validation, and the checks that sit between them. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes.

The eight regions are:

  1. Verification Checkpoint — An inspector checks the board and code against the blueprint.
  2. The Green Checklist — Every line is ticked, and the ticks only vouch for the build.
  3. Validation Checkpoint — The same board on a real bench, facing the real problem.
  4. Waveforms That Disagree — The measured trace and the simulated trace do not match.
  5. The Flaw That Travels — A small flaw in the blueprint rides through every verified stage.
  6. Independent Check — The same quantity computed by a route with different failure causes.
  7. Primary Source Check — Going to the original paper, datasheet, or standard.
  8. Cross-Model Check — Asking a different model or a fresh session and comparing.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Verification asks whether the work was done right. Validation asks whether the right thing was done. A design can be fully verified against a specification that was wrong, and it will be wrong in exactly the way the specification was. Agents make this easy to miss, because an agent will faithfully implement the question as you stated it. If the question was framed badly, every verified result answers the wrong thing.

The three checks on the poster all guard the verification side. An independent check has failure causes different from the thing checked. A primary source check goes to the original document. A cross-model check is a cheap screen in which agreement is weak evidence and disagreement is a flag. None of them settles validation on its own. The poster does not claim any check proves a result is true. It shows which question each check can answer. The numbers in the chapter's examples are illustrative.

docs.title: Where Does Your Data Go?
docs.text:
Open the interactive poster full screen

Use Explore mode to hover over or click a panel and read where data goes when you use a hosted model, what changes when you run one yourself, and how to sort documents before you paste. Use Quiz mode to read a clue and click the panel it describes.

The eight regions are:

  1. Out Through the Window — A hosted model sends your documents out of the lab.
  2. The Cloud End — At the far end, the provider's terms decide retention, access, and training.
  3. Inside the Lab Boundary — A model you run keeps documents inside the lab.
  4. You Maintain It — Self-hosting brings setup, security, and upkeep work.
  5. Green Lane — Public material that may go to any tool.
  6. Yellow Lane — Internal and unpublished material that needs a decision first.
  7. Red Lane — Obligated data that stays off hosted tools.
  8. The Lab Policy Sheet — The one-page lab AI policy that writes the rules down.

docs.title: Static Poster
docs.text: The full-size poster above is a static copy of the interactive version, handy for printing, sharing, or viewing without JavaScript.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Placing unpublished results in a hosted AI tool is a disclosure to a third party under the provider's terms, and a disclosure cannot be undone. Research holds more than your own results: participants' personal data, sponsor data, and vendor files under non-disclosure agreements. The remedy is a small classification that people can apply without looking it up, and a one-page lab policy that says which class may go to which tool.

The three traffic-light lanes simplify the four data classes of Chapter 18, and the classification there is illustrative. Policies on AI use, data protection, export control, and ownership differ between institutions, funders, journals, and countries, and they change. This poster is not legal advice. It also does not rank any product. Chapter 19 teaches the questions to ask of any hosted or self-hosted agent, and the claims it records about products are vendor-stated.

The seven columns are:

  1. Ada: Chief of Staff — Your assistant and the coordinator of all six other agents. Ada keeps your knowledge graph, email, and calendar.
  2. Scout: Novelty and Prior-Art Search — Searches papers, patents, and code to answer "is this idea really new?"
  3. Marisol: Events and Speakers — Runs the department seminar calendar and the speaker pipeline, from invitation to confirmation.
  4. Penny: Lab Budgets and Finance — Tracks grant spending, forecasts overruns, and drafts purchase requests and expense reports.
  5. Rosa: Grant Writing — Finds funding calls and drafts, critiques, and tracks proposals through the deadline.
  6. Pixel: Presentations and Web — Builds slide decks, posters, and figures, and keeps your university web page current.
  7. Kai: Conferences and Proposals — Tracks calls for papers, vets venues, and drafts abstracts, talk proposals, and travel.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: One general-purpose assistant that does everything is hard to check, because you cannot tell which of its jobs went wrong. A team of narrow agents is easier to supervise: each has one job, one color, one task list, and clear rules about what it does alone, what it asks about first, and what it never does. Seeing the whole team in one picture shows where the work is divided, and where the hand-offs are, such as Scout's prior-art summary feeding Rosa's proposal or Kai's travel estimate feeding Penny's budget. In every column the pattern is the same: the agent drafts and prepares, and a person sends, submits, signs, and pays.

docs.title: Adoption Plan Prioritizer
docs.text: Run the Adoption Plan Prioritizer MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An adoption plan is the staged introduction of AI research practices into a research group or a personal workflow. The sequence matters, because several steps are prerequisites for the safe use of the later ones. This MicroSim asks you to prioritize six steps:

Step Description A Write the lab AI use policy, with the data classes and permitted tools (Chapter 18). B Set up a shared repository with an instruction file and a project knowledge base (Chapters 5 and 6). C Pilot one skill on one repeatable task at autonomy level 1 or 2, such as citation verification (Chapters 7, 9, and 11). D Add verification checks and a reproducibility package to the pilot (Chapters 13 and 17). E Scale to a small agent team on one project, with review gates (Chapter 10). F Review the metrics at 90 days, such as time saved, review load, and errors that escaped, and decide what to expand or stop.

An order is valid when A comes before C, B before C, C before D, D before E, and E before F. A and B may be in either order, so there are two valid orders. When an order is invalid, the sim names the first violated dependency: reading your sequence from the top, the first step that comes before one of its prerequisites (if step C comes before both A and B, A is named).

Learning objective: prioritize six adoption steps for a research group into an order that respects their dependencies, and state the dependency that justifies each constraint.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. The six steps start in a scrambled order. The question on screen is Which steps must come first, and why?
  2. Pick a step in the drop-down list below the drawing. The list shows each step's current position, for example Step C (#4), and the picked step is outlined in dark blue.
  3. Press Earlier or Later to move the picked step up or down one position. All controls work with the Tab key and Enter or Space.
  4. Press Submit Order. The sim reports Valid order. with the list of dependencies and their reasons, or Invalid: C needs A first. (for example) with the reason for that dependency. It then shows both valid orders and the dependency graph; the broken dependency is drawn as a dashed arrow marked with a cross.
  5. On a narrow screen the feedback opens on its own page; press Next Page to read more and to return to the steps.
  6. Only the first submission counts as evidence. You may rearrange the steps and submit again afterward; later submissions are marked as practice, and the status line keeps the result of the first one.

  • Bloom level: Evaluate
  • Bloom verb: prioritize

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Prioritize (5 min): Before moving anything, decide which steps must come before the pilot and which must wait for it. Arrange the steps and submit once.
  2. Justify (5 min): Read the reason for each dependency. Explain why A and B may be swapped without effect, and why scaling to a team is not the first step after a pilot.

docs.title: Evidence of Mastery
docs.text:
• The learner arranges six steps in a sequence and submits. The order is correct when every dependency holds (A before C, B before C, C before D, D before E, E before F).
  • Mastery: a valid order on the first submission. The status line shows whether the first submission was valid.
  • Reading the step descriptions, and later practice submissions, are exploration and are not evidence.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 20: Case Studies and Capstone Project - the section "Adopting These Practices" is the source of the six steps and their dependencies.

docs.title: Agent Autonomy Level Assigner
docs.text: Run the Agent Autonomy Level Assigner MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Agent autonomy is a dial, not a switch, and the right setting depends on the task and not on how capable the model is. This MicroSim asks you to recommend an autonomy level for each of eight illustrative research tasks from three attributes of the task:

  • Reversible? Can the effect be undone?
  • Leaves your control? Does the result leave your control, by being sent, published, or written to a shared system? (reach)
  • Verifiable quickly? Can you or a script check the result quickly and objectively?
Level Name The agent may 0 Suggest only Propose; you perform the action 1 Approve each step Act after you approve each action 2 Act within a boundary Act freely inside a defined scope, and stop at gates for your approval 3 Act and report Act unattended and report afterwards

The answer for every task follows from the assignment rule in Chapter 9, applied in this order: if the result leaves your control and cannot be verified, the level is 0; if it leaves your control and can be verified, the level is 1; if it stays local but cannot be undone, the level is 1; if it is local and reversible but cannot be checked quickly, the level is 2; if it is local, reversible, and verifiable, the level is 3. The tasks are invented for illustration.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the task card. The question on screen is How much should the agent do on its own? The card shows the three attributes of the task, and the four levels are listed below it with what the agent may do at each one. No level is chosen at the start.
  2. Press Level 0, Level 1, Level 2, or Level 3 to choose a level. You can change your choice until you submit.
  3. Press Submit. Each task gets one attempt. The sim shows Correct: level n. or The rule gives level n., the reason for the answer, and the rule that applied. The rule's level is outlined and marked with a check mark; a wrong choice is marked with an X.
  4. Press Next Task to continue. The eight tasks always come in the same order.
  5. After task 8, press See Score. The summary shows n of 8 correct, whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met, and how many tasks fell at each level. Start Over returns to task 1.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will recommend an autonomy level from 0 to 3 for each of eight research tasks from its reversibility, reach, and verifiability, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

  • Bloom level: Evaluate
  • Bloom verb: recommend

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Agent autonomy, reversibility, reach, verifiability, and the four autonomy levels, all defined in the section "Autonomy and Supervision" of Chapter 9.

docs.title: Evidence of Mastery
docs.text: For each of the eight tasks the learner commits one of the four levels. A level is correct when it equals the level given by the assignment rule. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the task attributes is exploration and is not evidence.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• A capable model deserves more autonomy on every task.
  • Anything local is safe to run unattended.
  • If a result is outward-bound, a quick look at it is enough.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 9: Supervising Agents and Defining Agent Roles - the section "Autonomy and Supervision" defines the three task properties, the four autonomy levels, and the assignment rule used for the answer key.

docs.title: Personal Agent Comparison Criteria Matcher
docs.text: Run the Personal Agent Comparison Criteria Matcher MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Personal agents change from month to month, but the questions a researcher should ask of them do not. This MicroSim practises turning a worry about an agent into the comparison criterion that addresses it. Each of eight questions belongs under exactly one of eight criteria:

Criterion What it covers Where it runs Where the computation and the data are located: your laptop, the vendor's cloud, or a server you manage Blast radius How far a failure, compromise, or injected instruction can spread Approval model The policy that decides which actions need a human Usage metering How consumption is counted, capped, and billed Data exposure What happens to the data given to the agent: training, retention, access Memory Whether you can inspect and control what the agent keeps between sessions Claim verification Independent evidence behind what the vendor advertises Activity audit The record of the agent's actions that is available for review

The criteria come from the section "Risks That Define the Criteria" in Chapter 19. The questions are invented for illustration and do not describe any one product. The order of the criterion buttons is shuffled for each learner, so the position of a button tells you nothing about the answer.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is Which criterion does this question test?
  2. Press one of the eight criterion buttons below the drawing area. Your choice is marked with a filled circle and a dark background. You can change it until you submit.
  3. Press Submit. Each question gets one attempt. The feedback reads Correct: criterion. (with a check mark) or This asks about criterion. (with an X), followed by the "Why" sentence. The correct criterion's button is marked with a check mark and a solid border; a wrong pick is marked with an X and a dashed border.
  4. Press Next Question to continue. The questions come in a fixed order.
  5. After question 8, press See Score. The end screen shows n of 8 correct, whether you met the mastery threshold of 7, and a one-line test for each criterion that you could run on a real product. On narrow screens, press More Tests to page through the tests.

All controls are buttons that can be reached with the Tab key and pressed with Enter or Space. To try again with a new criteria order, reload the page.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Learning objective: The learner will classify each of eight questions about a personal agent under the comparison criterion it addresses, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Bloom level and verb: Understand (L2), classify.

Evidence of mastery: For each of eight questions the learner commits one of eight criteria. A classification is correct when it equals the answer key. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the list of criteria is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions to watch for:

  • A comparison is about features and price only.
  • A vendor's statement about safety is itself the verification.
  • Where an agent runs is the same as what it can reach.

Duration: 10 minutes.

Prerequisites: agent blast radius, usage metering, agent data exposure, vendor claim verification, overnight activity audit, cloud agent computer, self-hosted agent, and the approval model, as defined in the sections "What Makes an Agent Personal and Always-On" and "Risks That Define the Criteria" of Chapter 19.

Follow-up: Pick one agent you might use and run two of the one-line tests from the end screen with a throwaway account and synthetic data. Record what you found for each criterion.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 19: Always-On Personal Agents for Research - the section "Risks That Define the Criteria" defines the eight criteria used in this MicroSim.

docs.title: Agent Failure Log Triage
docs.text: Run the Agent Failure Log Triage MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Agents fail in recognizable ways, and naming the pattern is the first step to catching it. This MicroSim shows six short excerpts of an agent log, written as raw log lines the way you would meet them after an overnight run, and asks you to differentiate which failure mode each one shows:

Failure mode What it means Premature completion The agent reports success without having run the check that defines success. Hallucinated result The agent reports a number or file that no tool produced. Scope drift The agent fixes something nobody asked it to touch. Test weakening Faced with a failing test, the agent edits the test and not the code. Wrong arguments The agent calls the right tool with the wrong path, parameter, or units. Runaway loop The agent repeats an action without progress.

Each excerpt shows exactly one of the six modes. After each answer the sim gives the reason and the mechanical defense for that mode from Table 2 of Chapter 9. The log lines are invented for illustration.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the log excerpt in the white box. The question on screen is What went wrong here? Lines that start with a time stamp are log entries; lines in gray italics are notes about the log. The six failure modes are listed below the excerpt with their definitions.
  2. Choose a failure mode in the drop-down below the drawing. You can change the choice until you submit.
  3. Press Submit. Each excerpt gets one attempt. The sim shows Correct: mode. or This is mode., the reason, and the mechanical defense for that mode. The correct mode is outlined and marked with a check mark; a wrong choice is marked with an X. On a narrow screen the list shows the mode names only after you submit, so that the feedback fits.
  4. Press Next Excerpt to continue. The six excerpts always come in the same order.
  5. After excerpt 6, press See Score. The summary shows n of 6 correct and whether the mastery threshold of 5 was met. Start Over returns to excerpt 1.

docs.text:
The learner will differentiate six agent failure modes from six excerpts of an agent log, with at least 5 of 6 attributed correctly.

  • Bloom level: Analyze
  • Bloom verb: differentiate

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: The six agent failure modes defined in the section "Logging, Failure Modes, and Runaway Agents" of Chapter 9.

docs.title: Evidence of Mastery
docs.text: For each of the six log excerpts the learner commits one of the six failure modes. A choice is correct when it equals the mode in the answer key. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration and is not evidence.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• A passing test run means the work is correct.
  • An agent that touched extra files was being thorough.
  • Repeated tool calls mean the agent is working hard.

docs.text: 1. Chapter 9: Supervising Agents and Defining Agent Roles - the section "Logging, Failure Modes, and Runaway Agents" defines the six failure modes, and its Table 2 gives the mechanical defense for each.

docs.title: Agent Knowledge Graph Update Architecture
docs.text: Run the Agent Knowledge Graph Update Architecture MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Agents communicate through four levels, and each level controls its own knowledge graph:

  1. Personal Researcher Agents at the bottom, controlled by each researcher.
  2. EECD Department Agents, managed by the Electrical Engineering and Computer Design department.
  3. College of Science and Engineering (CSE) Agents.
  4. University of Minnesota Agents at the top.

Every level holds the same three knowledge nodes: Annual Budget, AI Usage Policy, and NSF Grant Award. Because each level owns its own copy, a fact is only true at a level once that level's agent has updated its node. Three buttons send an update through the levels so you can see which agent hands the fact to which, and in what order the nodes change.

Button Direction What happens Budget Information Top-down A new annual budget is issued at the University level. Each agent updates its Annual Budget node and passes the budget to the agent below. NSF Grant Award Bottom-up NSF notifies a researcher that a grant was awarded. The researcher agent updates its node and reports upward, so each level's NSF Grant Award node changes. AI Usage Policy Change Both ways from CSE The CSE agent adopts a policy that allows researchers to use Claude Desktop. It informs the University above and the EECD department below, and the change reaches the researcher agents.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the starting state. Every node shows its old value: FY2026, Claude Desktop ✗, and 0 awards. Nothing moves until you press a button.
  2. Press Budget Information, NSF Grant Award, or AI Usage Policy Change.
  3. Watch the colored message travel between agents. The status line under the graph says which step is happening, such as "Step 3 of 7".
  4. When a message reaches a knowledge node, the node pulses and changes to its new value (FY2027 ✔, Claude Desktop ✔, 1 award ✔).
  5. Press Reset to return every node to its starting value, then try another button. The three event buttons are disabled while an update is running.
  6. Hover over any node for a short description of what it holds.

docs.text:

        height="532px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will explain how a knowledge update travels through a four-level agent hierarchy and which agents must update their own knowledge graph for the fact to become true at every level (Bloom: Understand, verb: explain).

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty (AI for EE Research).

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• What an AI agent is and what a knowledge base is (see Chapter 6 and Chapter 8).
  • Awareness that a university has several organizational levels (department, college, university).

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Press each of the three buttons in turn, pressing Reset between them. Before each press, predict which nodes will change and in what order, then compare your prediction with the run.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): For each event, name the agent that originates the update and the agents that only relay it. In the policy event, explain why the CSE agent sends the change in two directions.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Without the sim, sketch a fourth event of your own (for example, a new data-retention rule from the University). State where it starts, which direction it flows, and which node each agent must update.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• A learner who has met the objective can say that each level updates its own knowledge graph, so one message must be relayed by every agent between the source and the destination.
  • They can identify that Budget Information starts at the top, NSF Grant Award starts at the bottom, and the AI Usage Policy Change starts in the middle and fans out in both directions.
  • Watch for the misconception that a change at one level is automatically visible at the others. In this architecture a level's graph stays out of date until its agent updates it.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 8: Agents, Tool Use, and Subagents - describes how agents pass work and information to other agents.
  2. Chapter 6: Knowledge Bases and Skill Anatomy - describes the knowledge bases that each agent in this sim keeps up to date.
  3. vis-network documentation - the JavaScript network library used to draw the graph.

docs.title: Agent Loop Stepper
docs.text: Run the Agent Loop Stepper MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An agent does not plan everything in one step and then execute. It works in a loop: the model decides on an action and emits a tool call, the harness runs the tool, and the result is added to the context, where the model reads it before deciding again. This MicroSim steps through one short loop so that you can infer each next action from what the agent has observed so far.

The task, shown at the start, is: "The ENOB of capture-07.csv is 6.1 bits but the converter should give about 9. Find out why." The agent has three tools: read_file, run_python, and list_files. The files, results, and numbers are invented for illustration, and the sim labels them "Illustrative data".

At each of five steps you see three candidate next actions. Exactly one is correct: the one that follows from the results observed so far and does not exceed the scope of the task. You predict before the agent's actual choice is shown, so your mental model of the loop is tested at every step.

The strip of five boxes across the top shows the stages of one pass through the loop from the chapter: Decide (model), Call (model), Run (harness), Observe (harness to model), and Repeat or stop (model). The active stage has a thick border and a triangle marker.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the task, the tools, and the Context panel, which lists the calls and results the agent has seen so far. At the start it says Nothing yet. and the question on screen is What should the agent do first?
  2. Read candidates A, B, and C, then press Choose A, Choose B, or Choose C. The press commits your prediction, and each step allows one attempt.
  3. Read the feedback. A correct prediction shows Correct. with the reason. An incorrect one shows the agent's action and the reason. The agent's action is outlined and marked The agent's action with a check mark; a different prediction is marked Your prediction with an X.
  4. Watch the stage strip: the model emits the call, the harness runs it, and the result appears in the Context panel marked [new]. On wide screens the full sequence stays listed under the feedback.
  5. Press Next Step to continue. At step 5 the agent gives a final answer instead of a tool call, so the Run and Observe stages are marked skipped and the loop stops.
  6. After step 5, press See Full Loop. The summary shows n of 5 correct, whether you reached mastery (4 of 5), and the whole loop as a list of calls and results with your prediction at each step.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Tool use, tool definition, tool call, and the agent loop, from the section "Tool Use and the Agent Loop" in Chapter 8
  • The roles of the model and the harness: the model emits a tool call, and the harness executes it and returns the result to the context

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will infer the agent's next tool call at each of five steps of a loop that diagnoses a low ENOB result, given the task and the results observed so far, with at least 4 of 5 correct.

  • Bloom level: Understand
  • Bloom verb: infer

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Prediction (5 min): Step through the loop once. Before each choice, say in one sentence what the latest result tells the agent.
  2. Discussion (5 min): Using the summary list, trace how each result shaped the next call. Identify where the loop would have gone wrong if the agent had acted before measuring (step 3) or had edited the project file instead of testing on a copy (step 4).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Evidence of mastery: at each of five steps the learner commits one of three candidate next actions before the agent's actual choice is shown. A prediction is correct when it equals the action marked correct in the specification. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct.
  • Stepping forward after the reveal is exploration and is not evidence of mastery.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The model runs the tools itself. (The stage strip shows that the harness runs every call.)
  • The agent decides everything in one planning step and then executes. (Each action depends on the previous result.)
  • An error result ends the loop. (Every result goes back to the model, and the loop stops only when the model judges the task complete or a limit is reached.)

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 8: Agents, Tool Use, and Subagents - the section "Tool Use and the Agent Loop" defines tool use, tool calls, the harness, and the five stages of the loop used in this sim.

docs.title: Agent Permission Boundary Judge
docs.text: Run the Agent Permission Boundary Judge MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Permissions are the rules a harness checks before it runs a tool call: a call is allowed, needs your approval, or is denied. This MicroSim asks you to judge ten actions that an agent might propose in an ADC project against a short, illustrative policy. The policy has three outcomes, so you must weigh reversibility and scope, not only choose between allow and deny.

The rules apply in this order, and the first match decides:

Rule Condition Outcome 1 Reads or writes any path outside the project directory, or reads credentials or key files Deny 2 Any command that downloads and executes code, or uses elevated privileges Deny 3 Writes to data/raw/ Deny 4 Deletes files, installs packages, pushes to a remote, or sends data over the network Ask 5 Reads files in the project, or edits files in scripts/ or docs/, or runs a Python script from scripts/ Allow

The policy and the actions are invented for illustration, and the sim labels the policy "Illustrative policy". The domain example.com used in one action is reserved for documentation.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the policy and action 1. The question on screen is What does the policy say about this action?
  2. Press Allow, Ask, or Deny. The press commits your judgment, and each action allows one attempt.
  3. Read the feedback. A correct judgment shows Correct: .; an incorrect one shows The policy gives . Both are followed by the matching rule number and the reason. In the policy, the rules checked before the match are marked no match, the deciding rule is outlined and marked first match, and later rules are marked not checked.
  4. Press Next Action to continue. After action 10, press See Score.
  5. The summary shows n of 10 correct, whether the mastery threshold of 8 was met, and the actions the policy sends to Ask. These are the approvals the researcher would see.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)
