docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• File access, shell commands, and code execution, from the section "Reaching Files, Shells, and Code" in Chapter 8
  • Sandboxing, permissions, and permission modes, from the section "Sandboxing and Permissions" in Chapter 8

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will judge, for each of ten proposed agent actions, whether a stated permission policy allows it, requires approval, or denies it, with at least 8 of 10 correct.

  • Bloom level: Evaluate
  • Bloom verb: judge

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Judgment (5 min): Judge all ten actions. For each one, find the first rule that matches before you press a button.
  2. Discussion (5-10 min): Look at the three Ask actions in the summary. For each, say what makes it irreversible or outward-bound. Then compare action 2 (edit a script, Allow) with action 4 (overwrite raw data, Deny): both change a file inside the project, so what separates them?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Evidence of mastery: for each of ten actions the learner commits one of three outcomes. An outcome is correct when it equals the outcome given by the policy. Mastery is at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.
  • Reading the policy is exploration and is not evidence of mastery.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any action inside the project directory is safe. (Overwriting raw data is inside the project and is denied.)
  • A command is safe if it is common. (pip install and git push are common and still need approval.)
  • Approval is needed for everything that changes a file. (Edits in scripts/ and docs/ are allowed, because version control can undo them.)

docs.text: 1. Chapter 8: Agents, Tool Use, and Subagents - the sections "Reaching Files, Shells, and Code" and "Sandboxing and Permissions" define the tool families, permissions, and the policy pattern used in this sim.

docs.title: AI Use Disclosure Decision Helper
docs.text: Run the AI Use Disclosure Decision Helper MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A general principle such as "disclose substantive AI use" is hard to act on until it is written as specific rules and tried on real cases. This MicroSim gives you a five-rule lab policy and asks you to apply it to eight scenarios from an electrical engineering project. The policy is an illustrative lab policy, not a real venue's policy. Real journal, conference, and institutional policies differ and change, so read the current author guidelines of each venue at submission time.

Rule Statement 1 Text drafted or substantially rewritten by an AI tool that appears in a submitted manuscript is disclosed in the paper. 2 AI use to generate or analyze data, code, or figures that contribute to reported results is disclosed in the paper, with the tool and version. 3 Grammar, spelling, and formatting assistance does not need to be disclosed. 4 AI use for brainstorming or literature search that does not appear in the paper is recorded in the project log only. 5 An AI system is never listed as an author.

For each scenario you choose one of four actions: Disclose in the paper, Record in the project log only, No disclosure needed, or Not permitted. The policy has gradations on purpose, so that you separate a disclosure in the paper from a project log entry and from no record at all. After the eighth scenario the sim assembles a draft disclosure statement from the scenarios that required disclosure in the paper. The draft is illustrative and is not legal advice: the tool name, model version, and date of use are left as placeholders to fill in from your project log.

Learning objective: apply a five-rule illustrative lab disclosure policy to eight scenarios of AI use and give the required action for each, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the policy at the top and scenario 1 in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is What does the policy require here?
  2. Choose an action from the drop-down list below the drawing area and press Submit. Each scenario has one attempt, and the answer cannot be changed after you submit it.
  3. Read the feedback. A correct answer shows Correct. with a check mark; an incorrect answer shows The policy gives the required action, with an X. Both show the rule number and the reason, and the matching rule is outlined and marked with an arrow in the policy.
  4. Press Next Scenario to continue. The scenarios come in a fixed order.
  5. After scenario 8, press See Score. The summary shows n of 8 correct, whether you met the mastery threshold of 7, and a draft disclosure statement built from the scenarios that required disclosure in the paper. Reload the page to start again.

docs.title: Citation Chaining Explorer
docs.text: Run the Citation Chaining Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Citation chaining is finding papers by following the citation links of a paper you already have. Backward chaining follows a paper's reference list to the earlier work it builds on. Forward chaining follows the papers that cite it to the later work that builds on it.

The graph shows eight papers. They are illustrative: the papers, years, and links are invented for this exercise. An arrow from X to Y means X cites Y. The seed paper S (2022) is highlighted, older papers sit on the left, and newer papers sit on the right.

Paper Year Role S 2022 Seed paper A 2018 Cited by S B 2019 Cited by S C 2020 Cited by S F 2017 Cited by B and by C D 2023 Cites S E 2024 Cites S and C G 2025 Cites D

You answer five questions in a fixed order. The question on screen is Which papers does this procedure find? Each question names a procedure, such as backward chaining one step from S, and you select the set of papers it finds. The seed paper S is never part of an answer. After each answer the sim highlights the edges the procedure follows and explains why.

docs.text:
1. Click any paper in the graph, or use the Paper details buttons, to read its year, role, the papers it cites, and the papers that cite it. You can also drag papers to see the links more clearly. This is exploration and is not scored.
  2. Read the question in the right-hand panel (below the graph on narrow screens).
  3. Check every paper that answers the question. Your selections are marked in the graph with a dot (●). Then press Submit answer (or press Enter on a checkbox). Each question has one attempt.
  4. Read the feedback. A correct answer shows "Correct." and the reason. An incorrect answer shows the correct set and the reason. In both cases the correct papers are marked with a check mark (✓), a wrong pick with an X (✗) and a dashed border, and the edges the procedure follows are drawn thick.
  5. Press Next question to continue. After question 5 the panel shows your score as n of 5 correct and whether you met the mastery threshold of 4. Compare the years of the papers each direction of chaining reached.

docs.title: Citation Verification Judge
docs.text: Run the Citation Verification Judge MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A fabricated citation is the signature hallucination of research use: it is well formed, so it passes a glance. Citations fail in four distinct ways, and this MicroSim asks you to judge which one applies to each of eight records, using the evidence of a simulated database lookup rather than the look of the citation.

Verdict Meaning Verified The paper exists, the details match, and the paper supports the claim Wrong details The paper exists, but year, venue, volume, pages, or an author is wrong Unsupported claim The paper exists and the details are right, but it does not say what the model claimed Fabricated No such paper exists

The verdict follows a fixed order of checks. If the exact title is not found, or the DOI resolves to a different paper, the verdict is Fabricated. Otherwise, if the authors, venue, or year do not match the database, the verdict is Wrong details. Otherwise, if the paper's text does not support the claim, the verdict is Unsupported claim. Otherwise the verdict is Verified.

All eight records are invented for this exercise. Authors, titles, claims, and DOIs are not real, and the DOI prefix 10.9999 is not assigned. Each lookup result is marked with a symbol as well as a color: a check mark for yes, an X for no, an exclamation mark for a DOI that resolves to a different paper, and a dash for not applicable.

Learning objective: judge each of eight model-generated citations as verified, wrong details, unsupported claim, or fabricated, using the results of a simulated database lookup, with at least 7 of 8 judged correctly.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read record 1: the model's citation and the claim the model attached to it. The question on screen is Is this citation safe to use as written?
  2. Open the four lookup checks in any order with Check DOI, Check title, Check details (authors, venue, and year), and Check text (does the paper's text support the claim). Each button reveals that check's result for the record.
  3. Choose a verdict from the list and press Submit. You have one attempt per record.
  4. Read the feedback. Correct shows the verdict and the reason. Not quite shows the reason, the correct verdict, and the misconception the record tests. All four lookup results are opened after you submit.
  5. Press Next Record. After record 8, press See Score to see n of 8 correct, whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met, and the missed verdicts grouped by the misconception each exposes. On a narrow screen, press More Missed Records to page through the list.

docs.title: Context Selection Budget
docs.text: Run the Context Selection Budget MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Including everything in the context window is the wrong default. It costs tokens, it risks truncation, and irrelevant material gives the model more to be distracted by. This MicroSim asks you to prioritize nine candidate context items for one task:

"Check whether the ENOB reported in Section 4 of my draft is consistent with the measurement procedure in Section 3."

The window is 8,000 tokens. A completion reserve of 1,500 tokens is held back, so the context budget is 6,500 tokens. Each item lists its size as is and, for three of the items, its size if compressed. You give each item one verdict:

Verdict Tokens it adds to the running total Include The size as is Compress The size if compressed (only for items that list one) Omit 0

Including every item as is totals 33,000 tokens, so you must choose. The test for each item is the question on screen: Would the answer change if this item were missing? The task, items, sizes, and budget are invented for illustration, and the sim labels them illustrative.

Learning objective: prioritize nine candidate context items for a stated task by assigning each one the verdict include, compress, or omit, so that the total fits a stated token budget and at least 8 of 9 verdicts match the answer key.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the task in the box at the top and the budget statement below it. The meter shows the running total against the 6,500-token budget; the hatched part to the right is the 1,500-token completion reserve.
  2. Choose an item in the Item drop-down list (the selected row is outlined and marked with ▶), then press Include, Compress, or Omit. Compress is available only for items that list a compressed size. The selection moves to the next item, and the running total updates after every choice. You can change any verdict before you submit.
  3. When all nine items have a verdict, press Submit. If the total is over 6,500, the submission is refused with the message Over budget by n tokens. Compress or omit something. Change a verdict and submit again.
  4. After the one accepted submission, the sim shows n of 9 correct, your final total, the correct total of 4,350 tokens, and whether you met mastery. Each item then shows Correct or Incorrect with the correct verdict and the reason. For a wrong verdict it also says whether you dropped a needed item, or how many tokens the choice adds and whether that alone would push an otherwise correct selection over the budget. Press Next Page to see the rest of the items.

Try including the related-work section along with an otherwise correct selection. The total becomes 6,850 tokens, which is 350 over the budget.

docs.title: Context Window Budget Calculator
docs.text: Run the Context Window Budget Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The context window is a shared budget: the completion draws from the same pool of tokens as the prompt. This MicroSim asks you to calculate how many tokens remain for the answer and to decide whether a requested completion fits, using the rule from the chapter:

Remaining = window - (system prompt + history + attachment + latest message)

When an attachment is given in words, convert it to tokens with words / 0.75. A request fits when the remaining tokens are at least the requested completion. A negative remaining figure means the prompt alone overflows the window.

The MicroSim has two parts:

Part What you do Three challenges Type the tokens remaining and choose "fits" or "does not fit". Each challenge allows two attempts. Exploration mode Move four sliders (window, system prompt, history, attachment) and watch a stacked bar of the window, the remaining space, and whether a 6,000-token completion fits.

All window sizes and component sizes are illustrative; they are not the limits of any specific model. In the stacked bar each prompt component has its own color and a letter (S, H, A, M), the remaining space is a dashed outline, overflow past the window limit is hatched, and the requested completion is a bracket under the bar.

Learning objective: calculate the number of tokens left for a completion from a context window size and the sizes of the prompt components, and state whether a requested completion fits.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1. The question on screen is How many tokens are left for the answer?
  2. Type the tokens remaining in the answer box (commas are allowed, and a negative number means the prompt overflows the window). Choose fits or does not fit for the requested completion, then press Submit. Both answers are checked together.
  3. If the answer is wrong on the first attempt, a hint appears: check that the completion shares the window with the prompt, add all four components, then subtract from the window. Try again.
  4. After a correct answer, or after a second wrong answer, the worked subtraction and the stacked bar for that challenge appear. A second wrong answer counts the challenge as missed. The running count Challenges correct: n of 3 is shown at the top.
  5. Press Next Challenge, and after challenge 3 press Open Exploration Mode.
  6. In exploration mode, move the four sliders. The latest message is fixed at 400 tokens and the requested completion at 6,000 tokens. Set Attachment to 22,000 tokens (two 8,250-word papers) and notice that the decision changes from "fits" to "does not fit" although no single component looks large.

docs.title: Measurement Data Cleaning Decision Simulator
docs.text: Run the Measurement Data Cleaning Decision Simulator MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Every cleaning choice changes the answer, and nothing in the cleaned file marks that a choice was made. This MicroSim asks you to judge eight anomalies in a batch of 40 devices whose offset voltages were measured in millivolts. The batch and its lab notebook excerpts are synthetic, invented for this exercise, and the sim says so on screen.

For each anomaly you commit one of the four responses from the section "Cleaning Without Hiding" in Chapter 12:

Action When it applies Keep Variation is physical or consistent with expected noise Exclude with log A documented cause, such as a duplicate, a missing-value code, or a known fault Correct and log A documented systematic error, such as a unit mismatch Remeasure The data cannot support the analysis, such as a stuck or missing channel

The criterion is the documented cause. A value with no documented cause is kept, however surprising it looks. Exclusion needs a documented cause. Missing or unusable measurements are sent for remeasurement, not cleaned. Two of the eight anomalies are surprising values that should be kept, and two are problems that cleaning cannot fix.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the anomaly in the dark-blue box and the lab notebook excerpt below it. The question on screen is What should happen to this data?
  2. Press one of the four action buttons: Keep, Exclude with log, Correct and log, or Remeasure. The chosen button gets a thick border and bold text. You can change your choice until you submit.
  3. Press Submit. You get one attempt per anomaly.
  4. Read the feedback. A correct choice shows Correct: action. with a check mark; an incorrect choice shows The better response is action. with an X. Both are followed by the "Why" sentence and the Cleaning log entry that this case would add to the log. The correct action's button is marked with a check mark and a wrong pick with an X.
  5. Press Next Anomaly to continue. The eight anomalies come in a fixed order.
  6. After the eighth anomaly, press See Score. The summary shows n of 8 correct, whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met, and how many rows the actions you chose kept, excluded, corrected, and sent for remeasurement. The lot B unit mismatch and capture 12 are listed by name because the batch description does not give them a row count.

Reload the page to start again.

docs.title: Data Sensitivity Sorter for AI Tools
docs.text: Run the Data Sensitivity Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Placing data in a hosted AI tool is a disclosure to a third party under that provider's terms, and a disclosure cannot be undone. A research group needs a small data classification that people can apply without looking it up, with a rule for what each class may be given to. This MicroSim uses the illustrative classification from Chapter 18 and asks you to judge which tools may receive eight items of research data.

Class Examples May be given to 0 Public Published papers, public datasets, open-source code Any tool 1 Internal Lab notes on setup, scripts, draft text without new results An approved hosted tool, or a local model 2 Unpublished Unpublished measurements and designs of the group A local model, or a hosted tool with the advisor's written approval 3 Obligated Data under NDA, export-controlled technical data, personal data of participants, vendor files under license A local model only, and only if the agreement allows; otherwise no AI tool

An item that falls in two classes takes the more restrictive one. Each class is tested by two items, including edge cases such as an open-source script and a draft with no new results. The classification is an illustrative policy; your institution, sponsor, and agreements decide the real rules.

Learning objective: judge which class of AI tool an item of research data may be given to under a four-class illustrative policy, for eight items, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the classification at the top and item 1 in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is Which tools may receive this?
  2. Choose one of the four tool classes from the drop-down list below the drawing area (Any tool; Approved hosted tool or local; Local model, or hosted with the advisor's approval; Local model only, if the agreement allows) and press Submit. Each item has one attempt.
  3. Read the feedback. A correct answer shows Correct. and the item's class, with a check mark; an incorrect answer shows This item is the class and the tool class it allows, with an X. Both show the reason, and the item's class is outlined and marked with an arrow in the classification.
  4. Press Next Item to continue. The items come in a fixed order.
  5. After item 8, press See Score. The summary shows n of 8 correct, whether you met the mastery threshold of 7, and the eight items grouped by class, each marked with a check mark or an X for your answer. Reload the page to start again.

docs.title: Embedding Vector Search Explorer
docs.text: Run the Embedding Vector Search Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Vector search ranks stored passages by the cosine of the angle between each passage vector and the query vector:

\[ \cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\lVert \mathbf{a} \rVert \, \lVert \mathbf{b} \rVert}. \]

This MicroSim draws six stored passages and three queries as arrows in a two-dimensional toy embedding space, so the geometry can be seen. The two axes are an illustrative "analog–digital" axis and an illustrative "learning" axis. Real embeddings have hundreds to thousands of dimensions and no named axes. All vectors, titles, and queries are invented for illustration and are not the output of a real embedding model.

ID Passage title Vector (x, y) D1 SAR ADC offset calibration (0.95, 0.20) D2 Delta-sigma noise shaping (0.85, 0.35) D3 Transformer accelerator dataflow (0.15, 0.95) D4 Edge-inference quantization (0.30, 0.90) D5 LDO stability compensation (0.70, -0.45) D6 Analog and digital mixed-signal learning (0.60, 0.60)

The search always returns two results (top-k with k = 2), ranked by descending cosine similarity, with ties broken by the lower passage number. A result clears the threshold when its cosine similarity is at least 0.90. Similarities are rounded to 0.001. The key lesson is that the search always returns something: a weak second result comes back looking just like a strong one.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the query text and look at the angles between the orange dashed query arrow and the six blue passage arrows. The question on screen is Which two passages will vector search return?
  2. Choose the First result and the Second result, in order, and a Threshold mark (clears threshold or below threshold) for the second result. Press Submit. Each query gets one attempt; Submit stays disabled until you pick two different passages and a mark.
  3. Read the feedback. The table now lists all six passages in rank order with their cosine similarities and a check or X for the 0.90 threshold; the two returned passages are highlighted, drawn in dark blue, and labeled #1 and #2. A shaded wedge around the query shows the region where cosine similarity is at least 0.90. A correct answer shows Correct: with the two passages; a miss shows the correct ranking with the cosine values. Both are followed by the reason.
  4. Press Next Query. After Q3, press Open Exploration. The final count n of 3 correct stays on screen.
  5. In exploration, drag inside the plot (or use the arrow keys) to move the query vector and watch the ranking and threshold marks update. Move the query far from every passage and notice that two results still come back.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will infer, from the angles between vectors in a two-dimensional toy embedding space, which two stored passages vector search returns for each of three queries and whether the second result clears a similarity threshold of 0.90.

  • Bloom level: Understand
  • Bloom verb: infer

docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research

  2. Exploration (3 min): Drag the query vector between the passage clusters and into the empty lower-left quadrant. Record a query position where the second result falls below the threshold and one where even the first result does.
  3. Reflection (2 min): Write one sentence explaining why a retrieval pipeline needs a similarity threshold, using Q3 as the example.

A query is correct when both retrieved passages and their order match the answer key and the threshold mark matches. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct.

docs.title: Failure Case Root Cause Analyzer
docs.text: Run the Failure Case Root Cause Analyzer MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A failure case is a specific instance in which something went wrong, described with its cause, how it was found, and what changed. The visible symptom is rarely the root cause. This MicroSim asks you to attribute six failure cases to the missing practice that let each one through, and connects each one to the control from an earlier chapter that would have caught it.

The six root causes are:

Root cause Control that would have caught it Missing sanity check A numerical check against the nominal resolution (Chapter 13) Unverified model claim A primary source check with the location of the claim (Chapters 11 and 17) Unreviewed diff Diff review and a number check (Chapters 5 and 15) Environment drift A pinned environment and a rerun of known-answer tests (Chapter 13) Scope too broad Single-purpose skills with their own tests (Chapter 7) Untraceable claim A claim-to-source table with measured, cited, or expected labels (Chapters 11 and 15)

Each failure case has exactly one correct root cause and exactly one control. All six cases are invented or adapted for illustration and are labeled "illustrative" on screen. They come in a fixed order, and each case gets one attempt.

Learning objective: attribute each of six failure cases to its root cause and to the control that would have caught it, with at least 5 of 6 attributed correctly.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read failure case 1 in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is What was missing that let this through?
  2. Choose one of the six root causes in the drop-down list below the drawing. The cause you pick is outlined and marked with an arrow in the list on screen.
  3. Press Submit. The choice is committed and cannot be changed.
  4. Read the feedback. A correct choice shows Correct: and the cause; an incorrect choice shows The root cause is and the correct cause. Both show the control that would have caught the failure and the "Why" sentence. In the list, the correct cause is marked with a check and a wrong pick with a cross.
  5. Press Next Case to continue. After case 6, press See Score to see n of 6 correct, whether the mastery threshold of 5 was met, and a table of the six causes with their controls. Reload the page to start again.

docs.title: Falsifiable Hypothesis Sorter
docs.text: Run the Falsifiable Hypothesis Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A research hypothesis has a form that an experiment could show to be wrong: under stated conditions, a stated change produces a stated effect of at least a stated size. This MicroSim asks you to distinguish falsifiable hypotheses from statements that no experiment could contradict.

The sim shows eight statements, one at a time, in a fixed order. All of them are invented for illustration. For each one you answer the question Could any measurement show this to be wrong? by choosing Falsifiable or Not falsifiable. A checklist on screen restates the rule: a falsifiable statement names a measurable quantity, a threshold or a direction and size of effect, and the conditions under which it is tested, so that some possible observation would contradict it. A statement missing any of these, or that is true under every outcome, is not falsifiable.

The not-falsifiable statements fail in different ways. Some have no metric, some leave the conditions open, one is true whatever happens, and one explains away every disagreement in advance. No single cue, such as the presence of a number or a technical tone, is enough to sort them.

Learning objective: distinguish falsifiable hypotheses from statements that no experiment could contradict, among eight statements, with at least 7 of 8 classified correctly.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the statement in the dark-blue box and the question above it: Could any measurement show this to be wrong?
  2. Press Falsifiable or Not falsifiable. Each statement gets one attempt, and the answer is committed at once.
  3. Read the feedback. A correct answer shows Correct. with a check mark and the "Why" sentence. An incorrect answer shows This statement is falsifiable. or This statement is not falsifiable. with an X and the "Why" sentence. For a not-falsifiable statement the feedback also names what is missing.
  4. Press Next to go to the next statement. After statement 8, press See Score.
  5. The final screen shows n of 8 correct, whether you met the mastery threshold of 7, and the correct classification of every statement. Reload the page to start again.

Feedback uses a symbol and words as well as color: a check mark for correct and an X for incorrect.

  2. For each statement you missed, use the checklist to name the element (metric, threshold or effect size, or conditions) that is present or missing, or say why the statement is true under every outcome.
  3. Rewrite statement 2, "Calibration makes the ADC better", as a falsifiable hypothesis by adding a metric, a threshold, and conditions.

  • Reading the checklist of properties is exploration and is not evidence.

docs.title: Figure Caption Critic
docs.text: Run the Figure Caption Critic MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A good figure caption makes the figure readable without searching the body text for context. It states what is plotted, the conditions under which the data were obtained, how to read any markers or error bars, and makes no claim the figure cannot support. This MicroSim asks you to critique six captions against that checklist and name the main defect, or judge that there is none.

The checklist is applied in a fixed order, and the first property that fails is the main defect:

Order Judgment Property checked 1 Vague Does it say what is plotted against what? 2 Missing conditions Does it state the conditions of the data? 3 Undefined symbols Are all symbols and markers defined? 4 Overclaims Does it claim only what the figure shows? No defect None of the four fails.

All six captions and their values are invented for illustration and are labeled "illustrative" on screen. Length is not a cue: one long caption has no defect, and one short caption fails. When a caption has a defect, the sim offers a short corrected caption, marked as a suggestion with a dashed border. The suggested captions were written for this sim and are illustrative too.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the caption in the dark-blue box and the checklist below it. The question on screen is Could a reader understand this figure from the caption alone?
  2. Press the button for the judgment you choose. The choice is highlighted in the button row and marked with an arrow in the checklist, and you can change it until you submit.
  3. Press Submit. Each caption gets one attempt, and the judgment cannot be changed after you submit.
  4. Read the feedback. A correct judgment shows Correct: <judgment>. and an incorrect one shows The main issue is <judgment>., followed by the reason. The correct judgment is outlined and marked with a check mark, and a wrong pick is marked with an X. Where the caption has a defect, a suggested corrected caption appears below the reason.
  5. Press Next to go to the next caption. The six captions come in a fixed order.
  6. After caption 6, press See Score. The summary shows n of 6 correct and whether the mastery threshold of 5 was met.

All buttons can be reached with the Tab key and pressed with Enter or Space.

docs.title: From Generative AI to Agent
docs.text: Run the From Generative AI to Agent MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Four terms appear in a row as a chain: Generative AI, Large Language Model, AI Assistant, and AI Agent, joined by three links. The question on screen is What changes at each step from generative AI to an AI agent?

Each link asks what the second term adds to the first. You choose one of four options and commit. Three of the options are common misconceptions, such as the idea that a larger model or a friendlier tone is what turns an assistant into an agent. After each commit the sim reveals the correct capability, and if you chose a distractor it explains why that choice belongs somewhere else in the chain.

The chain ends with the point the chapter makes: an AI agent is an AI assistant plus tools and a loop. It acts, observes the result, and chooses the next step.

You can open any node at any time to read its definition. Opening a node is exploration and is not scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click any node in the diagram, or use the Open a node buttons below it, to read that term's definition. This step is optional and is not scored.
  2. Look at the exercise panel. It shows Link 1 of 3: Generative AI → Large Language Model and asks What does the second term add to the first?
  3. Select one of the four options, then press Commit answer. You can also use the arrow keys to move between options and press Enter to commit.
  4. Read the feedback. A correct choice shows "Correct" and the correct option. An incorrect choice shows why that option does not fit this link, followed by the correct option. You cannot change an answer after you commit it.
  5. Press Next link to move on. A link cannot be answered until the previous link has been answered. Each answered link is marked in the diagram with a check mark (correct) or an X (incorrect).
  6. After the third link the panel shows your final score as n of 3 correct. Mastery is 3 of 3.
  7. Press Restart at any time to begin a new run. The order of the options is reshuffled on every run.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will explain what capability each of the three links in the chain from generative AI to AI agent adds, by selecting the correct capability for all three links (Bloom: Understand, verb: explain).

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The six terms defined in the section "The Vocabulary of Generative AI" of Chapter 1:

  • generative AI
  • large language model
  • AI assistant
  • AI agent
  • tool
  • loop

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Open each of the four nodes and read its definition. For each pair of neighboring terms, say out loud what the second term has that the first does not. This step is not scored.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Work through the three links in order. Before you commit each answer, predict the capability in your own words, then compare your prediction with the options. After each commit, read the feedback, including the explanation for any distractor you chose.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Restart so the options are reshuffled, and answer all three links without opening the nodes. Then, without the sim, write one sentence that explains the difference between an AI assistant and an AI agent.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Mastery: 3 of 3 links correct, counting the first commit on each link.
  • Opening nodes to read definitions is exploration and does not count as evidence.
  • A learner who has mastered the objective can state, in one sentence, that an agent adds tools and a loop to an assistant: it acts, observes the result, and chooses the next step.
  • Watch for the three misconceptions the distractors target: that an assistant and an agent differ only in branding, that a larger model is what makes an agent, and that an agent is a chatbot with a friendlier tone or a longer memory.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator - the section "The Vocabulary of Generative AI" defines the four terms in this chain and states that an agent adds tools and a loop to an assistant.
  2. vis-network documentation - the JavaScript network library used to draw the chain.

docs.title: Markdown Syntax Matcher
docs.text: Run the Markdown Syntax Matcher MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Reading Markdown is easy; writing it so that it renders the way you meant takes practice. This MicroSim gives you eight rendered results, such as a level-2 heading, a bulleted list, a fenced Python code block, a link, or a two-column table, and three candidate sources for each. Your job is to use Markdown syntax: pick the source that produces the result.

The wrong options are the near-miss errors people actually make: a missing space after ## or -, quotation marks used where backticks are needed, link brackets in the wrong order, or a table without its separator row. After each answer the sim draws the rendered preview of the source you chose next to the preview of the correct source, following the CommonMark rules with the GitHub Flavored Markdown table extension. Most wrong options differ from the right one by a single space or character, and the previews show what that difference costs.

The option order is shuffled for each item when the page loads, so the letter of the correct option tells you nothing.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the Rendered result box. The question on screen is Which source produces this result?
  2. Read the three sources, shown as literal text and labeled A, B, and C.
  3. Press Option A, Option B, or Option C to select a source. The selected option gets a pointer and a black outline, and you can change the selection until you submit.
  4. Press Submit. Each item has one attempt. The correct option is outlined in blue with a check mark; a wrong choice is outlined in orange with an X.
  5. Read the feedback. A correct answer shows Correct. and the reason. A wrong answer shows the reason and two rendered previews: your choice and the correct option.
  6. Press Next Item, and after item 8 press See Score. The final screen shows n of 8 correct, whether you met the mastery threshold of 7, and the misconception behind each item you missed.

docs.text:
The learner will use Markdown syntax for headings, lists, tables, code, links, and emphasis by choosing, for each of eight described rendered results, the source text that produces it, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

  • Bloom level: Apply
  • Bloom verb: use

1. A heading needs no space after the hash characters.
  2. A list item needs no space after the marker.
  3. A table works without a separator row.
  4. Quotation marks or single quotes make code.

docs.title: MicroSim Suitability Judge
docs.text: Run the MicroSim Suitability Judge MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A MicroSim is not always the right medium. Before you specify or generate one, you have to judge whether the content would be understood better by changing something. This MicroSim gives you one criterion and eight pieces of research content, and asks you to apply the criterion and to decline to build a sim when the criterion is not met.

The criterion, which stays on screen throughout, is:

A MicroSim suits content with a parameter the learner can change, or a process the learner can step through or predict, where seeing the response builds understanding.

Every item is invented for illustration and is labeled "illustrative". Each item has exactly one correct answer: MicroSim or Static figure or text. The eight items come in a fixed order and you get one attempt at each. After each judgment the sim says whether you were right and gives the reason, naming the parameter or process where there is one. After item 8 it shows how many of the eight you judged correctly and whether you reached the mastery threshold of 7.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the criterion and the item in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is Would a learner understand this better by changing something?
  2. Press MicroSim or Static figure or text to choose a medium. The chosen button is outlined and bold, and you can change the choice until you submit.
  3. Press Submit. Your judgment is final. The feedback is Correct. (with a check mark) or The better medium is ... (with an X), followed by the "Why" sentence.
  4. Press Next Item to continue. After item 8, press See Score to see n of 8 correct and whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

All buttons can be reached with the Tab key and pressed with Enter or Space.

docs.text:
The learner will judge, for each of eight pieces of research content, whether an interactive MicroSim or a static figure or text is the better medium, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

  • Bloom level: Evaluate
  • Bloom verb: judge

• For each of the eight items the learner commits "MicroSim" or "static figure or text". A judgment is correct when it equals the answer key.
  • Mastery: at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.
  • Reading the criterion is exploration and is not evidence of mastery.

docs.text:
• Interactive is always better than static.
  • Any technical content should become a simulation.
  • A table of values is equivalent to a sim of the function.

docs.title: Model Choice Scenario Sorter
docs.text: Run the Model Choice Scenario Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
There is no best model, only a best model for a task under constraints. This MicroSim asks you to recommend one of three access paths for each of eight illustrative research scenarios:

Access path Meaning Chat interface Hosted model used through a web or desktop application Hosted API Hosted model called from a script Local open-weight model A downloadable model run on hardware the researcher controls

For each scenario you also name the single deciding factor: Privacy or data policy, Scale and automation, Reproducibility over time, or Capability and effort. Only the access path is scored; the factor is feedback that helps you check your reasoning.

The scenarios are written so that each path is correct for some of them. A single rule such as "always use the strongest model" or "local is always safest" fails on at least two items. All scenarios are invented for illustration.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is Which access path would you recommend, and why?
  2. Choose an access path from the first list and the deciding factor from the second list, then press Submit. Each scenario gets one attempt, and your choice cannot be changed after you submit.
  3. Read the feedback. A correct answer shows Correct: followed by the path; a miss shows The better fit is followed by the path. Both are followed by the reason. The better-fit path is outlined in blue and marked with a check; a wrong pick is outlined in orange and marked with an X. A gray line compares your deciding factor with the one the reasoning turns on.
  4. Press Next Scenario to continue. After scenario 8, press See Score.
  5. The summary shows n of 8 correct, whether you met the mastery threshold of 6, and, for each missed scenario, the misconception it exposes. If the list is long, press More Missed Scenarios to page through it.

A missed scenario is linked to the misconception that matches the path you over-applied: choosing a local model where it was not the better fit exposes "a local model is always the safest or cheapest choice"; choosing a hosted API exposes "the strongest hosted model is the right choice for every task"; and choosing a chat interface exposes "a chat interface is adequate for any task because the model is the same".

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will recommend one of three access paths, chat interface, hosted API, or local open-weight model, for each of eight research scenarios, with at least 6 of 8 recommendations matching the reasoning in the chapter.

  • Bloom level: Evaluate
  • Bloom verb: recommend

docs.text:
1. Exploration (3 min): Before starting, reread Table 1 in Chapter 3 and write one question you would ask about any research task to decide its access path (for example, "Can this data leave the site?").
  2. Practice (7 min): Work through the eight scenarios. For each, commit an access path and a deciding factor before reading the feedback.
  3. Reflection (5 min): For each missed scenario, read the misconception it exposes and write one sentence explaining which constraint in the scenario should have decided the choice.

docs.title: Numerical Sanity Check Judge
docs.text: Run the Numerical Sanity Check Judge MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A numerical sanity check cannot prove that a result is right, but it can prove that a result is wrong. This MicroSim asks you to judge eight reported results, one at a time and in a fixed order, and to give each one of five verdicts:

Verdict What it means Plausible The result violates none of the checks Exceeds a limit A definitional or physical limit is broken, such as ENOB above the nominal resolution or efficiency above 100 percent Disagrees with a hand calculation The result differs from a paper estimate by a factor of 2 or more, such as an RC cutoff that is not near \( 1 / (2\pi R C) \) Violates scaling A linear system does not double its output when its input is doubled Impossible value The quantity can never take that value, such as a negative standard deviation

All eight results are invented for illustration. Three of them are plausible, so that you do not learn to treat every number as suspect. The results include the 17.98-bit ENOB that comes from using 20 log10 on a power ratio and the RC low-pass filter with R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF, whose cutoff is 1.59 kHz.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the reported result in the box. The question on screen is Is this result plausible, and if not, which check does it fail?
  2. Choose one of the five verdict buttons. The chosen button is marked with a filled circle (◉). You can change your choice until you submit.
  3. Press Submit. Each result gets one attempt. The sim shows Correct: . (with a check mark) or The verdict is . (with a cross), the "Why" sentence, and, when the result has a problem, the quick calculation that exposes it.
  4. Press Next to continue. After result 8, press See Score to see n of 8 correct and whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.
  5. Optional: check Show the checks to read a one-line hint about each kind of check. Reading the hints is exploration and does not affect the score.

docs.text:
The learner will judge each of eight reported results as plausible or as violating one of four kinds of sanity check, with at least 7 of 8 judged correctly.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:

  • The RC low-pass cutoff \( f_c = 1 / (2\pi R C) \) and the ENOB of an ADC

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Judge (5 min): Work through the eight results with one attempt each. Before you submit, write the quick calculation you would use to test the result.
  2. Review (5 min): For each result you judged incorrectly, compare your quick calculation with the one the sim showed. Decide which misconception led you astray: trusting a number because it is printed to many digits, calling any surprising result an error, or trusting a result because the simulator is well known.

docs.title: Evidence of Mastery
docs.text:
• For each of the eight results the learner commits one of five verdicts. A verdict is correct when it equals the answer key.
  • Mastery: at least 7 of 8 verdicts correct on the first attempt.
  • Reading the hint about each check is exploration and is not evidence.

docs.title: Orchestrator Review Load Calculator
docs.text: Run the Orchestrator Review Load Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Researcher attention, not compute, limits the size of an agent team. This MicroSim turns the chapter's load formula into a planning tool. The daily review load, in minutes, is

\[ L = f\, n_p\, k_p\, r_p + n_e\, k_e\, r_e + c, \]

where \( f \) is the fraction of planning outputs reviewed, \( n_p \) and \( n_e \) are the numbers of planning and execution agents, \( k_p \) and \( k_e \) are the outputs per agent per day, \( r_p \) and \( r_e \) are the review minutes per output, and \( c \) is the time spent resolving conflicts. The load fits when it is no more than the attention available times 60.

The nine quantities and their ranges are:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Planning agents n_p 0 40 1 20 agents Execution agents n_e 0 20 1 10 agents Planning outputs per agent per day k_p 1 4 1 1 outputs Execution outputs per agent per day k_e 1 4 1 1 outputs Review time per planning output r_p 2 15 1 6 minutes Review time per execution output r_e 5 30 1 15 minutes Conflict resolution c 0 120 10 30 minutes per day Attention available 1 8 0.5 4 hours per day Fraction of planning outputs reviewed 0.25 1.0 0.25 1.0 fraction

All values are illustrative. The sim opens with the default team and 4 hours of attention, and asks How many hours of review does this team need each day? Three challenges follow in a fixed order:

  1. What is the daily review load in hours for the default team?
  2. With attention fixed at 4 hours, 10 execution agents, and every planning output reviewed, what is the largest number of planning agents that fits?
  3. With 20 planning agents and attention fixed at 4 hours, what is the largest fraction of planning outputs, from 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, that can be reviewed?

During the challenges the sliders show the challenge's values and are locked, and the quantity you are solving for is shown as ?. After each challenge ends, the sim shows the worked calculation and a stacked bar that compares the load (planning, execution, and conflict minutes) with a dashed line at the attention available, and states in words whether the load fits. After the third challenge, exploration opens and all nine sliders unlock.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the challenge and type your answer in the box under the drawing area. Press Submit or Enter. If the box does not contain a number, the sim asks for one and does not count the attempt.
  2. You have two attempts per challenge. A first wrong answer gives the hint "Check that each term is agents x outputs x minutes." A second wrong answer shows the worked calculation and counts the challenge as missed. The running count n of 3 correct is shown at the top.
  3. Read the worked calculation and the bar, then press Next challenge.
  4. After the third challenge, press Start exploring. Move any of the nine sliders and watch the bar and the verdict. Halve the review time per planning output (6 to 3), press Restore defaults, then halve the review time per execution output (15 to 7 or 8), and compare how much each change saves.

The sliders are native controls that can be reached with the Tab key and moved with the arrow keys.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will calculate the daily review load of an agent team from its size and per-output review times, and adjust the team or the review fraction to fit a stated attention budget, in three challenges.

  • Bloom level: Apply
  • Bloom verb: calculate

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Researcher attention, span of control, review checkpoint, and the load formula \( L = n_p k_p r_p + n_e k_e r_e + c \), all from the section "Review, Approval, and Researcher Attention" of Chapter 10.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (6 min): Work the three challenges in order. Write each term of the load formula on paper before you submit.
  2. Explore (5 min): After the challenges, compare halving the review time per planning output with halving it per execution output. Then set your own team size and attention, and find the largest team that fits.
  3. Reflect (3 min): Write one sentence on why reviewing a sample of the cheapest, most reversible outputs is not the same as skipping review.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Evidence of mastery: for each of the three challenges the learner types a value and submits, and a value is correct when it equals the answer key (5.0 hours, 10 planning agents, a fraction of 0.5). Mastery is 3 of 3 correct.
  • Changing the quantities in exploration mode is not evidence.
  • Watch for three misconceptions: that review load grows only with the number of execution agents, that more agents always means more done, and that sampling review is the same as skipping review.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 10: Orchestrating Agent Teams - the section "Review, Approval, and Researcher Attention" gives the load formula, the 300-minute load of the default team, and the 240-minute load when half of the planning outputs are reviewed.
  2. Span of control - Wikipedia article on the number of subordinates one supervisor can manage effectively.
  3. p5.js reference - the JavaScript library used to draw the bar and create the sliders.

docs.title: Overnight Activity Audit
docs.text: Run the Overnight Activity Audit MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An always-on agent works while you are away, so each morning you review what it did. This MicroSim practises that audit. The agent was given one task with explicit permissions:

Each night, search arXiv for new papers on SAR ADC calibration and append their titles to docs/reading-queue.md. Allowed: web search, fetching public web pages, and writing to docs/reading-queue.md. Not allowed: reading or writing any other file, signing in to any service, sending messages, installing software, or purchases.

You read ten lines of the agent's log, one at a time, and decide whether each action stayed inside the task. An action is in scope when it is covered by the Allowed list and out of scope otherwise. Some out-of-scope actions look harmless, such as reading a file, which is the point: scope, not apparent harm, is the test. For every out-of-scope line, the sim names the control that would have prevented it: a permission rule, a sandbox, or an approval gate.

The task and the log are invented for illustration and are labeled "illustrative log". They do not describe any real product.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the task and its Allowed and Not allowed lists in the white panel, then the log line in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is Did the agent stay inside the task?
  2. Press In scope or Out of scope. Your choice is marked with a filled circle and a dark background. You can change it until you submit.
  3. Press Submit. Each line gets one attempt. The feedback reads Correct. (with a check mark) or This line is in scope / out of scope. (with an X), followed by the "Why" sentence. For an out-of-scope line it also names the control that would have prevented the action. The correct button is marked with a check mark and a solid border; a wrong pick is marked with an X and a dashed border.
  4. Press Next Line to continue. The lines come in a fixed order.
  5. After line 10, press See Morning Report. The end screen shows n of 10 correct, whether you met the mastery threshold of 9, and a morning report listing the five out-of-scope actions with the control that would have prevented each one.

All controls are buttons that can be reached with the Tab key and pressed with Enter or Space. To try again, reload the page.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Learning objective: The learner will examine ten lines of an agent's overnight activity log against a stated task and permission list, and flag each as in scope or out of scope, with at least 9 of 10 correct.

Bloom level and verb: Analyze (L4), examine.

Evidence of mastery: For each of ten log lines the learner commits "in scope" or "out of scope". A classification is correct when it equals the answer key. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the task statement is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions to watch for:

  • An action that looks helpful is in scope.
  • Reading a file is harmless.
  • An action that is allowed by the platform is allowed by the task.

Duration: 10 minutes.

Prerequisites: overnight activity audit, agent blast radius, and least privilege, as defined in the section "Risks That Define the Criteria" of Chapter 19 and in Chapter 9.

Follow-up: For each action in the morning report, write the one permission rule, sandbox setting, or approval gate you would configure before letting the agent run another night, and say which of the audit questions it answers: what did it do, was each action within the task, what did it spend, and did anything leave your control?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 19: Always-On Personal Agents for Research - the sections "Risks That Define the Criteria" and "Auditing Overnight Activity" describe the audit procedure used here.
  2. Chapter 8: Agents, Tool Use, and Subagents - defines sandboxing and permissions.
  3. Chapter 10: Orchestrating Teams of Planning and Execution Agents - defines the human approval gate.

docs.title: Paper Section Sorter
docs.text: Run the Paper Section Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Readers rely on the standard structure of a research paper: they go to the results for the numbers and to the discussion for the limits. Each section answers one reader question, and a sentence belongs in the section whose question it answers. This MicroSim asks you to classify ten sentences from one invented paper on offset calibration for a SAR ADC into one of six sections:

Section The reader's question Abstract Should I read this? Introduction Why does this matter? Related work What is already known? Method What exactly was done? Results What was found? Discussion What does it mean, and what are the limits?

All ten sentences and their values are invented for illustration and are labeled "illustrative" on screen. Because they come from one paper, you can compare how the same numbers and ideas appear in different sections. Watch for three traps: a sentence with a number is not always a result, a contribution statement can appear outside the abstract, and a limitation belongs in the discussion.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the sentence in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is Which reader question does this sentence answer? The six sections and their reader questions are listed below the sentence.
  2. Press the button for the section you choose. The choice is highlighted in the button row and marked with an arrow in the list, and you can change it until you submit.
  3. Press Submit. Each sentence gets one attempt, and the choice cannot be changed after you submit.
  4. Read the feedback. A correct choice shows Correct: <section>. and an incorrect one shows This belongs in <section>., followed by the reason. The correct section is outlined and marked with a check mark, and a wrong pick is marked with an X.
  5. Press Next to go to the next sentence. The ten sentences come in a fixed order.
  6. After sentence 10, press See Score. The summary shows n of 10 correct, whether the mastery threshold of 8 was met, and all ten sentences grouped by section, each marked with a check mark (classified correctly) or an X (classified incorrectly, with the section you chose). If the groups do not fit on one screen, press More Sections to page through them.

All buttons can be reached with the Tab key and pressed with Enter or Space.

docs.title: Personal Knowledge Graph Query Explorer
docs.text: Run the Personal Knowledge Graph Query Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A folder of notes lets you find a note you already know exists. A typed graph lets you derive a fact that no single note states, by chaining relationships. This MicroSim shows a small, illustrative personal knowledge graph for an ADC research project: ten entities of six types (Experiment, Dataset, Design, Paper, Concept, Person) joined by twelve typed, directed relationships such as USED, TESTED, REVISES, REPORTS, CITES, ABOUT, and AUTHORED. The entities and links are invented for illustration.

The question on screen is Which entities answer this, by following the relationships? Five questions follow in a fixed order. They rise from one hop ("Which experiments used Dataset A?") to three hops ("Which papers report an experiment that tested the design that ADC Design v3 revises?"). For each one you select the set of entities that answers it and submit. An answer counts as correct only if your set equals the answer set exactly, with no missing and no extra entities.

After each submission the sim highlights the path that produces the answer set in thick blue edges, labels each edge on the path with its number and type, and shows the reason, for example Dr. Rivera authored Paper Beta (edge 12), and Paper Beta cites Paper Alpha (edge 9).

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore the graph. Each node shows its name and its entity type. Arrows point from the first entity to the second. Hover over an edge to read its type, or hover over a node (or move the keyboard focus to its button) to read all of its incoming and outgoing relationships. Exploring is not scored.
  2. Read the question in the exercise panel.
  3. Select the entities that answer it. Click a node in the graph, or press the matching entity button. A selected entity shows a check mark (✓). Click it again to remove it.
  4. Press Submit. You get one attempt per question. The sim says Correct or Incorrect, gives the correct answer set when you missed, highlights the path, and shows the reason. In the graph and on the buttons, ✓ marks a correct pick, ✗ marks an entity that is not in the answer, and ★ marks an answer you missed.
  5. Press Next question to continue.
  6. After question 5 the panel shows your score as n of 5 correct and whether you met the mastery threshold of 4. Press Start over to try the five questions again.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will solve five questions about a twelve-edge personal knowledge graph by following typed, directed relationships, and give each answer as the exact set of entities, with at least 4 of 5 correct (Bloom: Apply, verb: solve).

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Entity, relationship, typed relationship, graph schema, backlink, and graph querying, all defined in the section "From Files to a Knowledge Graph" of Chapter 6.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (3 min): Hover over the nodes and edges. For each relationship type, say in words what it means and which direction it points (for example, a Paper REPORTS an Experiment).
  2. Guided Practice (7 min): Answer the five questions in order. Before you select, trace the path with your finger from the entity named in the question, one hop at a time, and say whether each hop follows an edge in its direction or against it. After each submission, compare your path with the highlighted one.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Without the sim, write the chain of relationships that answers question 5, and explain why Paper Beta must be rechecked even though it never names Dataset A.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Evidence of mastery: for each of the five questions the learner selects the set of entities that answers it and submits. An answer is correct when the selected set equals the answer set exactly. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt.
  • Hovering over edges to read their types is exploration and is not evidence.
  • Watch for three misconceptions: that a relationship can be followed in either direction with the same meaning, that a question needing more than one hop cannot be answered from the graph, and that a paper not directly linked to a dataset is unaffected by that dataset.

docs.title: Project Instruction File Triage
docs.text: Run the Project Instruction File Triage MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A project instruction file such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md is read by an agent at the start of every session, so every line costs context on every turn. A useful file holds three kinds of content: project goals (what the project is for and what success means), project conventions (how routine work is done here), and project constraints (what the agent may not do, or may do only with approval). Everything else should be left out: transient notes go stale, vague exhortations cannot be checked, and secrets leak.

This MicroSim shows an illustrative draft instruction file for a SAR ADC project and asks you to judge each of its eleven lines against those criteria. Three of the eleven lines should be removed, so "keep it" is not a safe default.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the draft file. The highlighted line, marked with a pointer, is the one to judge. The question on screen is Is this line a goal, a convention, a constraint, or not worth putting in the file?
  2. Press Goal, Convention, Constraint, or Does not belong to select a label. You can change the selection until you submit.
  3. Press Submit. Each line has one attempt. The feedback box shows Correct: and the label (for example, Correct: Goal.) or This line is and the correct label (for example, This line is Constraint.), followed by the reason, and the next line is highlighted. Judged lines are marked in the file with a check mark or an X.
  4. After line 11, press See Score. The final screen shows n of 11 correct, whether you met the mastery threshold of 9, and where the content of each line that does not belong should live instead.

At narrow widths the lines you are not judging are shortened to one line each so that the whole file still fits; the highlighted line is always shown in full.

docs.text:
1. Anything useful to say to an agent belongs in the instruction file.
  2. A vague exhortation such as "be careful" is a constraint.
  3. A credential in a private repository is safe to include.

docs.title: Projecting AI Task Completion to 2030
docs.text:
Run the Projecting AI Task Completion MicroSim Fullscreen

To use this chart on any website, copy this line of HTML into your web page:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-for-ee-research/sims/projecting-ai/main.html" width="100%" height="762"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
METR measures how long a task an AI model can complete, where "long" means the time a human expert needs for the same task. The 50% time horizon is the task length a model completes successfully half the time, and the 80% time horizon is the task length it completes 80% of the time. This MicroSim puts release date on the horizontal axis and the time horizon on the vertical axis, and extends the exponential trend to 2030.

For an AI-assisted research group, the time horizon is a rough guide to how much work you can hand an agent in one go. A model with a 20-minute horizon suits a single function or a literature lookup. A model with a 12-hour horizon can plausibly take a larger piece of a project, though it still fails half of the tasks of that length, which is why the review habits in this book still apply.

docs.title: Data (METR Time Horizon 1.1)
docs.text:
The chart data is METR's published METR-Horizon-v1.1 results, retrieved on 2026-10-19 from benchmark_results_1_1.yaml. The file holds 26 models from GPT-2 (February 2019) to Claude Mythos Preview, an early version (April 2026).

  • Frontier (green): the best model METR had measured at the time of its release (METR's is_sota flag), 18 models.
  • Non-frontier (gray): other models measured on the same suite, 8 models.
  • Recent frontier models: Claude Opus 4.6 at about 12 hours (719 min) at 50% and 70 minutes at 80%, and Claude Mythos Preview (early) at about 17 hours (1,045 min) at 50% and 3.1 hours at 80%.

Reliability limit. METR notes that measurements above 16 hours are unreliable with its current task suite, so the Mythos Preview point is best read as "at least this long", and the tooltip says so. The trend line is anchored on Claude Opus 4.6, the newest model below that limit.

docs.title: Interactive Features
docs.text:
• Scale: Log shows the exponential pattern as a roughly straight line. Linear shows how far the latest models are above the rest.
  • Success Probability: 50% or 80%. The 80% horizons are several times shorter, and the gap shows how much reliability costs.
  • Doubling Time: switches the trend line between METR's two fitted doubling times, described below.
  • Trend Line: show or hide the projection.
  • Hover: shows the model name, the horizon in seconds, minutes, hours, or days, and the release date.

docs.title: The Doubling Time
docs.text:
METR's data file gives two doubling times, both fitted without points above 16 hours:

Fit Doubling time Notes All-time (2019 onward) 187.8 days (about 6.2 months) The default. Close to the 7 months in METR's March 2025 paper. Since 2023 128.7 days (about 4.2 months) Interval 104 to 158 days. Recent models have been improving faster.

The trend line is horizon = reference × 2^(days since reference ÷ doubling time), starting from Claude Opus 4.6 (February 2026) at 12.0 hours for the 50% horizon:

Date 6.2-month doubling 4.2-month doubling January 2027 about 41 hours (1.7 days) about 71 hours (3 days) January 2028 about 156 hours (6.5 days) about 505 hours (21 days) January 2030 about 96 days about 3 years

The last cell is a warning sign, not a forecast. Nobody expects tasks of that length to be measured or even to exist in a form that fits the benchmark.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
1. A projection, not a prediction. Exponential trends end. Compute, cost, or a lack of very long tasks to measure could all bend the curve.
  2. Long tasks are poorly measured. There are far fewer very long tasks than short ones, and the longest ones often have estimated rather than timed human completion.
  3. Software tasks. The suite is mostly software engineering and research-engineering work. Other kinds of work may differ.
  4. Model set. The chart shows only what METR has published. Models it has not measured, for example many open-weight models, are missing. Earlier versions of this chart used the older Time Horizon 1.0 suite and included models such as Grok-4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and several DeepSeek and Qwen models; those are not in the current v1.1 file.
  5. Not comparable across suites. Time Horizon 1.1 re-estimated older models, so numbers from older charts and papers (for example GPT-5 at about 2 hours 17 minutes) will not match the 203 minutes shown here.

docs.title: How to Update the Data
docs.text:
Edit the modelData object in script.js. All horizons are in minutes:

{ name: 'Model Name', horizon50: 100.0, horizon80: 20.0, date: 'YYYY-MM-DD' }

The METR file reports p50_horizon_length and p80_horizon_length in minutes, with release_date for the date. If the doubling times change, edit doublingOptions and the two button labels in main.html. If a newer model passes 16 hours, consider changing TREND_REFERENCE to the newest model below the limit, or noting the new reliability limit.

docs.title: Prompt Chain Builder
docs.text: Run the Prompt Chain Builder MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Prompt chaining breaks a long task into separate prompts, where the output of one becomes the input of the next, with a check between them. This MicroSim asks you to implement a six-step chain for the goal:

"Produce a verified comparison table of five SAR ADC papers by Walden figure of merit."

The Walden figure of merit is

\[ \text{FoM} = \frac{P}{2^{\text{ENOB}} \cdot f_s}, \]

with \( P \) in watts and \( f_s \) in hertz, giving energy per conversion step in joules, so lower is better.

You do two things. First, arrange the six step cards into an order in which every step comes after the steps it needs. The order is partly forced and partly free: one step can sit in more than one place, so there are three valid orders, not one. Second, choose one of three candidate acceptance checks for each step. Only one check per step is testable, meaning a script or a second reader could decide it. The options are shown in a shuffled order, so their position carries no information. The test row values in one of the checks (9.0 ENOB, 50 µW, 1 MS/s) are illustrative.

Learning objective: implement a six-step prompt chain by placing the steps in an order that respects their dependencies and choosing a testable acceptance check for each step, with a valid order and at least 5 of 6 testable checks.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the goal. The six cards, labeled Card A to Card F, start in a scrambled order under Your chain; step 1 runs first. The question on screen is In what order can these steps run, and how would you know each one worked?
  2. Choose a card in the first drop-down list. The selected card is outlined and marked with ▶, and its full text and its three candidate checks appear in the panel below.
  3. Press Move Up or Move Down to change the card's place in the chain. The drop-down list shows each card's current position, such as Card C (#3).
  4. Use the second drop-down list to choose Check 1, Check 2, or Check 3 for the selected card. The chosen check is outlined and marked with ●, and the chain shows which check each card has.
  5. When all six cards have a check, press Submit. The sim says Valid order. or names the first violated dependency in the form Invalid: <step> needs <step> first., where steps are named S1 to S6 with their card letters. It shows the score Order valid: yes or no; checks: n of 6, whether you met the mastery condition, and, for each step, whether your check was correct, the testable check, and the reason. Press Next Page to see the rest of the steps.
  6. Press Reset to try again with a new scramble. Only the first submission counts as evidence; its result stays on screen during later attempts.

docs.title: Prompt Component Sorter
docs.text: Run the Prompt Component Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
When a prompt misbehaves, the way to fix it is to find which component is missing or doing the wrong job. This MicroSim shows one assembled prompt, adapted from the worked prompt in Chapter 3, and asks you to distinguish which component each of its ten sentences carries:

Component What it controls Clear instruction The task and audience Constraint Sources, scope, length, and a sanctioned way to say "unknown" Output format The shape of the result Role Tone and perspective Few-shot example Format and judgment, shown by a worked instance

Sentences 9 and 10 are added to the chapter's prompt. All example values in the prompt are illustrative.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the assembled prompt. The highlighted sentence has a yellow background, a gold outline, bold text, and an arrow next to its number. The question on screen is Which component of the prompt does this sentence carry?
  2. Choose a component from the list below the drawing and press Submit. Each sentence gets one attempt.
  3. Read the feedback. A correct label shows Correct: with the label; a miss shows This sentence is with the correct label. Both are followed by the reason. The answered sentence is tagged in the prompt with its correct component, with a check if you chose it and an X if you did not.
  4. Press Next Sentence to highlight the next sentence. After sentence 10, press See Score.
  5. The summary shows n of 10 correct, whether you met the mastery threshold of 8, and a bar chart of how many sentences carry each component. Notice which component is the most numerous.

On narrow screens the prompt box shows a window of sentences around the highlighted one, with notes for the sentences above and below.
