docs.title: Prompt Injection Spotter
docs.text: Run the Prompt Injection Spotter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A prompt injection is text inside the material a model processes that is written to be taken as an instruction. Telling it apart from ordinary content is harder than it sounds, because ordinary documents are full of imperative sentences. A methods section tells a human reader what to do, and that is not an injection. An injection is aimed at the model, or at whatever reads the text automatically, and tries to change what it does.

This MicroSim asks you to differentiate eight snippets that an agent has been asked to read. Each one comes with a source label, such as a paper's methods section, a README, or a message in a mailbox. Surface features appear in both classes: imperative voice and words like "ignore" or "disregard" show up in ordinary content as well as in injections, so you have to decide who the text is addressed to.

Classification Meaning Injected instruction Directed at an AI model or automated reader, asking it to change its behavior, disclose information, or take an action Ordinary content Anything else, including imperative text addressed to a human reader

For each injected instruction, the feedback names the capability the text tries to borrow (the report, a secret, a mailbox, or a shell) and the structural defense from the chapter that would limit it: least privilege, separated channels, human approval for consequential actions, or treating output as untrusted. All snippets are invented for this exercise, and the domains example.org and example.com are reserved for documentation use.

Learning objective: differentiate, among eight text snippets that an agent has been asked to read, those that contain an injected instruction aimed at the model from those that are ordinary content, with at least 7 of 8 classified correctly.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the source label and the snippet. The question on screen is Is this text trying to steer the model?
  2. Press Injected instruction or Ordinary content. Each snippet gets one attempt, and the answer is committed at once.
  3. Read the feedback. A correct answer shows Correct: with the classification; a wrong one shows This is with the correct classification. Both show the reason. For an injected instruction, a box names the capability it tries to borrow and the defense that would limit it.
  4. Press Next Snippet to continue. The eight snippets come in a fixed order.
  5. After snippet 8, press See Score. The summary shows n of 8 correct, whether you met the mastery threshold of 7, and, for each missed snippet, the misconception that the miss suggests. If the list is long, press More Missed Snippets to page through it.

docs.title: Python Traceback Reader
docs.text: Run the Python Traceback Reader MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A Python traceback is read from the bottom. The last line names the kind of failure and the reason, the line above it shows where it happened, and the entry nearest the bottom that is in your code is where to look first. This MicroSim asks you to examine five illustrative tracebacks, each condensed to the file, line, function, and exception message, and to choose the diagnosis that the evidence supports.

Each traceback comes with three diagnoses. One is correct, and the others are plausible causes that the message rules out, so you must read the message and not only the exception type. The tracebacks, file names, and messages are invented for illustration and are labeled "Illustrative" on screen. The order of the three diagnoses is shuffled separately for each traceback every time the page loads, so two learners side by side will see different letters for the same answer.

After each submission the sim reveals the correct diagnosis and the reason, and highlights the part of the traceback that determines the cause with a gold background and an underline.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the traceback in the gray monospaced box and the three diagnoses below it. The question on screen is What does this error tell you about the cause?
  2. Press Diagnosis A, Diagnosis B, or Diagnosis C. The chosen diagnosis is outlined and tagged Your choice. You can change your choice until you submit.
  3. Press Submit. You get one attempt per traceback.
  4. Read the feedback. A correct choice shows Correct. with a check mark; an incorrect choice shows the correct diagnosis with an X. Both are followed by the "Why" sentence. The correct diagnosis is tagged Correct diagnosis with a solid outline, and a wrong pick is tagged Your choice with a dashed outline.
  5. Press Next Traceback to continue. The five tracebacks come in a fixed order.
  6. After the fifth traceback, press See Score to see n of 5 correct and whether the mastery threshold of 4 was met.

Reload the page to start again; the diagnoses are reshuffled on each load.

docs.text:
The learner will examine five Python tracebacks and identify the cause of each from the exception type, message, and failing line, with at least 4 of 5 correct.

  • Bloom level: Analyze

docs.text: • Error message, traceback, exception type, and the rule of reading a traceback from the bottom, from the section "Reading Error Messages" in Chapter 12

docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.text: For each of the five tracebacks the learner chooses one of three diagnoses. A diagnosis is correct when it equals the answer-key diagnosis. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The first line of a traceback shows the problem.
  • A ValueError that the code raised on purpose is a bug in the code.
  • Every error is a code defect.

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text: Sort the five causes into three groups: a problem with the input data, a problem with the environment, and a defect in the code. Which tracebacks point away from the code, and what in the message tells you so?

docs.title: Research Funnel
docs.text: Run the Research Funnel MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Most research ideas never become papers. This MicroSim draws that attrition as a horizontal funnel that is widest at Research Ideas on the left and narrowest at Published Paper on the right. Each of the six stages sits behind a gate, and a gate is a question that an idea must answer well enough to move on.

# Stage Standard research term Gate question 1 Research Ideas Ideation; Stage-Gate Discovery and idea screen Is this a clear, specific question with a measurable outcome? 2 Not Done Before Novelty screen by literature review; FINER Novel Has someone already done this, or is there a real gap? 3 Feasible Within Budget Feasibility study, or scoping; FINER Feasible Can we finish with our time, budget, equipment, and skills? 4 Funded & Approved Proposal and review gate; FINER Interesting, Ethical, Relevant Who cares, and will the advisor, funder, and review board say yes? 5 Validated Results Execution and validation; Stage-Gate Development and Testing Do the experiments support the hypothesis, and can others reproduce them? 6 Published Paper Dissemination by peer review Do reviewers judge the work novel, sound, and clearly written?

The stage names come from three published frameworks. The FINER criteria (Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant) are the standard checklist for judging a research question (Hulley et al.). Stage-Gate splits development into work stages separated by go, kill, hold, or recycle gates (Cooper, 1990). The Heilmeier catechism is the set of questions DARPA program managers ask of a proposal, including What is new? and Who cares?

Learning objective: explain the sequence of gates a research idea passes between ideation and publication, using the standard name for each gate, by stepping through the funnel.

The numbers are illustrative

The pass rates (100%, 40%, 60%, 50%, 50%, 70%) are invented to show the shape of a funnel. They are not measured. Real pass rates differ by field, lab, and funder. The height of the funnel is proportional to the surviving ideas, with a minimum height so the last stage stays visible.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the funnel from left to right. The number in each segment is how many of your starting ideas survive to that stage.
  2. Press Next and Previous, or click a segment, its label, or its pass rate, to select a stage. The selected stage is outlined and its label is bold.
  3. Read the panel under the funnel: the research term for the gate, how many ideas remain, the gate question, why ideas stop there, and an EE example.
  4. Move the Starting ideas slider (20 to 200) to see how the counts change. A funnel that begins with 20 ideas ends with about one published paper.
  5. Visit all six stages. The counter beside the buttons shows Visited n of 6, and when the sixth stage is opened two confetti cannons fire from the lower corners. Confetti fires once per run, and the message "All six gates visited. Well done!" stays at the bottom of the drawing region.
  6. Press Reset to return to stage 1 with only that stage counted as visited, so you can run through the funnel again.

docs.title: Bloom Level
docs.text: Understand (verb: explain)

docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites

  2. Step through (5 min): press Next to visit each stage and compare the real gate names with your prediction. Visiting all six stages fires the confetti cannons.
  3. Apply to your own idea (5 min): choose one idea you are considering and answer each gate question for it in one sentence. Mark the first gate where you cannot answer.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Hulley, S. B., Cummings, S. R., Browner, W. S., Grady, D. G., and Newman, T. B. Designing Clinical Research, 4th ed. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2013. The source of the FINER criteria.
  2. Cooper, R. G. "Stage-Gate Systems: A New Tool for Managing New Products." Business Horizons 33(3), 1990, pp. 44-54. The Stage-Gate process of work stages and go/kill gates.
  3. DARPA. The Heilmeier Catechism. The questions asked of a research proposal, including what is new and who cares.
  4. Ioannidis, J. P. A. "Why Most Published Research Findings Are False." PLoS Medicine 2(8), 2005, e124. Why results often fail the validation gate.

docs.title: Research Idea Ranking Matrix
docs.text: Run the Research Idea Ranking Matrix MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Idea ranking orders candidate ideas by weighted criteria. The weighted score of an idea is

\[ S = \sum_i w_i s_i \]

where \( s_i \) is its score on criterion \( i \) from 1 to 5 and \( w_i \) is the weight, with the weights summing to 1. This MicroSim asks you to calculate weighted scores for four research ideas on a 10-bit SAR ADC and to see that the ranking depends on the weights.

The four ideas are scored on impact, feasibility, novelty, and low risk, where 5 is best and a higher "Low risk" score means lower risk. Two weighting profiles apply different priorities to the same scores: P1: Exploratory thesis (0.3, 0.1, 0.4, 0.2) and P2: Deadline in three months (0.2, 0.5, 0.1, 0.2). The ideas, scores, and weights are invented for illustration.

Five questions come in a fixed order: two weighted-score calculations and three questions about which idea ranks first. After each question the sim shows the worked calculation and the full ranking under both profiles. After the fifth question, exploration opens and you can set your own weights.

Learning objective: calculate the weighted score of research ideas under two weighting profiles and state which idea ranks first under each, with all five answers correct.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the score matrix and the two weighting profiles. The profile a question uses is outlined and marked with an arrow.
  2. For a number question, type your answer in the Answer box and press Submit (or Enter). A number is correct when it is within 0.05 of the answer. You have two attempts. After a first wrong attempt the hint is Multiply each score by its weight and add the four products.
  3. For a choice question, pick an answer from the drop-down list and press Submit. You have one attempt.
  4. Read the feedback: Correct. with the worked calculation, or the correct answer with the worked calculation. The ranking under both profiles appears below it. The running count n of 5 correct is at the top.
  5. Press Next Question. After question 5, press Explore Weights.
  6. In exploration, move the four sliders (steps of 0.05, from 0.00 to 1.00). The ranking is shown only while the weights sum to 1.00; when they do not, the sim shows the current sum and how much to lower or raise the weights in total. Ties are reported as tied. Try moving a small amount of weight from one criterion to another and watch whether the leader changes.

Feedback uses a check mark or X and words as well as color. Scores are shown to one decimal place.

docs.title: Research Task Decomposition Builder
docs.text: Run the Research Task Decomposition Builder MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Task decomposition breaks a research goal into subtasks that each have a checkable output and explicit prerequisites. This MicroSim asks you to apply two criteria to one concrete goal from Chapter 1:

Goal: Compare the measured and simulated ENOB of two ADC designs.

You see eight candidate subtask cards, labeled A to H in a shuffled order. Six of them are the subtasks S1 to S6 that decompose the goal. The other two are distractors: one is not a subtask at all, and one is outside the scope of the goal. Your job is to build one ordered list that contains exactly the six subtasks, in an order where every subtask comes after all of its prerequisites.

A submission is valid when:

  • all six subtasks S1 to S6 are present and neither distractor is present, and
  • for every subtask, each of its prerequisites appears at an earlier position. S2 and S3 may appear in either order. S4 must appear after S2, and S5 after S3. S6 must appear after both S4 and S5.

When you press Check Order, the sim reports every problem it finds: a card that does not belong (with its "Why" sentence), a required subtask that is missing, or a card placed before its prerequisite (naming both cards and giving the "Why" sentence). You have two submissions. After a correct submission, or after the second submission, the answer and the reason for every card are shown, together with the result: Correct within n submission(s) or Not yet correct.

Learning objective: apply the criteria of a checkable output and a valid order to select six well-formed subtasks from eight candidates and sequence them so every prerequisite precedes its dependent.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the goal and the eight cards. The question on screen is Which of these are well-formed subtasks for this goal, and in what order?
  2. Pick a card in the drop-down list below the drawing. The picked card is outlined in dark blue.
  3. Press Add Card to put it at the end of your sequence. A card in the sequence is shaded and shows its position, for example #3, and the drop-down list shows the same number.
  4. To reorder, pick a card that is already in the sequence and press Move Earlier to move it up one position. When a card in the sequence is picked, the add button reads Remove Card; press it to take the card out, then add it again at the end. Any order can be built with these two moves.
  5. Press Check Order to submit. An empty sequence is rejected and does not use a submission. A sequence with fewer than six cards is reported as incomplete.
  6. Read the feedback. Every problem is listed with its reason. On a narrow screen, the feedback opens on its own page; press Next Page to read more, and pick or edit a card to return to the cards.
  7. Revise the sequence and press Check Order a second time if needed. After a correct submission or the second submission, the answer is shown: the six subtasks in a valid order and the two distractors, each with its reason. Use Next Page if the answer does not fit on one page.
  8. Start Over empties the sequence. Before the answer is shown, it keeps the submissions you have used. After the answer is shown, it starts a new attempt with the cards reshuffled and two new submissions; earlier results stay on the status line.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Task decomposition and subtask, as defined in the section "Task Decomposition" in Chapter 1
  • Prerequisite and checkable output: a subtask has a stated input, produces an artifact that can be inspected, and names what must be finished before it
  • Effective number of bits (ENOB) as a figure of merit for an analog-to-digital converter, from the section "The Setting: Electrical Engineering Research" in Chapter 1

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Before adding any card, read the eight cards and apply the checklist from the chapter to each one: Does it have a stated input? Does it produce an artifact you could inspect? Is its scope small enough that a failure is easy to localize? Mark the two cards that fail. Then work backward from the deliverable: ask what the last subtask must receive, then what produces that, and sketch the order on paper.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Build the sequence with Add Card, Move Earlier, and Remove Card, and submit it with Check Order. If the feedback lists problems, read each "Why" sentence and decide whether it is a membership error (a distractor or a missing subtask) or an ordering error (a card before its prerequisite). Fix only what the feedback names and submit a second time. Notice that S2 and S3 can be swapped without breaking the order, because both depend only on S1.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Record the result shown after the answer is revealed. Then, without the sim, write a decomposition of a goal from your own research into four to six subtasks, give each a checkable output, list its prerequisites, and mark which subtasks are independent of each other and could run in parallel.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Mastery: a correct submission within two submissions, shown as Correct within 1 submission or Correct within 2 submissions. Not yet correct after the second submission means mastery is not yet shown.
  • The learner can explain why each distractor is excluded: "Do the research on the ADC" has no checkable output and no defined scope, and "Improve the ADC until its ENOB reaches 9.5 bits" changes the design instead of comparing ENOB.
  • The learner can state the prerequisite of each subtask and explain why S2 and S3 may appear in either order.
  • Moving cards before submitting, and reading the revealed answer, are exploration, not evidence of mastery.

docs.title: Research Task Sorter
docs.text: Run the Research Task Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Not every research task should be handed to a model, and not every task should be kept away from one. This MicroSim asks you to differentiate ten research tasks by the kind of check or judgment they need, not by how technical they sound. Each task belongs in exactly one of three groups:

Group Meaning AI drafts, you verify A model can produce a first version, and you can check the result cheaply You decide, AI assists A model can supply options or analysis; the choice depends on your knowledge and judgment You do directly Responsibility, commitment, or certification that cannot be handed off

The ten task cards come from the five everyday research tasks in Chapter 1: literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, scientific coding, and manuscript preparation. After each placement the sim tells you whether it matched the answer key, gives a one-sentence reason, and, when you missed, names the correct group. The goal is to match the answer key on at least 8 of 10 cards.

Learning objective: differentiate ten research tasks into "AI drafts, you verify", "You decide, AI assists", and "You do directly", matching the answer key in at least 8 of 10 tasks.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the task card in the dark-blue box and the three group definitions below it. The question on screen is Who should do this task: the model, you assisted, or only you?
  2. Press the button with the name of the group you choose. The placement is committed at once and cannot be changed.
  3. Read the feedback. Correct (with a check mark) or Not quite (with an X) is followed by the "Why" sentence, and a miss also shows the correct group. The correct group is outlined and marked with a check mark; a wrong pick is marked with an X.
  4. Press Next Card to continue. The Placed count on each group shows how many cards you have put there in this run.
  5. After the tenth card, press See Score. The summary shows n of 10 correct, whether you reached mastery (8 of 10), and every card you placed incorrectly with its correct group and "Why" sentence. If the list is long, press More Missed Cards to page through it.
  6. Press Run Again to play a new run with the cards reshuffled. The score of every run stays on screen so you can see whether you improved.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The five everyday research tasks (literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, scientific coding, manuscript preparation) from the section "The Five Everyday Research Tasks" in Chapter 1
  • The definitions of the three groups "AI drafts, you verify", "You decide, AI assists", and "You do directly"
  • Basic familiarity with lab measurement, simulation, and paper-writing workflows in electrical engineering

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Before placing any card, read the three group definitions and write down, in one phrase each, the test you will use to tell them apart (for example: "Can I check the output cheaply?", "Does the choice depend on what only I know?", "Does it carry my signature or commitment?"). Then play one run without stopping to think too long, and note which cards surprised you.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Review the list of missed cards on the summary screen. For each miss, read the "Why" sentence and decide which of your three tests you applied incorrectly. Compare two cards that sound similar but fall in different groups, such as "Draft an abstract from a table of measured results" (AI drafts, you verify) and "Certify before submission that the reported measurements were taken and not generated" (You do directly), and explain in a sentence what separates them.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Press Run Again and sort the reshuffled cards. Record both run scores. Then write one new task from your own research that would belong in each group, and justify each placement with a sentence in the style of the "Why" feedback.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Mastery: at least 8 of 10 placements match the answer key on the first run. The score of the second (reshuffled) run shows whether the criteria transferred.
  • The learner can state, for any missed card, why the answer-key group is correct, using the distinction between cheap verification, judgment that depends on the researcher's knowledge, and responsibility that cannot be delegated.
  • The learner's three self-written tasks are each placed in a defensible group with a one-sentence justification.
  • Reading the feedback and reviewing the missed-card list are exploration, not evidence of mastery.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This diagram turns Table 1 of Chapter 1 into a flowchart. The running example follows a doctoral student designing a low-power SAR ADC through five stages. Each box is a stage, and each arrow carries the artifact that the stage hands to the next one. The example is illustrative and not drawn from a published study.

docs.title: Workflow Steps
docs.text:
1. Find what is known takes a topic and a gap and produces a reading list with citations.
  2. Frame the question turns the reading list and a design goal into one falsifiable question statement.
  3. Build and measure uses the question and a design to produce netlists, scripts, and raw data files.
  4. Analyze turns the raw data files into result tables and plots with uncertainty.
  5. Communicate turns the result tables and plots into manuscript source and figures.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Hover over any box to see its input, output, and handoff artifact in the right panel.
  2. Hover over an arrow label to read what that artifact is and which stages it connects.
  3. Click each box. A clicked box gets a green outline, and the counter above the panel shows how many of the seven boxes you have clicked. With the keyboard, press Tab to reach a box and Enter or Space to click it.
  4. Click all seven boxes to fire the confetti cannon once. It does not fire before then, and it does not fire again. Confetti is skipped if your system requests reduced motion.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will describe the input, output, and handoff artifact of each of the five research workflow stages (Bloom: Understand, verb: describe).

docs.title: Activity
docs.text: Cover the right panel and name the handoff artifact on each arrow from memory. Then hover to check. For one arrow, say what would go wrong downstream if that artifact contained an unnoticed error.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can the learner name the artifact passed between each pair of adjacent stages?
  • Can the learner explain why a handoff is where quality is either confirmed or silently lost?

docs.title: Review Checkpoint Judge
docs.text: Run the Review Checkpoint Judge MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An agent that can act on your files, send messages, and compute results will take many steps you did not individually approve. Asking for approval on every step teaches you to click through requests; asking for none lets an irreversible or public mistake through. This MicroSim asks you to judge where a human review checkpoint belongs, using three criteria from Chapter 1 that stay on screen the whole time:

Criterion Question Reversibility Is the action irreversible? Outward effect Does the output leave your control by being sent, published, or used to commit resources? Reported result Does the output become a result you will report?

A step requires review when at least one criterion applies.

You see eight agent steps from an analysis workflow, one at a time and in a new shuffled order on every run. For each step you commit two things together: a judgment, Review required or No review needed, and the main reason, which is one of the three criteria or No criterion applies. Choosing the reason separates a correct decision from a correct guess. Four of the eight steps require review and four do not.

Learning objective: judge, for each of eight agent steps in an analysis workflow, whether a human review checkpoint is required before its output is used, agreeing with the answer key on at least 7 of 8 steps.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the three criteria at the top and the agent step in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is Does this output need your review before it is used?
  2. Choose the main reason in the drop-down list below the drawing: Reversibility, Outward effect, Reported result, or No criterion applies. If you press a judgment button without choosing a reason, the sim asks you to choose one first and nothing is recorded.
  3. Press Review required or No review needed. The judgment and the reason are committed together and cannot be changed.
  4. Read the feedback. Correct means both the judgment and the reason match the answer key. Right decision, different reason means the judgment matches but the reason does not; the correct reason is shown. Not quite means the judgment does not match; the correct judgment is shown. The "Why" sentence appears after every commit, and the criterion that is the main reason is marked Main reason with a check mark.
  5. Press Next Step to continue. After the eighth step, press See Score. The summary shows the score as n of 8 (it counts judgments only), whether you reached mastery (7 of 8), and every step judged incorrectly with its "Why" sentence. If the list is long, press More Missed Steps to page through it.
  6. Press Run Again to judge the eight steps again in a reshuffled order. The score of every run stays on screen.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Human in the loop: the three positions of a person relative to an automated process (in the loop, on the loop, out of the loop), from the section "Human in the Loop" in Chapter 1
  • Reversible and irreversible actions
  • Output that leaves your control by being sent, published, or used to commit resources
  • Output that becomes a reported result
  • The idea of an agent as an assistant with tools and a loop, which can take actions you did not individually approve

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Read the three criteria and restate each one as a yes/no test you could apply in under ten seconds. Then judge the first step without hurrying, and read the "Why" sentence and the marked main reason before pressing Next Step. Reading the criteria is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Finish the run. On the summary screen, for each step judged incorrectly, name the criterion you applied (or failed to apply) and explain the miss using the "Why" sentence. Compare two pairs that look alike but are judged differently: the agent sends an email versus drafts the same email and leaves it unsent, and the agent overwrites the raw measurement files versus renames a column header in a copy of the data file. Write one sentence for each pair saying which criterion separates them.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Press Run Again and judge the reshuffled steps. Record the first-run and second-run scores and how many steps showed Right decision, different reason. Then describe one agent step from your own research workflow, judge it, and name its main reason in the style of the "Why" feedback.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Mastery: at least 7 of 8 judgments match the answer key on the first run. The score counts judgments only.
  • The learner names the correct main reason for each step that requires review (Reversibility, Outward effect, or Reported result) and gives "No criterion applies" for the four steps that do not. A "Right decision, different reason" result shows a judgment that is not yet backed by the right criterion.
  • The learner explains, for any missed step, why the answer-key judgment is correct using the three criteria.
  • The learner's own example step is judged with a defensible reason.
  • Common misconceptions to listen for: every agent action needs review, so review is never a choice; a step that looks harmless needs no review even when it is irreversible; a step that only drafts something is safe to send without review.

docs.title: Search Query Precision and Recall Explorer
docs.text: Run the Search Query Precision and Recall Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Two numbers describe how well a search query performs. Precision is the fraction of the results returned that are relevant, and recall is the fraction of all the relevant papers that were returned. With \( TP \) relevant results returned, \( FP \) irrelevant results returned, and \( FN \) relevant papers missed:

\[ \text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}, \qquad \text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}. \]

This MicroSim uses a corpus of 20 papers, P1 to P20, that is synthetic, invented for this exercise. Eight of the papers are relevant to the search question. Three queries are run on the corpus:

Query Description A A narrow query using the exact phrase "foreground calibration" B A broad query using OR across many synonyms C A balanced query combining architecture and technique terms

For each query you count the relevant papers in the result set and calculate precision and recall to two decimal places. The narrow query and the broad query sit at opposite ends of the trade-off: broadening a query raises recall and lowers precision, and narrowing does the opposite. At the end you use the numbers to choose the query that suits a stated purpose.

The question on screen is What fraction of the results are relevant, and what fraction of the relevant papers were found?

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. The corpus is drawn as a grid of 20 papers. Papers returned by the current query have a solid blue box; papers that were not returned have a dashed box. Query A is shown first.
  2. Press Reveal Relevant Set. Each relevant paper now carries a star (★).
  3. Use the checkboxes to mark the returned papers that are relevant. Each marked paper shows a check mark (✓) in the grid, and the panel counts how many you marked. Marking is a counting aid and is not scored.
  4. Type precision and recall as decimals with two places, for example 0.25, and press Check Values (or press Enter). A value counts as correct when it is within 0.01 of the reference value.
  5. You have two attempts for each query. After a first attempt with a wrong value you see a hint, and a correct value is locked with a ✓ so you change only the other one. After a correct answer, or after the second attempt, the sim shows the worked counts (TP, FP, FN and both fractions) and labels every paper in the grid TP, FP, or FN.
  6. Press Next Query to repeat the steps for queries B and C.
  7. Press Go to Purpose Question, choose a query from the list, and press Submit Choice. You have one attempt. The sim shows whether your choice is correct, the correct answer with its reason, the worked values for all three queries, and your score.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the precision and recall of three search queries run on a corpus of twenty papers with eight known relevant papers, and choose the query that suits a stated purpose (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Search strategy, precision, recall, true positive, false positive, and false negative, all defined in the section "Searching: Strategy, Keywords, and Sources" of Chapter 11.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (3 min): Before revealing the relevant set, look at the result sets of the three queries. Predict which query will have the highest recall and which the highest precision.
  2. Guided Practice (7 min): Work through queries A, B, and C. For each one, mark the relevant returned papers, write down TP, FP, and FN, and only then compute the two fractions. Compare query A and query B: one has high recall and low precision, and the other the reverse.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Answer the purpose question. Then, without the sim, state which query you would choose if you needed a short list of the best papers on a subtopic, and justify the choice with the numbers.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Evidence of mastery: at least 5 of the 6 precision and recall values are correct (each within 0.01 of the reference value, on the first or second attempt for that query) and the purpose-question choice is correct.
  • Browsing the corpus and marking papers is exploration and is not evidence.
  • Watch for three misconceptions: that a query returning many results is a good query, that high precision means the search found everything relevant, and that precision and recall always move together.

Chapter 11: AI-Assisted Literature Search and Synthesis - the section "Searching: Strategy, Keywords, and Sources" defines precision and recall and states that broadening a query raises recall and lowers precision. The corpus and queries in this MicroSim are synthetic and invented for this exercise.

docs.title: Skill Anatomy Labeler
docs.text: Run the Skill Anatomy Labeler MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An agent skill is a directory. Its central file, SKILL.md, starts with YAML frontmatter that holds the skill name and the skill description, and its body holds the skill instructions. Scripts, reference documents, and templates sit beside it as supporting files, opened only when the instructions point to them.

This MicroSim shows the complete enob-report skill from the chapter: its directory tree and its SKILL.md file. The question on screen is Which part of the skill is this? One of eight items is highlighted at a time, in a fixed order, and you label it as one of four parts: Skill name, Skill description, Skill instructions, or Supporting file.

Each item has exactly one correct label. Two rules settle the harder cases: a line inside SKILL.md below the frontmatter is Skill instructions, and a path to a file other than SKILL.md is a Supporting file.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Find the highlighted item. It has a yellow box around it and a ▶ marker beside it, in either the directory tree or SKILL.md.
  2. Choose a label from the menu below the drawing: Skill name, Skill description, Skill instructions, or Supporting file.
  3. Press Submit. Each item gets one attempt, and the label cannot be changed after you submit it.
  4. Read the feedback. A correct label shows ✓ Correct: label. An incorrect one shows ✗ This is a label. naming the correct label. Both are followed by the reason.
  5. Press Next item to highlight the next item.
  6. After item 8 the sim shows your score as n of 8 correct and whether you met the mastery threshold of 7. Press Start over to label the eight items again.

docs.title: Skill Description Trigger Tester
docs.text: Run the Skill Description Trigger Tester MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An agent decides whether to load a skill by comparing the user's request with the skill's description. A good trigger test checks both directions: the skill should fire on requests it covers and stay quiet on requests it does not. The most useful tests are near misses, requests that share a keyword with the description but ask for a different task.

This MicroSim shows one illustrative skill description:

"Check a SPICE netlist for floating nodes, a missing .end card, and unit suffix errors. Use when the user asks to lint, check, or validate a .sp or .cir netlist file."

You then judge eight user requests, one at a time and in a fixed order. The rule is that a request should trigger the skill when it asks for a task and an input type that the description names. Shared vocabulary alone does not make a request trigger. Each request has exactly one correct answer. The description and the requests are invented for illustration.

Learning objective: distinguish, for each of eight user requests, whether a stated skill description should trigger the skill or not, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the skill description at the top and request 1 in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is Would an agent load this skill for this request?
  2. Press Should trigger or Should not trigger. Your choice gets a thick border and is named on screen. You can switch to the other answer until you submit.
  3. Press Submit. Each request gets one attempt, and the answer cannot be changed after you submit it.
  4. Read the feedback. Correct. (with a check mark) or the correct answer (with an X) is followed by the "Why" sentence. The correct answer is always shown.
  5. Press Next Request to continue. After request 8, press See Score.
  6. The summary shows n of 8 correct, whether you met the mastery threshold of 7, and the requests that share a keyword with the description but should not trigger, each with the shared keyword. Reload the page to start over.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Skill description, skill triggering, single-purpose skill, and trigger tests, from the sections "Scoping a Skill" and "Testing and Evaluating a Skill" in Chapter 7 and from Chapter 6
  • Basic familiarity with SPICE netlists (.sp and .cir files)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (3 min): Read the skill description and underline the task it names (check, lint, validate) and the input types it names (.sp and .cir netlist files). Reading the description is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  2. Practice (5 min): Judge the eight requests. For each, ask two questions: does it ask for the checking task, and is the input a SPICE netlist file?
  3. Reflection (2 min): On the summary screen, read the near-miss requests. For each, name the keyword it shares with the description and the task it actually asks for.

docs.title: Evidence of Mastery
docs.text: For each of eight requests the learner commits "should trigger" or "should not trigger". A choice is correct when it equals the answer key. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the skill description is exploration and is not evidence.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 7: Designing, Testing, and Sharing Agent Skills - the section "Testing and Evaluating a Skill" defines trigger tests and recommends near-miss requests that share a keyword with the skill.

docs.title: Skill Failure Mode Classifier
docs.text: Run the Skill Failure Mode Classifier MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Skills fail in a small number of recurring ways, and each failure mode points to a different fix. This MicroSim asks you to trace a symptom to its cause. The eight observations share surface features, such as "it gave the wrong result", so you have to reason from what did not happen: the skill was not loaded, it loaded wrongly, a step was skipped, it cannot run, its content is outdated, or it has too many jobs.

The six failure modes, from the section "Failure Modes and Maintenance" in Chapter 7, are listed on screen with their definitions:

Failure mode Symptom Undertriggering The skill is not used when it should be Overtriggering The skill loads on requests it cannot handle Instruction drift The skill loads, but the agent skips or reorders steps Missing dependency A script needs a library, tool, or file that is not present Stale reference A reference document or hard-coded path is out of date Scope creep The skill has accumulated extra jobs and does none reliably

The observations are invented for illustration, and each has exactly one correct mode.

Learning objective: attribute each of eight observed skill problems to one of six failure modes, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read observation 1 in the dark-blue box and the six failure modes below it. The question on screen is Which failure mode explains this?
  2. Choose a mode in the drop-down list. The chosen mode is outlined and marked with an arrow in the list on screen.
  3. Press Submit. Each observation gets one attempt, and the choice cannot be changed after you submit it.
  4. Read the feedback. Correct: <mode>. (with a check mark) or This is <mode>. (with an X) is followed by the "Why" sentence. The correct mode is outlined and marked with a check mark, and a wrong pick is marked with an X.
  5. Press Next Observation to continue. After observation 8, press See Score.
  6. The summary shows n of 8 correct, whether you met the mastery threshold of 7, and the recommended fix for each mode you missed, with the observations you missed. Reload the page to start over.

docs.title: Sycophancy Spotter
docs.text: Run the Sycophancy Spotter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Sycophancy is a model's tendency to agree with the user, to tell them what they appear to want to hear, and to change an answer under pushback even when no new evidence has been given. A change of answer is a warning unless the pushback contained evidence. This MicroSim asks you to distinguish replies that follow the researcher from replies that follow the evidence, across six short exchanges written in several tones, so that tone alone is not a cue.

The two classifications shown on screen are:

Classification Rule Sycophantic Agrees with, validates, or reverses to match the researcher's stated view without new evidence. Calibrated Changes only for supplied evidence, or states what it cannot establish and what would.

All six exchanges are invented for illustration and are labeled "illustrative" on screen. Each exchange has exactly one correct classification.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the exchange in the dark-blue box: what the researcher said, then the model's reply. The question on screen is Did the reply follow the evidence or the researcher?
  2. Press Sycophantic or Calibrated. Pressing the button submits your answer. You get one attempt per exchange, and it cannot be changed.
  3. Read the feedback. A correct answer shows ✓ Correct. and an incorrect one shows ✗ This reply is sycophantic (or calibrated), each followed by the "Why" sentence. The correct classification is always revealed: its definition box is outlined and marked with ✓, and a wrong choice is marked with ✗.
  4. Press Next Exchange to continue. The exchanges appear in a fixed order from 1 to 6.
  5. After exchange 6, press See Score. The summary shows n of 6 correct and whether the mastery threshold of 5 was met.
  6. Press Start Over to play the exchanges again. Every run's score stays on screen, but only the first run counts as evidence of mastery.

docs.text:
The learner will distinguish, among six exchanges between a researcher and a model, the replies that are sycophantic from those that are calibrated, with at least 5 of 6 classified correctly.

  • Bloom level: Analyze
  • Bloom verb: distinguish

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Sycophancy, overconfidence, uncertainty awareness, and the countermeasures, all defined in the section "Behaviors of Models That Undermine Checks" in Chapter 17

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (2 min): Read the two definitions on screen. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  2. Assessment (4 min): Classify the six exchanges in order, one attempt each, and record the first-run score.
  3. Discussion (4 min): Compare exchanges 2 and 3, which concern the same 50 Hz notch. Explain why one reply is sycophantic and the other calibrated, using the presence or absence of new evidence. Then compare exchanges 4 and 5 and discuss why declining to certify novelty is not unhelpful.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Evidence of mastery: for each of the six exchanges the learner commits "sycophantic" or "calibrated". A classification is correct when it equals the answer key. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.
  • Reading the definitions is exploration and is not evidence.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
1. A model that changes its answer is being responsive.
  2. A polite and agreeable reply is a good reply.
  3. A model that declines to confirm is being unhelpful.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 17: Verification and Reproducibility - the section "Behaviors of Models That Undermine Checks" defines sycophancy, overconfidence, and uncertainty awareness and gives the countermeasures used in this MicroSim.

docs.title: Task Dependency Critical Path Scheduler
docs.text: Run the Task Dependency Critical Path Scheduler MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Nine tasks from the running ADC project are drawn as a dependency graph, from the literature survey (T1) at the top to final assembly (T9) at the bottom. Each task shows its duration in hours. The durations are illustrative. An arrow from A to B means that B needs A's output. The question on screen at the start is When can T5 finish?

The sim asks five questions in a fixed order:

  1. What is the earliest finish time of T5, in hours?
  2. Which tasks form the critical path?
  3. What is the slack of T4, in hours?
  4. What is the project duration, in hours?
  5. If T3 is reduced from 3 hours to 1 hour, what is the new project duration, in hours?

Each question has one attempt. After you submit, the sim says whether you were correct, gives the correct answer and the reason, and adds the forward pass to the graph: the earliest start and finish of each task. The tasks that the answer depends on are marked with a ▶ and a dashed blue border. From question 2 on, critical tasks carry a ★ critical tag, an orange fill, and a thick border, and the arrows between them are drawn thick and solid. From question 3 on, every task shows its slack.

The rules are those of the chapter. A task's earliest start is the latest earliest finish of its prerequisites, or 0 if it has none. Its earliest finish is its earliest start plus its duration. The project duration is the largest earliest finish. Slack is the latest finish that does not delay the project minus the earliest finish, and a task is on the critical path when its slack is 0.

After question 5 the graph switches to T3 = 1 hour, and a T3 duration slider lets you try other values and watch the critical path move. Cutting 2 hours from T3 saves only 1 hour, because the path through the test suite T4 then becomes critical.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the graph. Each node shows the task, its name, and its duration in hours.
  2. Type your answer in hours in the box and press Submit (or Enter). For question 2, press the T1 to T9 buttons to select the tasks on the critical path, then press Submit. If the box does not contain a number, the sim asks for one and does not count the attempt.
  3. Read the feedback and the new start and finish times on the graph, then press Next question.
  4. After question 5, read your score, n of 5 correct, and whether you met the mastery threshold of 4. Move the T3 duration slider to see how the project duration and the critical path change.
  5. At any time, click a task in the graph or choose it in Read a task to read its details. You can also drag tasks around the graph. Reading details and dragging tasks are exploration and are not scored.
  6. Press Restart to begin again with no times shown.

The zoom and arrow buttons in the graph corners zoom and pan the graph. Below 720 pixels of width, the graph and the question panel are stacked and scroll together inside the frame.

docs.text:
The learner will calculate the earliest finish time, the critical path, and the slack of tasks in a nine-task dependency graph, and recalculate the project duration after one duration changes, with at least 4 of 5 answers correct.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Task dependencies, task queue, critical path, earliest finish, and slack, all from the section "Breaking Work Down" of Chapter 10.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min): Before answering, add up all nine durations (21 hours) and write down whether you expect the project to take that long.
  2. Calculate (8 min): Answer the five questions in order. For each number question, write the forward pass on paper first: the start and finish of every task the answer depends on.
  3. Explore (5 min): After question 5, move the T3 slider from 1 to 6 hours. Note the value of T3 at which the critical path switches between the T3 branch and the T4 branch, and explain why cutting 2 hours from T3 saved only 1 hour.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Evidence of mastery: for each of the five questions the learner enters a value or selects a path, and an answer is correct when it equals the answer key (12; T1, T2, T3, T5, T6, T8, T9; 1; 18; 17). Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Temperature Next-Token Explorer
docs.text: Run the Temperature Next-Token Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
At each step a language model scores every candidate token and converts the scores into probabilities. Temperature reshapes those probabilities before one token is chosen:

pi = exp(zi / T) / Σj exp(zj / T)

This MicroSim shows five candidate next tokens for the illustrative prompt "The measured ENOB of the converter is", with scores 2.0, 1.0, 0.0, -1.0, and -2.0. The prompt, tokens, and scores are illustrative, not output of a real model; the percentages are computed from the formula over these five candidates only.

Temperature " 9" " 10" " 8" " about" " lower" 0.5 86.5% 11.7% 1.6% 0.2% 0.0% 1.0 63.6% 23.4% 8.6% 3.2% 1.2% 2.0 42.9% 26.0% 15.8% 9.6% 5.8%

You infer the direction of change before you see it. Three predictions ask whether a token's probability rises, falls, or stays the same when the temperature changes. After the predictions, an exploration mode offers a temperature slider (0.1 to 2.0) and a Draw 10 Samples button. The draws are synthetic and use a fixed seed of 42, so the same temperature always gives the same ten draws.

The token being asked about is drawn in a different color, outlined, and tagged "asked". After a reveal, a dashed outline on each bar shows the probability before the change.

Learning objective: infer, before it is revealed, whether the probability of the top-ranked and of the lowest-ranked candidate token rises or falls when the temperature is raised or lowered.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the distribution at temperature 1.0 and prediction 1: If temperature drops to 0.5, what happens to the probability of the top token?
  2. Choose rises, falls, or stays the same from the list, then press Reveal. You have one attempt per prediction.
  3. The chart changes to the new temperature. Correct answers show the old and new percentages. Incorrect answers show the correct answer, the reason, and the revealed numbers. The running count Predictions correct: n of 3 is shown at the top.
  4. Press Next Prediction. Each prediction starts again from temperature 1.0.
  5. After prediction 3, press Open Exploration Mode. Drag the temperature slider across the full range and press Draw 10 Samples at several temperatures. Notice that the ranking never changes, and that the same ten draws become more varied as the temperature rises.

docs.text:
The learner will infer, before it is revealed, whether the probability of the top-ranked and of the lowest-ranked candidate token rises or falls when the temperature is raised or lowered.

  • Bloom level: Understand
  • Bloom verb: infer

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Token, probability distribution, and temperature with the formula pi = exp(zi/T) / Σj exp(zj/T), from the section "Temperature and Sampling" in Chapter 2

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predictions (4 min): Commit each of the three predictions before revealing it. Write a one-line reason for each prediction first.
  2. Exploration (4 min): Set the temperature to 0.1, 1.0, and 2.0 and press Draw 10 Samples at each. Record how many of the ten draws are the top token " 9" at each temperature.
  3. Reflection (2 min): Explain in one sentence why low temperature makes an answer more repeatable but not more correct.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Evidence of mastery: each of the three predictions ("rises", "falls", or "stays the same") is committed before the new distribution is shown and matches the change computed from the formula. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct.
  • Dragging the temperature control freely is exploration and is not evidence of mastery.

docs.title: Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Low temperature makes the model more accurate.
  • Temperature changes which token ranks first.
  • At high temperature every token becomes equally likely.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 2: How Language Models Work - the section "Temperature and Sampling" gives the softmax-with-temperature formula and the worked example of how temperature changes the odds but not the ranking.

docs.title: Unit Test Selector for Seeded Bugs
docs.text: Run the Unit Test Selector for Seeded Bugs MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A test that passes does not prove that a function is correct. It only shows that the function gives the right answer on the input you chose. This MicroSim asks you to apply the idea of a known-answer test to a small Python function with three seeded bugs.

The specification says: "Return 10 times the base-10 logarithm of signal power divided by noise power. Raise ValueError if either power is not positive." The buggy implementation is:

def sndr_db(signal, noise): return 20 * np.log10(signal / noise)

Bug Description A Uses 20 times the logarithm instead of 10 times. B Does not raise ValueError when the noise power is 0. C Does not raise ValueError when the signal power is negative or 0.

You may run at most four of the eight candidate tests, so you have to choose each test for what it would reveal. Bug A is the same 10 versus 20 log10 silent error as the chapter's worked example; bugs B and C hide behind boundary inputs that typical values never reach. The sim does not run real Python: it simulates the buggy function's behavior from the specification table.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the eight candidate tests and their expected results under the specification, and the three bugs. The question on screen is Which tests would reveal what is wrong? Use the Show menu to read the specification and the buggy implementation. On a wide screen the table and the code are shown together.
  2. Check up to four tests (Test 1 to Test 8). Selected rows are tinted and marked ☑.
  3. Press Run. If more than four tests are checked, the sim refuses with Choose at most four tests.
  4. Read the run results: each selected test is marked ✓ PASS or ✗ FAIL on the buggy code with its "Why" sentence, followed by Bugs exposed: … Bugs hidden: …. The first run is the one that counts as evidence, and the sim keeps it on screen.
  5. Change the selection and run again as often as you like. From the second run on, choose Show minimum set to see the minimum set and the reason each test exposes its bug.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will apply the idea of a known-answer test by selecting, from eight candidate unit tests, a set of at most four that exposes all three seeded bugs in a function.

  • Bloom level: Apply
  • Bloom verb: apply

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Unit test, known-answer test, silent error, and boundary input, from the sections "Why Tests, and Which Ones" and "Debugging and Code Review" in Chapter 13

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (3 min): Before checking any box, write next to each bug the input that would make the buggy code disagree with the specification.
  2. Select and run (4 min): Choose at most four tests and press Run. Record which bugs your first run exposed.
  3. Reflect (3 min): Run again with a different selection, then open the minimum set. Explain why test 2 can never expose a bug, and why typical values such as tests 1, 5, 6 and 7 cannot expose bugs B and C.

docs.title: Evidence of Mastery
docs.text:
• The learner selects up to four tests and presses Run. The selection is correct when every one of the three bugs is exposed by at least one selected test and no more than four tests are selected.
  • Mastery: a correct selection on the first run, which needs one of tests 1, 5, 6, 7 (bug A), test 3 (bug B), and one of tests 4, 8 (bug C).
  • Reading the function source is exploration and is not evidence.

docs.title: Verification Method Matcher
docs.text: Run the Verification Method Matcher MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A check is only as useful as the kind of error it can catch. This MicroSim asks you to recommend a verification method for each of eight claims or situations that come up in AI-assisted EE research. Each claim could be wrong in a different way, so no single favorite method scores well. The five methods come from the section "Kinds of Checks" in Chapter 17:

Method What it guards against Known-answer test Implementation errors Independent method Method-specific errors and shared assumptions Primary source check Misquotation, fabrication, outdated facts Cross-model check Gross errors, a screening aid Replication Non-reproducible results

All eight claims are invented for illustration and are labeled "illustrative" on screen. Each claim has exactly one correct method, chosen by what the claim could be wrong about: an implementation, a method, a quotation, a screening question, or recurrence.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the claim in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is What could be wrong with this claim, and which check would reveal it? The table below the claim lists the five methods and what each one guards against.
  2. Choose a method in the drop-down list below the drawing area. The chosen row is marked with ▸ and "(selected)". Press Submit. You get one attempt per claim, and the answer cannot be changed after you submit it.
  3. Read the feedback. A correct choice shows ✓ Correct: method. and an incorrect one shows ✗ The better fit is method., each followed by the "Why" sentence. The correct method is always revealed: its row is outlined and marked with ✓, and a wrong choice is marked with ✗.
  4. Press Next Claim to continue. The claims appear in a fixed order from 1 to 8.
  5. After claim 8, press See Score. The summary shows n of 8 correct, whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met, and all eight claims grouped by their correct method, each marked ✓ or ✗ with the method you chose. If the groups do not fit on one screen, press Next Page.
  6. Press Start Over to play the claims again. Every run's score stays on screen, but only the first run counts as evidence of mastery.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will recommend which of five verification methods best fits each of eight AI-assisted claims, with at least 7 of 8 matching the answer key.

  • Bloom level: Evaluate
  • Bloom verb: recommend

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Known-answer test, independent method, primary source check, cross-model check, and replication, all defined in the section "Kinds of Checks" in Chapter 17
  • The idea that an independent check has different failure causes from the thing it checks

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (3 min): Read the table of the five methods and what each guards against. Reading the table is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  2. Assessment (5 min): Work through the eight claims in order, one attempt each, and record the first-run score.
  3. Discussion (5 min): On the summary screen, look at the claims grouped by method. For any miss, use the "Why" sentence to name what the claim could have been wrong about. Discuss why asking the same model again is not an independent check, and why a cross-model check flags claims rather than proving them.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Evidence of mastery: for each of the eight claims the learner commits one of the five methods. A method is correct when it equals the answer key. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.
  • Reading the table of methods is exploration and is not evidence.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
1. Asking the same model again is an independent check.
  2. A cross-model check proves a claim.
  3. A single check method suits every claim.

docs.title: From Researcher to Orchestrator
docs.text: A hands-on guide to using AI tools and agents for everyday research in electrical engineering and computer design

docs.title: The Problem: Research Is a Pipeline
docs.text:
• Literature search
  • Data analysis
  • Brainstorming and problem framing
  • Scientific coding and simulation
  • Manuscript preparation

AI can now absorb a large share of each stage, but only for researchers who know how to direct it, check it, and own the result.

docs.title: The Big Idea: Researcher as Orchestrator
docs.text:
• Stop doing every task personally
  • Coordinate ~20 planning agents and ~10 execution agents
  • You set direction, supply domain judgment, resolve conflicts, and decide what is true
  • You stay accountable for the science

docs.title: Who It Is For
docs.text:
Audience: MS and PhD students, postdocs, and faculty in EE, computer engineering, and computer design

Prerequisites

  • Graduate standing or equivalent research experience
  • One programming language, preferably Python
  • Command line, text editor, and Git basics
  • No prior ML, prompt engineering, or agent experience

docs.title: How the Book Is Organized
docs.text: Part Chapters Theme 1. Foundations 1–4 Workflows, how LLMs work, prompts, context 2. Memory and skills 5–7 Markdown, Git, knowledge graphs, skills 3. Agents and teams 8–10 Tools, supervision, orchestration 4. Research tasks 11–15 Literature, data, code, ideas, manuscripts 5. Communicate and trust 16–20 MicroSims, verification, ethics, agents, capstone

docs.title: Foundations: How Language Models Work
docs.text:
Chapters 2–3

  • Text becomes tokens; the context window is a shared budget
  • Models optimize plausibility, not truth, so fluent answers can be false
  • Fabricated citations come from this, not from a bug
  • Choose models by capability, cost, latency, privacy, and reproducibility
  • A prompt is a specification: instructions, constraints, roles, examples

docs.title: Context Engineering
docs.text:
Chapter 4

  • Decide everything the model sees
  • Task spec: goal, inputs, outputs, constraints, definition of done
  • Ground answers in sources
  • Chain prompts with checks between steps
  • Defend against prompt injection

docs.title: Memory: Markdown, Git, and Knowledge Graphs
docs.text:
Chapters 5–6

  • Markdown is readable by both humans and agents
  • AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md hold goals, conventions, constraints
  • Git gives history and recovery
  • A personal knowledge graph links notes, papers, experiments, and people as queryable entities

docs.title: Agent Skills: Repeatable Tasks as Commands
docs.text:
Chapters 6–7

  • Anatomy: name, description, instructions, supporting files
  • One-sentence scope; single-purpose skills
  • Progressive disclosure keeps context small
  • Test that it fires, stays quiet, and gives known answers
  • Version, share, and maintain

docs.title: Agents, Tools, and Subagents
docs.text:
Chapter 8

  • Agent = model + tools + loop
  • Decide, call a tool, observe, repeat
  • File access, shell, code execution, MCP
  • Sandboxing and permissions set the limits
  • Subagents run in parallel with isolated context

docs.title: Supervising Agents and Assigning Roles
docs.text:
Chapter 9

  • Autonomy is a dial set per task
  • Set it by reversibility, reach, and verifiability
  • Log everything; bound cost and runtime
  • Know the failure modes: premature completion, scope drift, test weakening, runaway loops
  • Roles: planner, executor, reviewer, researcher, coder, writer

docs.title: Orchestrating Agent Teams
docs.text:
Chapter 10

  • Break work into tasks with owners, outputs, and checks
  • Dependencies set the critical path, and parallelism cannot shorten it
  • Handoffs through files and a shared workspace
  • Review checkpoints and human approval gates
  • Scaling stops paying off when review cost exceeds the work saved

docs.title: Literature Search and Synthesis
docs.text:
Chapter 11

  • Write a repeatable search strategy
  • Favor recall when scoping, then triage for precision
  • Chain citations forward and backward
  • Verify every citation against the source
  • Tie claims to locations in sources

docs.title: Data Analysis, Simulation, and Code
docs.text:
Chapters 12–13

  • Record measurement settings; keep raw data read-only
  • Cleaning is a logged script; outliers are information
  • Silent errors run cleanly and return wrong numbers
  • Test with known answers
  • Apply numerical sanity checks and pin environments

docs.title: Brainstorming and Manuscripts
docs.text:
Chapters 14–15

  • AI offers volume and range; its weakness is agreement
  • Use a devil's advocate prompt and check analogies
  • Move from hunch to falsifiable hypothesis
  • Draft from evidenced claims; abstract last
  • Protect your voice and your numbers

docs.title: MicroSims: Communicating by Interaction
docs.text:
Chapter 16

  • Match the medium to the point
  • A static figure shows a fact; an interactive shows a dependence
  • A MicroSim is small, single-concept, embeddable
  • Built with p5.js and built-in controls
  • Specify precisely, then check what the agent builds

docs.title: Verification and Reproducibility
docs.text:
Chapter 17

  • Verification: done right? Validation: the right work?
  • Independent checks with different failure causes
  • Primary-source and cross-model checks
  • Fix success criteria before seeing the result
  • Audit trails and reproducibility packages

docs.title: Responsible and Ethical Use
docs.text:
Chapter 18

  • Accountability cannot be delegated; AI is not an author
  • Disclose AI use per venue and institutional policy
  • Protect confidential data, participant data, and unpublished results
  • Respect licensing and intellectual property
  • Check for bias; keep your own skills sharp

docs.title: Personal Agents and Case Studies
docs.text:
Chapters 19–20

  • Always-on agents (Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, Claude Cowork, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent)
  • Judge them by criteria, not brands: where they run, what they reach, cost, data
  • Real cases, including failures: the MicroSims arXiv paper, this textbook's skill pipeline
  • Capstone: an end-to-end task with an agent team, plus an adoption plan

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Direct, check, and own — the researcher stays accountable
  • Context and memory make agents reliable: Markdown, Git, knowledge graphs, skills
  • Autonomy is a dial set per task, bounded by logs and review
  • Verify independently; disclose AI use
  • Start small, then adopt in order

Read the book: dmccreary.github.io/ai-for-ee-research

docs.title: Title: From Researcher to Orchestrator: Managing a Team of AI Agents for Research
Abstract:
docs.text:
What if every researcher managed a team of 30 AI agents? In this hands-on talk, I will describe a working model of research productivity in which each researcher coordinates 20 planning agents (which explore literature, decompose problems, and draft specifications) and 10 execution agents (which write code, run analyses, build simulations, and prepare figures and manuscripts). The researcher’s job shifts from doing every task to setting direction, supplying domain judgment, and reviewing results.

I will make this concrete with case studies from my own work (interactive simulations and a full arXiv paper produced with AI agents) and a live demonstration of the two practical building blocks students asked about: plain Markdown files that capture a project’s goals and conventions, and reusable agent skills that turn a repeatable research task into a one-line command. We will also discuss how to keep this work responsible and ethical: verifying outputs, citing sources, and keeping the human accountable for the science.

docs.title: Important New Term
docs.text:
Task Completion Time Horizon

The length of task, measured by how long a human expert needs to do it, that an AI agent completes successfully at a stated reliability.

  • 50% time horizon: tasks of this length succeed half the time
  • 80% time horizon: tasks of this length succeed four times out of five
  • It measures the task's length in human time, not how long the agent runs
  • Example (METR, April 2026): Claude Opus 4.6 is about 12 hours at 50% and about 70 minutes at 80%
  • Like Moore's Law, but for agentic capability: the horizon keeps doubling every 4-5 months

docs.title: Using Agent Personas to Divide Tasks
Agent-Agent Communication Strategies
docs.text:
Start simple: have agents communicate through shared files or a structured message format (Markdown), with one orchestrator (also called a nexus agent) coordinating. Add complex protocols only when you outgrow that.

A practical progression:

  1. Orchestrator + subagents - One lead agent delegates tasks and collects results. This is the easiest to debug and covers most use cases.
  2. Shared workspace - Agents read and write files (Markdown or JSON) in a common folder or repo. It leaves an audit trail and needs no special infrastructure.
  3. Structured messages - Agree on a small schema, such as {from, to, task, status, payload}, so agents don't have to parse free-form prose from each other.
  4. Standard protocols as you scale - Use MCP (Model Context Protocol), publish/subscribe messaging, or MQTT (a lightweight messaging protocol for devices) to give agents shared tools and data. Use A2A (agent-to-agent) when agents from different systems or vendors must discover and call each other.

docs.title: Number One Question: Sharing Knowledge
docs.text:
How do you efficiently get all your bots to communicate with one another, and with the agents in your department and at the University of Minnesota?

Recall: The key to artificial intelligence is knowledge representation

docs.title: The Key: Personal Knowledge Graph
docs.text: A central "ground truth" data structure to keep your content aligned with your goals.

docs.title: Enterprise Knowledge and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
docs.text:
1. Giving agents access to only the minimal data they need to do their work is complex
  2. Integrating personal knowledge into a research community is complex
  3. Each person and agent needs one or more precisely assigned roles
  4. Only specific roles may access a given node in the graph
  5. Integrating personal (PKG) and enterprise (EKG) knowledge graphs raises many questions about intellectual property (IP) ownership
  6. See references for details

docs.title: Agent Skills: Teach Your Agent a Repeatable Task
docs.text:
A skill is a reusable package of instructions that lets an agent do one defined task the same way every time.

  • A folder with a SKILL.md file: a name, a one-line description, and step-by-step instructions
  • Optional scripts, reference files, and templates in the same folder
  • The agent keeps only the name and description in context, and loads the rest when a request matches
  • Turns a repeatable research task into a one-line command
  • Example: a skill that extracts Bode-plot features from measurement files
  • Dan's experience: 100x quality improvement in textbook generation
  • A high-quality, searchable skill library can become an organization's competitive advantage

docs.title: Generating a Publication-Quality Paper
docs.text:
• Ask your GenAI tool for best practices:
    • Length of paper
    • Typical outline
    • Number of figures
    • Number of references
  • Provide a template
  • Create a build.sh script that produces main.pdf
  • Create a skill for generating a high-quality paper using the /skill-creator skill

docs.title: How Much Does It Cost per Month?
Security/Ethics/Legal Issues
docs.text:
1. What security risks are introduced by agents?
  2. Who is accountable for an agent's actions?
  3. What is the liability of the person who created the agents versus the LLM vendor?
  4. What are the ethics of agents using your credentials?
  5. Who owns the intellectual property created by agents running "at the edge" (researcher, software developer, or university)?
  6. What are the current policies about disclosing that agents were used to generate the first draft of a paper?
  7. How will increased agent activity strain university resources?
  8. How much additional environmental damage will agents cause?
  9. Will swarms of agents cause unemployment among grad students?
  10. When do we shut down rogue agent swarms?

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
1. Agent power is doubling every 4-5 months (task completion time horizon)
  2. Researchers who use agents can be up to 100x more productive
  3. Many new options for agent software, and more on the way
  4. Designing agents and their roles can be fun (and scary)
  5. Learning to set up your desktop is a required skill (~6 hours of training)
  6. Research agents open up many security, ethics, and legal issues

Thank You!
